rationale: D294 names workQueue and keeps it generic, D290/D264/D266/D279 keep queue lifecycle outside messageBus and reserve ack/cursor for messaging, D184 requires shared DataIssue, D291/D293 provide shared bounded-flow and size-capacity policy vocabulary, and D128/D129 keep WorkItem/process orchestration above this layer. A commands/records/status/issues core mirrors messageBus discipline while using queue-specific lifecycle terms instead of ack/nack. Keeping available/work/deadLetter as projections preserves describe-visible topology, avoids default graph bloat, and prevents pull/read operations from becoming hidden reservation or completion commands.

layer: L6 / executor adapter contract tests and mock adapters / CSP-8 Layer C
question: How should real LLM, tool, human, and provider bindings be tested, replaced, and dry-run without live credentials, provider spend, or hidden adapter behavior?
decision: GraphReFly adds or reserves an executor adapter contract test harness and mock-adapter surface as provider-neutral test infrastructure, not as a production executor runtime. The harness consumes pure data such as AgentRequest, ExecutorProfile, ExecutorRoute, PromptBundle, ToolDefinition, ToolCatalog, credential/config scope refs, policy facts, and fixture transcripts, drives ExecutorBinding and ExecutorBridge boundaries, and asserts graph-visible facts, statuses, issues, audit records, stream events, artifact refs, and terminal ExecutorOutcome. Core contract scenarios cover success, failed, blocked, canceled, timeout, needs_approval, stream deltas before terminal outcome, stale callback after terminal, duplicate terminal rejection, cancel supported and unsupported, abort propagation, reconcile found/not_found/ambiguous/already_completed, missing credentials, permission denied, sandbox denied, schema mismatch, tool unavailable, retry/fallback visibility, backpressure/drop/coalesce evidence, large-output artifact refs, and redaction evidence before display/export/prompt continuation. Core tests must not call live providers or require credentials. Provider helper packages may ship mock adapters, golden lowering/normalization tests, fixture transcripts, and optional live-provider tests, but live tests are explicit user opt-in and outside the core gate. Mock adapters have two first-class roles: a zero-spend dry-run adapter that lets users verify whether the whole graph, routing, continuation, tool-call, approval, artifact, budget, and backpressure flow can run end-to-end; and an executable I/O contract reference that shows replacement-adapter authors the expected request shapes, stream event shapes, status/issue/audit material, tool-call/result envelopes, and terminal outcome shapes. The harness asserts GraphReFly public facts and adapter contracts, not provider SDK private objects, and it must not use monkeypatching, hidden queues, hidden runners, private retries, or direct WorkItem/domain mutation.
rationale: D251 defines ExecutorBinding, D252 defines ExecutorBridge, D253 locks provider lowering/normalization, D254 and D268 require tool-call correlation and continuation lineage, D275 requires cancellation/timeout propagation, D277 requires audit/redaction evidence, D288-D293 define stream/backpressure/size policy, and D271/D273 constrain tool side effects and sandbox scopes. Without a shared contract harness, adapter replaceability would remain aspirational and users would need paid provider calls to know whether a graph can run. Mock adapters make dry-run behavior cheap and inspectable while documenting the exact boundary expected from real OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama, Gemini, OpenRouter, CLI, MCP, browser, and human adapters.

layer: L6 / LLM multi-tool-call scheduling and join policy / CSP-8 Layer C
question: When one LLM response contains multiple tool calls, how should GraphReFly schedule them, observe completion or blockage, and continue the same LLM conversation without hidden recursion inside adapters?
decision: A single LLM response that requests one or more tool calls creates a visible tool-call series for that LLM turn. The series carries stable correlation such as requestId, operationId, turnId, inputId, responseId when available, toolCallSeriesId, toolCallId, callIndex, providerCallId when available, executorId, routeId, profileId, promptBundleId, and sourceRefs. Each tool call is lowered through ToolCatalog, ToolDefinition, ExecutorRoute, permission/sandbox policy, budget policy, and a tool-capable ExecutorBinding into an independent graph-visible execution request; the LLM adapter must not directly invoke tools, mutate WorkItems, or recursively call itself with tool results. Sibling tool calls may be scheduled concurrently only when explicit policy admits it; otherwise they are scheduled serially or by dependency order. Either way, admission, dispatch, waiting, result, blocked, needs_approval, timeout, canceled, failed, retry/fallback, and backpressure facts are visible. The continuation for that LLM turn is triggered only by a visible join projector over the tool-call series, not by a tool binding or LLM adapter private callback. By default, required tool calls must reach terminal tool-result outcomes before continuation; optional calls may be omitted, summarized, degraded, or converted to visible issues only under explicit policy. Join output preserves the provider-visible ordering and identity required for tool-result prompts, normally by callIndex and toolCallId, and records missing, duplicate, stale, unauthorized, blocked, or malformed tool results as DataIssue/status/audit evidence. The joined continuation reuses D268 continuation lineage and prompt-cache affinity: same conversation lineage, same selected LLM route/model/profile unless visible fallback policy changes it, and cache/material hints are carried forward rather than recomputed secretly. A stuck required tool call leaves the series in visible waiting, blocked, timeout, or canceled state; it must not silently disappear, auto-succeed, or let the LLM continue with fabricated results. Multiple rounds of tool calls are represented as subsequent visible LLM turns and tool-call series within the same lineage, with bounded retry/loop policy and budget evidence.
rationale: D242 and D246 define LLM tool-use continuation, D254 defines tool-call correlation, D268 locks continuation lineage and prompt-cache affinity, D243/D248 define ToolCatalog filtering, D271 constrains tool side effects, D275 defines cancellation/timeout, D257 defines budget accounting, D288-D293 define stream/backpressure/size evidence, and D298 makes mock/dry-run adapter behavior contract-testable. Multi-tool-call responses are common in OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, OpenRouter, Ollama-compatible, and local tool-use loops, but letting adapters invoke tools inline would violate F-DISPATCH-ALL, inspectability, no hidden async runner, and WorkItem mutation boundaries. A visible series plus join projector keeps concurrency explicit while preserving provider ordering and continuation cache affinity.

layer: L6 / workQueue derived state, leases, visibility timeout, and retry transitions
question: How should workQueue derive state and accept claim, lease, completion, failure, cancellation, scheduling, visibility timeout, and retry transitions without hidden worker runtime or wall-clock mutation?
decision: workQueue state is derived from the append-only records ledger plus explicit policy and clock/deadline facts, not from a mutable authoritative work map. The common derived states are scheduled, ready, leased, retry-wait, completed, canceled, and dead-lettered. Only ready work is claimable. scheduled and retry-wait work becomes available only when visible clock/deadline inputs make its notBeforeMs or retryAtMs eligible; available() must not read wall-clock time as a hidden side channel. claim on ready work emits work-claimed with workId, leaseId, attempt, workerId, claimedAtMs, leaseExpiresAtMs, and policy refs; each accepted claim starts a new monotonically increasing attempt for that work. renew-lease is accepted only for the current active lease and emits lease-renewed with the new leaseExpiresAtMs; stale, expired, unknown, terminal, or mismatched lease renewal emits DataIssue/status and must not extend ownership. release is accepted only for the current active lease and emits work-released; released work becomes ready unless an explicit schedule/retry policy record places it later. complete is accepted only for the current active lease/attempt and emits attempt-completed plus work-completed; later fail, complete, release, or renew commands for that lease or attempt are stale issues. fail is accepted only for the current active lease/attempt and emits attempt-failed; retry policy then emits retry-scheduled with retryAtMs or work-dead-lettered when retries are exhausted, non-retryable, or policy rejects retry. cancel emits work-canceled for any nonterminal work according to queue policy and invalidates active leases; later worker commands become stale issues. schedule emits work-scheduled for nonterminal work according to policy; scheduling terminal work is rejected. visibility timeout is represented by visible lease-expired records or equivalent status/issue material produced from explicit graph-local clock/deadline inputs; it is not a hidden timer callback and it does not mutate state without a record. After lease expiration, the prior lease can no longer complete/fail/release/renew; the work becomes ready or retry-wait according to policy. Duplicate commandId handling reuses shared dedupe/idempotency policy: duplicates either replay accepted status or emit duplicate-command issues, never produce a second lifecycle record. All transition rejection reasons flow as DataIssue with stable coordinates such as workId, leaseId, attempt, workerId, commandId, currentState, and expectedState. The state machine is queue-generic and must not mention WorkItem, AgentRequest, EffectRun, ExecutorOutcome, provider tool calls, or domain workflow completion.
rationale: D299 defines the command and record vocabulary, D294 keeps workQueue generic, D264/D266/D279 reserve ack/cursor semantics for messageBus, D184 provides DataIssue, D209 requires retry to reuse existing resilience mechanisms, and D291/D293 provide bounded-flow and size-capacity vocabulary. A record-derived state machine gives leases and retries real queue semantics while preserving replay honesty, explainability, and concurrency safety. Making lease expiration depend on visible clock/deadline facts keeps async timers outside the sync core and prevents available() from becoming a hidden scheduler or wall-clock peek.

layer: L6 / agent loop bounds and stop conditions / CSP-8 Layer C
question: How should GraphReFly bound multi-turn LLM/tool continuation loops and decide when to continue, stop, block, or fail without hiding an autonomous agent loop inside adapters?
decision: LLM/tool continuation is represented as a graph-visible loop series, not as a private recursive loop inside an LLM adapter, tool adapter, executor binding, or runner. Each LLM turn, tool-call series, join result, continuation request, approval wait, retry/fallback attempt, and terminal answer remains correlated through stable lineage such as requestId, operationId, conversationId or lineageId, turnId, toolCallSeriesId, promptBundleId, executorId, routeId, profileId, attempt, sourceRefs, and budget refs. Every loop has explicit finite policy bounds; v0 policy may include maxTurns, maxToolRounds, maxToolCalls, maxParallelToolCalls, maxRetries, maxRepeatedPatterns, maxWallTime, maxTokens, maxCost, maxArtifacts, maxOutputSize, maxErrors, maxApprovals, and maxBlockedWaits. Defaults must not imply an infinite autonomous loop. Continue decisions are produced by visible projectors over normalized LLM outcomes, tool-call series state, joined tool results, approval state, budget/usage evidence, route availability, and policy facts. Stop conditions include terminal LLM answer, required human approval, user cancellation, required tool blocked/timeout/canceled/failed without admitted fallback, permission or sandbox denial, route/provider unavailable, schema invalid, malformed or unsupported tool call, budget exhausted, repeated identical or no-progress tool-call pattern, max loop bound reached, too many errors, and explicit policy stop. Each stop emits visible status, DataIssue where applicable, audit/evidence, and an ExecutorOutcome or higher-level agent outcome; it must not silently stop, fabricate successful tool results, or mutate WorkItems directly. no-progress detection is advisory policy over visible facts, not semantic judgment by a hidden agent; users may replace or tune the detector. Dry-run/mock adapters from D298 must exercise the same loop bounds and stop conditions so users can validate a graph without provider spend. Resuming after a blocked/approval/waiting state requires new visible input facts and preserves lineage; it is not a private continuation callback.
rationale: D242, D246, and D297 define LLM tool-use continuation and multi-tool-call joins; D268 requires continuation lineage and prompt-cache affinity; D257 defines budget policy and usage accounting; D275 defines cancellation and timeout propagation; D271 and D273 constrain tool side effects and sandbox scopes; D277 requires audit/redaction evidence; D288-D293 define stream/backpressure/size evidence; and D298 requires mock/dry-run contract coverage. Without explicit loop bounds, a valid-looking tool-use design could become an uninspectable autonomous agent runner. Finite visible loop policy preserves user control, dry-run testability, cache affinity, and no-autonomous-decisions while still supporting multi-round tool-use workflows.

layer: L6 / user-replaceable AgentDecision boundary / CSP-8 Layer C
question: Where should the decision about continuing an LLM, requesting tools, waiting, asking a human, spawning or updating work, or stopping an agent loop live, and how can users replace that decision logic without granting adapters hidden mutation authority?
decision: AgentDecision is a graph-visible, user-replaceable policy/projector surface over normalized execution facts, not a hidden loop inside an LLM adapter, ExecutorBridge, tool binding, human adapter, or WorkItem runtime. An AgentDecision projector consumes visible inputs such as ExecutorOutcome, normalized LLM output, tool-call series and join state, PromptBundle material, WorkItem and EffectRun state, AgentRequest status, budget and usage evidence, approval facts, route/profile availability, permission/sandbox status, DataIssue/status/audit facts, user policy, and loop bounds. It emits only visible decision/proposal/command facts such as continue-llm, request-tools, wait-tools, request-human-approval, propose-domain-action, propose-work-spawn, stop-success, stop-blocked, stop-failed, retry, fallback, or require-review. It must not call providers, execute tools, wait on promises, mutate WorkItems, apply domain actions, append WorkItemEvents, dispatch ExecutorBindings, authorize itself, or hide retries/continuations. WorkItem close, resolve, approve, verify, patch, spawn, re-lane, and similar mutations remain proposals/admissions until D239 domain action application emits WorkItemEvent facts. The default AgentDecision may be a reference projector or bundle, but users can replace it with their own node or graph as long as it preserves the public input/output contract, stable sourceDecisionId/correlation refs, visible issue/status/audit behavior, finite loop policy from D300, and executor/tool continuation contracts from D297. Replacement decision logic may be deterministic rules, policy tables, small local functions, or LLM-assisted only by issuing new visible AgentRequest facts; it may not perform private async execution. D298 mock adapters and contract harnesses must include AgentDecision replacement fixtures so users can dry-run the whole graph and see expected inputs and outputs before connecting paid or side-effecting adapters.
rationale: D242 already routes LLM tool calls through explicit AgentDecision and AgentRequest proposals, D246 materializes tool results as prompt material by policy, D268 preserves continuation lineage and cache affinity, D297 makes multi-tool-call joins visible, D300 bounds continuation loops, D239 separates domain action application from proposals, D251/D252 keep bindings and ExecutorBridge from creating decisions or mutating WorkItems, and D298 makes adapter replacement dry-runnable. A replaceable AgentDecision surface is the narrow point where user policy belongs: it can decide what the agent should try next while preserving graph-visible causality, no hidden async runner, no autonomous domain mutation, and no provider/tool adapter lock-in.

layer: L6 / AgentDecision intent envelope vocabulary / CSP-8 Layer C
question: What minimal intent/proposal envelope should user-replaceable AgentDecision projectors emit so continue-LLM, tool requests, human waits, WorkItem actions, retries, fallbacks, and stops stay composable without each decision implementation inventing a private command format?
decision: AgentDecision output uses a small provider-neutral intent envelope vocabulary, not adapter-specific commands or direct domain mutations. Each emitted intent carries stable coordinates such as decisionId or sourceDecisionId, intentId when the intent is an independently tracked proposal subject, intentKind, targetKind, required or optional policy, correlation refs such as requestId, operationId, effectRunId, parentRequestId, turnId, toolCallSeriesId, toolCallId, inputId, promptBundleId, workItemId, routeId, profileId, executorId, attempt, sourceRefs, policyRefs, budgetRefs, reason, confidence or priority when policy needs it, issueRefs, auditRefs, and an intent payload. v0 intentKind values are open at the application layer but the default Layer C vocabulary includes continue-llm, request-tool, request-tools, wait-tools, request-human-approval, propose-domain-action, propose-work-spawn, retry, fallback, require-review, stop-success, stop-blocked, stop-failed, and no-op. targetKind describes the lowering destination, such as llm-request, tool-request, human-request, workitem-action, workitem-spawn, executor-route, effect-run, agent-loop, or custom. Intent payloads are narrow and typed by targetKind; they may reference PromptBundle material, ToolDefinition ids and args envelopes, approval needs, WorkItem action proposal material, retry/fallback policy refs, or stop/status material. AgentDecision intents are proposals: they do not execute tools, call providers, mutate WorkItems, apply actions, authorize themselves, or dispatch ExecutorBindings. Dedicated lowerers/projectors consume intents and emit the corresponding existing facts, such as AgentRequest proposals, tool-call request proposals, human approval requests, WorkItem domain action proposals/admissions, retry/fallback request proposals, status/outcome facts, DataIssue, and audit. Unknown intentKind, unsupported targetKind, missing required refs, malformed payload, unauthorized target, duplicate intentId, stale sourceDecisionId, or policy mismatch emits visible issue/status/audit rather than executing a best-effort command. Users may replace AgentDecision implementations as long as they emit this envelope and keep the same visible lowerer contracts. D298 mock adapters and contract harnesses should include fixture examples for each default intent kind so replacement authors can see expected input and output shapes.
rationale: D302 establishes AgentDecision as the user-replaceable policy/projector boundary, but without a shared envelope every replacement would invent its own private command dialect. D242 routes LLM tool use through AgentDecision and AgentRequest proposals, D246/D297 define tool-result continuation and joins, D300 bounds agent loops, D239 keeps WorkItem mutation behind domain action application, D251/D252 prevent bindings and ExecutorBridge from creating decisions or mutating domain state, and D298 requires dry-run contract visibility. A small intent envelope keeps decision logic replaceable and inspectable while preserving narrow lowering boundaries and avoiding a new hidden runtime or command bus.

layer: L6 / AgentDecision intent lowerers and conflict policy / CSP-8 Layer C
question: How should AgentDecision intent envelopes be lowered into AgentRequest proposals, human approval requests, WorkItem action proposals, retry/fallback requests, statuses, and outcomes, and how should multiple simultaneous or conflicting intents be handled without hidden imperative choice?
decision: AgentDecision intent lowering is performed by explicit graph-visible lowerer/projector nodes, not by AgentDecision itself, LLM adapters, ExecutorBridge, tool bindings, or WorkItem runtimes. Lowerers consume D303 intent envelopes plus the relevant current facts and policies, route by intentKind and targetKind, preserve sourceDecisionId, intentId, sourceRefs, correlation refs, policyRefs, issueRefs, and auditRefs, and emit the corresponding existing proposal/status/outcome facts. continue-llm lowers to an LLM AgentRequest proposal or PromptBundle continuation proposal; request-tool and request-tools lower to tool-call AgentRequest proposals; request-human-approval lowers to human-task/approval request facts; propose-domain-action and propose-work-spawn lower only to WorkItem action proposal or spawn proposal facts; retry and fallback lower to visible retry/fallback request proposals or statuses; stop-success, stop-blocked, and stop-failed lower to agent/effect/run status or outcome facts; no-op lowers only to optional audit/status evidence. Lowerers must not execute tools, call providers, dispatch bindings, mutate WorkItems, apply domain actions, authorize themselves, wait on promises, or create hidden queues. Multiple intents from the same sourceDecisionId are evaluated under explicit ordering and conflict policy. v0 default ordering treats stop/review/block intents, required waits, human approval, retries/fallbacks, request intents, and domain-action proposals as policy-comparable classes, but the lowerer must emit visible issue/status/audit when policy cannot prove compatibility. Conflicts include stop plus request, multiple terminal stop intents, duplicate intentId, duplicate request for the same toolCallId/inputId, required and optional disagreement for the same target, retry and fallback both targeting the same failed attempt without policy precedence, domain action proposal plus failed/blocked stop without review policy, stale sourceDecisionId, missing parent request, unauthorized targetKind, malformed payload, or unsupported intentKind. Conflict handling must be deterministic and graph-visible: emit a DataIssue/status and either block, require-review, or lower only the policy-admitted subset with audit evidence. Lowerers may be split by targetKind for modularity, but they share the envelope contract and conflict semantics so users can replace AgentDecision without replacing every downstream bridge. D298 mock/dry-run fixtures must include multi-intent and conflict cases.
rationale: D302 makes AgentDecision user-replaceable, and D303 defines a common intent envelope, but a shared lowering boundary is needed so replacement decisions do not smuggle execution into custom code or invent private command buses. D242, D246, and D297 require LLM/tool continuation to pass through visible request and join facts; D239 reserves WorkItem mutation for domain action application; D251/D252 keep binding dispatch inside ExecutorBridge after admission/routing; D300 bounds loops and stop conditions; and D298 requires dry-run contract coverage. Explicit lowerers preserve composability, deterministic conflict reporting, and sourceDecisionId traceability while keeping decision, lowering, execution, and domain mutation as separate replaceable surfaces.

layer: L6 / AgentDecision replay stability and idempotency / CSP-8 Layer C
question: How should AgentDecision and intent lowering behave under graph replay, restart, duplicate inputs, mock dry-run, adapter reconcile, and repeated subscriptions without issuing duplicate tool calls, LLM continuations, human requests, or WorkItem action proposals?
decision: AgentDecision and AgentDecision intent lowering must be replay-stable and idempotent over graph-visible inputs. A decision projector derives or emits stable sourceDecisionId values from durable input coordinates such as effectRunId, requestId, parentRequestId, outcomeId, promptBundleId, toolCallSeriesId, workItemId, policyRefs, and sourceRefs; it must not use wall-clock time, random ids, subscription order, object identity, provider SDK handles, or private adapter state to decide whether an intent is new. Intent envelopes carry stable intentId when the intent becomes an independently tracked proposal subject, or a deterministic idempotencyKey when the lowered target owns the durable id. Lowerers use sourceDecisionId, intentId, idempotencyKey, targetKind, inputId/toolCallId/workItemId/requestId, and sourceRefs to decide whether duplicate inputs replay the same proposal/status/outcome, are ignored as already-lowered with audit evidence, or emit duplicate/stale DataIssue. Replaying the same normalized LLM outcome must not issue another tool request, LLM continuation, human approval request, retry/fallback proposal, or WorkItem action/spawn proposal unless a new visible decision input or explicit retry/fallback/override policy changes the idempotency key. Mock dry-runs use the same deterministic ids and idempotency rules as live adapters so dry-run traces predict live graph shape without provider spend. Adapter reconcile may attach external operation refs to existing requests/outcomes, but it must not cause AgentDecision to generate a second intent for the same source decision. Derived views such as Canvas timelines, WorkspaceGraph projections, tool-call joins, and loop summaries may compute local view ids, but those ids do not grant replay authority or side-effect identity. Unknown, conflicting, missing, or unstable ids emit visible issue/status/audit facts and block or require review according to policy rather than best-effort duplicate execution.
rationale: D302 makes AgentDecision replaceable, D303 defines intent envelopes, D304 defines lowerers and conflict handling, D297 and D300 allow multi-round tool/LLM loops, D239 keeps WorkItem mutation behind action application, D251/D252 keep bindings and ExecutorBridge from creating decisions, D274 already requires executor idempotency and external operation reconcile, and D298 requires dry-run contract coverage. Without replay-stable decision and intent ids, restoring or re-subscribing the graph could duplicate paid calls or side effects while still appearing graph-visible. Deterministic idempotency keeps the model compatible with replay, mock adapters, external reconcile, and user-replaceable decision logic.

layer: L6 / AgentDecision dry-run trace and explainability / CSP-8 Layer C
question: How should users, Canvas, WorkspaceGraph, and adapter authors understand why an AgentDecision emitted particular intents, lowerers accepted or rejected them, and dry-run traces differ from live execution without leaking secrets or creating a second telemetry runtime?
decision: AgentDecision, intent lowerers, and dry-run/mock execution emit graph-visible explainability evidence as secret-free trace envelopes correlated to existing decision, intent, request, outcome, policy, and source refs. This evidence is not a new TraceStore, AuditLog, durable trace id family, Canvas-private debugger, or execution authority. Trace envelopes may include eventKind, phase, sourceDecisionId, intentId, targetKind, requestId, operationId, effectRunId, workItemId, toolCallSeriesId, promptBundleId, routeId, profileId, executorId, policyRefs, budgetRefs, approvalRefs, permission/sandbox refs, sourceRefs, consideredInputRefs, selectedIntentRefs, rejectedAlternativeRefs, matchedPolicyRefs, reason codes, stopReason, confidence or priority when policy uses it, dryRun flag, mockFixtureRef, expectedInputShapeRef, expectedOutputShapeRef, issues, auditRefs, artifact refs, redaction/sensitivity metadata, and optional summaries. Trace evidence explains decisions and lowerer behavior such as selected continuation, waiting on tools, requesting approval, blocking on budget, permission denial, retry/fallback selection, stop condition, malformed intent, duplicate idempotency key, or rejected alternative. It must not inline raw prompts, credentials, headers, provider request/response bodies, tool stdout/stderr above policy limits, filesystem contents, browser DOM snapshots, human private input, SDK objects, or raw artifacts except through D270 artifact envelopes and D277 redaction policy. Trace evidence must not authorize dispatch, execute tools, continue prompts, retry, fallback, mutate WorkItems, apply domain actions, or override conflicts; those remain separate visible policy/request/outcome flows. Dry-run/mock adapters from D298 use the same trace envelope as live flows and mark dryRun/mock material explicitly so users can compare expected graph shape, adapter input/output contracts, loop bounds, conflicts, and stop reasons without provider spend. Canvas, WorkspaceGraph, dashboards, and test harnesses may render or filter trace evidence, but the source of truth remains the graph facts and envelopes, not UI-local explanations. Missing, unsupported, redacted, summarized, or external-only trace material emits visible issue/status/audit rather than pretending full explanation is available.
rationale: D302 makes AgentDecision user-replaceable, D303 defines intent envelopes, D304 defines lowerers and conflict policy, D305 requires replay-stable idempotency, D298 requires dry-run and mock-adapter contract visibility, D270 defines artifact refs, D277 defines audit/redaction evidence, D257 records budget evidence, D239 preserves WorkItem mutation boundaries, and R-describe/D39 make graph inspection first-class. Without an explainability envelope, users could replace AgentDecision but still be unable to see why it chose a tool call, stop, retry, approval, or domain proposal. Keeping trace as secret-free evidence rather than a telemetry runtime preserves inspectability, dry-run usefulness, redaction safety, and separation between explanation and execution.

layer: L6 / workQueue admission boundary / messageBus substrate
question: How should workQueue admission consume messageBus messages, emit durable admission outcomes, and advance the messageBus subscription cursor without turning ack into work completion or hiding poison-message handling?
decision: workQueue admission is messageBus-backed, not a direct payload-to-record shortcut. A workQueue instance consumes a bound messageBus topic/subscription; each consumed retained message sequence must produce exactly one durable workQueue-visible admission outcome before the messageBus subscription cursor may advance. Accepted payloads emit a work-admitted record with stable messageBus coordinates such as topic, seq, subscriptionId, commandId/correlation refs when available, workId, payload refs, policy refs, and admission timestamp/evidence. Deterministic non-admission emits a work-rejected or admission-rejected record plus DataIssue/status material with stable coordinates and rejection reasons such as malformed payload, schema invalid, payload too large/ref-only required, policy rejected, duplicate rejected, unknown queue binding, closed queue, or unsupported work kind; after that durable rejection outcome exists, ack is allowed because replay can explain why the message did not become claimable work. Transient or retryable ingestion failures, including policy/runtime exceptions, unavailable required clock/policy input, reducer fault, or inability to emit the durable admission outcome, must not ack; they leave the subscription cursor unchanged and emit retryable DataIssue/status/audit so the message can be retried or explicitly recovered. messageBus ack for the workQueue ingestion subscription means only that the message has a durable workQueue-visible admission outcome, not that the work has completed, failed, been canceled, or reached a terminal queue state. claim, lease, renew, release, complete, fail, retry, cancel, and dead-letter lifecycle semantics remain over workQueue records after admission. available(), work(workId), and deadLetter() projections are read/pull surfaces and must not admit, reject, ack, seek, claim, or complete work. Convenience submit helpers may publish to the bound messageBus topic and return correlation material, but they do not directly append workQueue records or advance cursors.
rationale: D299 says submit enters through a bound messageBus topic/subscription path and that messageBus ack means durable ingestion into workQueue records, while D264/D266/D279 reserve ack/cursor semantics for messaging and keep job lifecycle out of messageBus. Without an explicit admission outcome boundary, poison messages would either permanently wedge the subscription cursor or be silently acked with no replay-visible explanation. Requiring work-admitted or work-rejected/admission-rejected before ack preserves replay honesty, keeps messageBus as retained log plus independent cursor substrate, keeps workQueue lifecycle in its own records ledger, and separates deterministic rejection from transient ingestion failure. The shape also reuses DataIssue, bounded-flow, size-capacity, dedupe, retry, and policy evidence from D184/D291/D293 while avoiding a hidden adapter-owned admission runtime.

layer: L6 / AgentDecision fixture corpus and executable examples / CSP-8 Layer C testing
question: What canonical fixture corpus should demonstrate and test replacement AgentDecision, intent lowerers, mock adapters, dry-run traces, tool-call joins, and stop conditions without requiring provider credentials or turning examples into a hidden runtime or benchmark?
decision: GraphReFly adds or reserves a canonical AgentDecision fixture corpus as testing and documentation infrastructure, not as a production runtime, provider benchmark, evaluation suite, or normative model quality test. Fixtures are secret-free, provider-neutral graph fact bundles plus expected graph-visible outputs: normalized executor outcomes, AgentDecision inputs, emitted D303 intent envelopes, D304 lowerer outputs, D305 idempotency behavior, D306 trace evidence, D298 mock-adapter I/O, optional describe/profile/observe snapshots, and expected issues/status/audit/outcomes. The required v0 corpus covers at least: simple terminal LLM answer; single tool call and continuation; multiple tool calls with deterministic ordering and join; optional tool omitted under policy; required tool blocked; approval required; permission or sandbox denied; budget stop; retry then success; fallback route selected; malformed tool call; unsupported tool; conflict intents; duplicate replay/idempotency; stale lowerer input; domain action proposal without mutation; WorkItem spawn proposal without direct create; artifact/ref output including JSON/file/large text summaries; redaction/sensitivity handling; cancellation/timeout; no-progress or repeated-pattern stop; and full dry-run end-to-end graph shape. Fixtures must use stable ids, deterministic clocks or recorded clock facts, deterministic ordering, explicit policy refs, explicit sourceRefs, and redacted or synthetic payloads. They must not call live LLMs, tools, MCP servers, CLIs, browsers, provider SDKs, networks, filesystems, or human inboxes unless a separate opt-in live integration harness wraps them. Expected provider request bodies, raw prompts, credentials, headers, private SDK objects, and raw large artifacts are not canonical fixture truth; if examples need them, they appear only as redacted summaries, artifact refs, or provider-helper-specific golden lowering tests outside the core corpus. Users replacing AgentDecision or adapters can run the corpus to validate expected input/output envelopes and dry-run graph behavior. The corpus may be implemented as JSON/JSONL fixtures, typed builders, snapshot tests, or docs examples, but the authoritative assertions are graph-visible facts and envelopes, not UI screenshots or provider transcripts.
rationale: D298 requires mock adapters and contract tests to show expected replacement-adapter I/O and zero-spend dry runs; D302-D306 define the replaceable AgentDecision boundary, intent envelope, lowerers, idempotency, and explainability trace; D297 and D300 define multi-tool joins and loop bounds; D239 prevents domain proposals from becoming direct WorkItem mutation; D270 and D277 require artifact/ref and redaction discipline. Without a shared fixture corpus, these contracts would be hard to learn and replacements would drift while still passing ad hoc tests. A provider-neutral executable corpus makes dry-run behavior concrete, gives users examples to copy, and keeps tests focused on GraphReFly facts rather than provider SDKs, UI demos, or paid live calls.

layer: L6 / AgentDecision package and export surface / CSP-8 Layer C / CSP-9
question: How should AgentDecision contracts, intent envelopes, lowerers, traces, fixtures, mock adapters, provider golden tests, WorkItem-specific mappings, and Canvas renderers be packaged in @graphrefly/ts without bloating root exports or mixing provider-neutral facts with runtime-private adapters and UI surfaces?
decision: AgentDecision v0 uses focused static package subpaths that preserve D125 and D283 dependency direction. Provider-neutral AgentDecision facts, types, intent envelopes, trace evidence types, replaceable projector contracts, idempotency helpers, policy helper types, and generic lowerer contracts live under a focused executor/agent-decision surface such as @graphrefly/ts/executors/agent-decision, or an equivalent static child of the executor application-infrastructure subpath. They are not root exports by default and must not import provider SDKs, framework bindings, Canvas/UI code, WorkspaceGraph product code, filesystem/network implementations, or runtime-private binding clients. Generic lowerer helpers that only translate AgentDecision intents into provider-neutral AgentRequest/status/outcome/audit/DataIssue facts may live with that surface. WorkItem-specific lowerers, action-proposal mappers, and WorkspaceGraph integrations live under orchestration or solution subpaths that consume AgentDecision contracts; they must not be required by the neutral executor agent-decision surface. D298 mock adapters, D308 fixture corpus, dry-run harnesses, and contract assertions live under testing-focused subpaths such as @graphrefly/ts/testing/executors or @graphrefly/ts/testing/agent-decision, with optional re-export from provider-helper test entrypoints when useful. These testing surfaces may depend on the neutral executor contracts and fixture data, but production executor contracts must not depend on testing. Concrete OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Ollama, OpenRouter, MCP, CLI, browser, HTTP, human inbox, or custom provider helpers keep provider SDKs and golden lowering/normalization tests in their focused adapter/helper subpaths; they may consume AgentDecision fixture shapes but must not make provider request bodies canonical AgentDecision facts. Canvas, WorkspaceGraph UI, dashboards, and framework renderers may consume trace/fixture facts and render explainability, but UI renderers live under solutions, framework adapters, or app packages, not in the neutral AgentDecision contract surface. Package exports are static, tree-shakeable, and explicit; v0 has no dynamic plugin discovery, auto-installed providers, root-level curated adapter registry, ambient credential lookup, or monolithic agent module that combines decision, lowerer, bridge, provider bindings, fixtures, and UI rendering. Experimental internals may remain unexported until their contracts are locked; once exported, they must keep provider-neutral facts separate from runtime-private configuration and side-effecting adapters.
rationale: D125 defines capability/application subpaths and dependency direction, D249 keeps provider helpers separate from provider-neutral facts, D283 defines the focused executor package surface, D298 and D308 define mock/fixture testing infrastructure, D302-D306 define AgentDecision contracts, lowerers, idempotency, and trace evidence, D239 keeps WorkItem mutation in orchestration/domain application, D240 keeps Canvas and WorkspaceGraph as consumers, and D238 keeps UI/framework boundaries focused. Without an explicit export split, implementation pressure would naturally collapse AgentDecision, mock adapters, provider SDK helpers, WorkItem mappers, and Canvas explainability into a single convenient module. Static focused subpaths keep the replaceable contract small, prevent optional dependencies from leaking into core imports, and make user replacement, testing, and provider integration possible without root bloat or hidden runtime ownership.

layer: L6 / workQueue messageBus binding and submit shape
question: How should workQueue declare its messageBus binding, queue identity, submit helper, and admission policy inputs without owning topic lifecycle or bypassing the retained log/subscription cursor substrate?
decision: workQueue v0 requires an explicit messageBus binding rather than owning a hidden queue runtime or auto-creating topics. The public construction shape includes a stable queueId, a bus reference, and a binding with topic, stable subscriptionId, and optional from coordinate such as earliest, latest, or an explicit sequence. queueId identifies the queue and may be used by helpers to derive deterministic default topic or subscription names, but any derived names must be stable, describe-visible, and user-overridable; they must not depend on random ids, runtime process identity, subscription order, wall-clock time, or hidden registries. Topic lifecycle remains messageBus-owned: creating, closing, rejecting, allowing, or dead-lettering unknown topics is handled through messageBus ensure-topic, close-topic, topicPolicy, catalog, status, and DataIssue facts. workQueue construction must not silently ensure a topic, mutate the bus catalog, seek a subscription, or repair unknown/closed topic issues. submit convenience helpers publish MessageBusCommand facts to the bound topic and may return command/correlation material, but they do not append workQueue records, admit work, claim work, or advance cursors directly. Admission consumes the bound subscription.available projection, applies queue admission policy, size-capacity, dedupe/idempotency, bounded-flow, retry, and other shared policy inputs as graph-visible facts or static policy configuration, then emits work-admitted or work-rejected/admission-rejected records according to D307. The admission policy boundary decides only admission outcome and work metadata such as workId, priority, notBeforeMs, payload refs, tags, and policy refs; it must not claim, lease, complete, fail, cancel, retry terminal work, dispatch workers, or mutate orchestration WorkItems. Test-only direct message or record injection may exist in fixtures or contract harnesses, but the public queue substrate path is messageBus-backed explicit binding.
rationale: D294 names workQueue as the generic application-infrastructure queue above messageBus, D299 says submit enters through a bound messageBus topic/subscription path, D301 keeps lifecycle transitions over workQueue records and visible policy/clock facts, and D307 requires a durable admission outcome before messageBus ack. The remaining API gap is the binding and submit shape. Explicit bus binding keeps dependency direction visible, makes subscription cursor identity durable, and preserves describe truth. Keeping topic lifecycle in messageBus prevents workQueue from becoming a second topic catalog or hidden auto-provisioning runtime. Restricting submit to publish sugar preserves the retained-log foundation, while limiting admission policy to accepted/rejected outcomes prevents admission from smuggling claim/lease/worker assignment or orchestration behavior into the queue boundary.

layer: L6 / workQueue work identity, dedupe, and idempotency
question: How should workQueue derive workId values, recognize duplicate submissions or duplicate admitted messages, and report idempotent or duplicate outcomes without relying on payload equality or messageBus command dedupe?
decision: workQueue v0 separates message identity, work identity, and dedupe identity. The source message coordinate is queueId plus messageBus topic and per-topic seq; it explains where an admission attempt came from but is not itself the business work identity unless policy chooses that default. The default work identity is replay-stable and derived from queueId, topic, and seq, so every retained message admits at most one distinct work item without needing payload equality. submit or admission payloads may carry an explicit workId, idempotencyKey, or domain work key, but those keys participate in duplicate recognition only when an explicit WorkQueueDedupePolicy admits them. Payload equality, object identity, wall-clock time, random ids, subscription order, and process-local counters must not be used as dedupe bases. Once a work-admitted record establishes a workId, that workId is immutable for the lifetime of that work. messageBus commandId dedupe remains publish-command dedupe only; it may replay or reject duplicate publish commands before a new message seq exists, but it does not replace workQueue dedupe for distinct retained messages that share an idempotency key or provided workId. Duplicate admission must never append a second work-admitted record for the same accepted work identity. The queue dedupe policy chooses whether duplicates produce idempotent replay status, such as admission-deduped with existingWorkId and original admission refs, or deterministic non-admission, such as work-rejected/admission-rejected plus DataIssue(code:'duplicate-work') and existingWorkId. Both outcomes are durable workQueue-visible admission outcomes and therefore allow the ingestion ack required by D307. Duplicate windows, retention, and eviction of dedupe memory reuse shared policy vocabulary where available; if a dedupe entry has been evicted, the queue must either treat the later message as new under the documented policy or emit a visible issue/status explaining that duplicate recognition is no longer guaranteed. Duplicate complete, fail, claim, renew, release, cancel, and schedule commands are governed separately by the lifecycle commandId/lease/attempt rules from D301; admission dedupe does not authorize lifecycle mutation.
rationale: D299 identifies workId as the durable queue identity and says duplicate or stale commands emit DataIssue/status, D301 requires duplicate commandId handling to reuse shared dedupe/idempotency policy, D307 requires every consumed message to have a durable admission outcome before ack, and D310 makes submit a messageBus publish helper rather than a direct record append. The remaining ambiguity is whether workId comes from message seq, caller input, commandId, payload equality, or a business idempotency key. Defaulting to queueId/topic/seq gives replay-honest behavior with no hidden hash or payload comparison, while explicit idempotencyKey/provided-workId policy supports real submit retries and business duplicate suppression. Separating messageBus commandId dedupe from workQueue admission dedupe preserves the retained log/cursor boundary and avoids silently dropping distinct messages. Requiring duplicate outcomes to be durable facts prevents poison-message wedges and keeps duplicate handling inspectable.

layer: L6 / workQueue available projection and claim ordering
question: How should workQueue expose available work, accept claims, and resolve concurrent or stale worker attempts without making reads reserve work or hiding ordering and fairness policy?
decision: workQueue available() is a read-only candidate projection, not a reservation operation. It derives possibly stale claim candidates from workQueue records plus explicit policy and clock/deadline facts; it must not emit lifecycle records, reserve work, mutate derived state, ack messageBus cursors, seek subscriptions, or assign workers. Reservation is created only by accepted claim commands that emit work-claimed records. A claim may target explicit workId values observed from available() or request next/batch candidates under explicit claim policy using fields such as workerId, commandId, limit, requestedWorkIds, and policy refs. The claim projector evaluates current derived state at claim time, not the stale available page, and only ready work may be claimed. Accepted claims emit work-claimed with workId, leaseId, attempt, workerId, claimedAtMs, leaseExpiresAtMs, and policy refs, starting the lease/attempt semantics defined by D301. Concurrent or stale claims for the same work are resolved by graph wave and record order in the single-thread graph concurrency domain; later losing claims emit DataIssue/status such as not-ready, already-leased, stale-candidate, unknown-work, terminal-work, batch-partial, or policy-rejected rather than mutating hidden state. Ordering and fairness are graph-visible claim policy, not a hidden scheduler, worker assignment runtime, or pull-to-reserve side effect. v0 default ordering is FIFO by stable admission order; priority, deadline, notBeforeMs, retryAtMs, worker affinity, queue partitions, or custom ordering participate only when represented by explicit records/policy facts. claim batching is bounded by explicit limit/maxBatch policy, and partial success must be visible through accepted work-claimed records plus issues/status for rejected candidates. availablePullId params may page/filter/sort candidates for reading, but must not reserve, claim, complete, fail, cancel, seek, ack, or mutate queue state.
rationale: D299 makes available(), work(workId), and deadLetter() on-demand projections and says claim is the only operation that reserves work. D301 states that only ready work is claimable and that claim creates a new attempt and lease through work-claimed records. D307-D311 make admission and identity replay-honest, but worker competition still needs a clear read-versus-reservation boundary. Treating available() as read-only preserves pullable projection semantics and prevents PULL/read operations from becoming hidden mutations. Letting claim evaluate current state at command time explains stale pages and concurrent worker races without distributed locks. Making ordering and fairness explicit policy keeps workQueue inspectable, reusable, and independent of orchestration or hidden worker assignment runtimes.

layer: L6 / workQueue replaceable claim policy and capacity fit
question: How should workQueue model claim-time capacity, token-like work sizes, worker capability matching, and custom worker/work predicates without hardcoding a token-bucket scheduler or enumerating every matching combination?
decision: workQueue claim selection is governed by a replaceable graph-visible claim policy/projector over ready work candidates, worker facts, active leases, capacity and size evidence, queue policy, and graph-local clock/deadline facts. Core workQueue may define generic metadata vocabulary for work such as priority, tags, requirements, cost or size usage evidence, notBeforeMs, deadlineMs, policy refs, and source refs, and generic worker facts such as workerId, capabilities, current usage, active leases, capacity policy, availability, and policy refs. These fields are evidence for claim policy; they do not form an exhaustive built-in matching matrix. The core must not hardcode combinations such as priority greater than a threshold, tenant affinity, model/provider routing, GPU memory fit, token budgets, role ownership, or domain-specific worker eligibility. Users may replace or supply claim policy projectors that filter, rank, reject, batch, or partition candidates using those facts and any domain metadata, as long as outputs remain visible accepted candidates, rejected candidates, policy refs, reason codes, DataIssue/status/audit, and the final reservation still occurs only through work-claimed records. Capacity-aware and rate-limited claim recipes may reuse D291 bounded-flow/rate-limit vocabulary and D293 size-capacity vocabulary, including token-like units such as tokens, bytes, items, events, lines, or custom units. Token bucket is allowed as one reusable recipe or helper when explicitly selected, but it is not the core workQueue claim model and must not become a hidden scheduler. If capacity information is missing, estimated, stale, unsupported, exceeded, or unmeasurable, claim policy emits visible issues/status and either rejects, degrades, or requires review according to policy rather than silently treating capacity as unlimited or zero. claim limit/maxBatch remains a count bound unless an explicit capacity policy adds weighted admission. Partial batch success must emit accepted work-claimed records plus visible rejected-candidate issues/status for capacity or predicate failures. Worker capacity accounting is derived from workQueue records, active lease facts, explicit worker/capacity facts, and policy evidence; it is not a private mutable worker registry.
rationale: D312 makes available() read-only and claim the only reservation operation, with ordering and fairness controlled by explicit claim policy. The user pointed out that token bucket and worker capacity fit are useful but cannot cover the full matching space: some work may be token-heavy, some workers may accept only certain priorities or capabilities, and domain combinations are open-ended. D291 already reserves shared bounded-flow/rate-limit policy and D293 reserves shared size-capacity vocabulary, while the current TS rateLimitBundle is a fixed-window helper rather than a generic token bucket. Therefore workQueue should reuse shared policy/evidence vocabulary and allow token-bucket-style recipes, but keep core claim policy replaceable and graph-visible. This preserves inspectability, avoids hidden worker assignment runtimes, and prevents workQueue from freezing domain-specific scheduling semantics.

layer: L6 / workQueue lease expiration materialization
question: How should workQueue materialize lease expiration from graph-local clock/deadline facts without hidden timers, read-side mutation, or projection-only ownership changes?
decision: workQueue lease expiration is represented by a first-class visible lease-expired record for the affected workId, leaseId, attempt, and workerId. Expiration is evaluated only from explicit graph-local clock/deadline facts such as nowMs, clockRef, leaseExpiresAtMs, and policy refs; it must not read wall-clock time or run a hidden timer callback. available(), work(workId), deadLetter(), snapshot, and other pull/read projections may expose expired-eligible candidates and expiration evidence, but they must not append lease-expired records, mutate queue state, claim work, or reject worker commands. lease-expired records are materialized only by mutation-bearing inputs such as an explicit expire-leases maintenance command, a claim command that needs to reclaim expired work, or a stale lifecycle command touching an already-expired lease. Materialization is idempotent: a given active lease/attempt can produce at most one lease-expired record, and duplicate expiration commands replay existing status or emit duplicate/stale issues rather than appending a second record. Once lease-expired exists or the current command materializes it, the old lease can no longer complete, fail, renew, or release; those commands emit DataIssue/status with stable coordinates. After expiration, policy determines whether the work becomes ready immediately, emits retry-scheduled, or emits work-dead-lettered, all through visible records/status. Claim over expired work must materialize the prior lease expiration before emitting the new work-claimed record in the same accepted transition batch. No private worker registry, background sweeper, or projection-only ownership mutation may be the source of truth.
rationale: D301 requires workQueue state to derive from records plus explicit policy and clock/deadline facts, and forbids hidden timer callbacks or wall-clock mutation. D312 makes available() read-only, and D313 keeps worker/capacity accounting graph-visible rather than private. Leaving expiration as projection-only would make worker ownership changes harder to audit, while a hidden timer or sweeper would violate the sync-core and inspectability floor. A first-class lease-expired record preserves replay honesty, lets claims and stale worker commands explain exactly why ownership changed, and still allows read projections to show expired-eligible candidates without mutating state.

layer: L6 / workQueue retry and dead-letter disposition
question: How should workQueue turn failed attempts into retry-scheduled or dead-lettered work without letting workers decide terminal state or inventing a queue-specific retry engine?
decision: workQueue treats fail as an attempt outcome, not as worker authority to choose retry or terminal queue state. An accepted fail command for the current active lease/attempt emits attempt-failed with stable workId, leaseId, attempt, workerId, commandId, failure evidence, DataIssue refs, retryable hints when provided, policy refs, and clock refs. The same accepted mutation-bearing evaluation must emit exactly one disposition record: retry-scheduled or work-dead-lettered. retry-scheduled records carry the failed attempt refs, retryAtMs, delayMs, retry policy refs, reason codes, and source failure refs; they do not create the next attempt. The next attempt is created only by a later accepted claim after retryAtMs is eligible. work-dead-lettered records carry terminal reason, failed attempt refs, exhausted policy evidence, source refs, and issue/status/audit refs. Retry and backoff semantics reuse the shared GraphReFly resilience mechanism, including RetryPolicy, BackoffPolicy, shouldRetry, nextRetryDelayMs, backoffDelayMs, and retry/status vocabulary; workQueue must not define a parallel queue-specific retry policy or hidden retry engine. Worker-provided retryable or nonretryable flags, failure categories, error values, artifact refs, size evidence, or provider/domain codes are evidence consumed by retry policy, not direct authority. If required retry policy, clock/deadline facts, or failure material are missing or invalid such that no durable disposition can be computed, the fail command is rejected with visible DataIssue/status and must not emit a half-transition attempt-failed without retry/dead-letter disposition. deadLetter() is a read-only workQueue projection over work-dead-lettered records; it must not republish messages, ack messageBus cursors, recover work, claim work, or mutate terminal state. Reprocessing dead-lettered work in v0 requires an explicit new submit/admission path or later reviewed recovery command; terminal work-dead-lettered records are not resurrected by projection reads.
rationale: D301 says fail emits attempt-failed and then either retry-scheduled or work-dead-lettered via shared retry policy, while D209 requires CSP-8 retry to reuse the existing GraphReFly retry/resilience mechanism end to end. D307 separates messageBus ack from work completion, and D312/D314 keep reads and expiration from mutating state. Making retry/dead-letter a visible disposition after attempt-failed preserves replay honesty and keeps workers from owning queue policy. Requiring an atomic failed-attempt-plus-disposition transition avoids an ambiguous failed-pending state, while keeping retry-scheduled separate from claim preserves the invariant that claim alone creates attempts and leases.

layer: L6 / workQueue completion evidence and terminal boundary
question: How should workQueue complete work without becoming a domain-result bus, WorkItem mutator, or unbounded artifact carrier?
decision: workQueue treats complete as successful completion of the queue lease/attempt, not as authority to mutate domain state or publish execution results elsewhere. An accepted complete command requires the current active lease/attempt and emits attempt-completed plus work-completed in the same mutation-bearing evaluation. The records carry stable coordinates such as workId, leaseId, attempt, workerId, commandId, completedAtMs or clock refs, policy refs, source refs, optional result/evidence refs, DataIssue refs when relevant, audit refs, and size/redaction evidence. Completion evidence may include small inline values only under explicit size/redaction policy; large outputs, files, provider raw responses, stdout/stderr, binary/media, or sensitive material must use D270 artifact/ref/summary envelopes and D293 size-capacity evidence. work-completed is terminal for the queue item: later claim, fail, complete, renew, release, retry, schedule, or lease-expire commands for that work or lease emit stale/terminal DataIssue/status rather than mutating state. workQueue completion must not append WorkItemEvents, apply domain actions, close or resolve WorkItems, emit ExecutorOutcome, ack messageBus cursors, publish to messageBus topics, or dispatch follow-up workers by itself. Domain-specific result handling is a separate projector/composition over work-completed evidence and the relevant domain policies. Duplicate complete command handling reuses lifecycle command idempotency: exact duplicate accepted commands replay status or emit duplicate-command material, never a second attempt-completed or work-completed record. If completion evidence violates size, schema, redaction, authorization, or policy requirements, the complete command is rejected with visible DataIssue/status and the active lease remains governed by renew, release, fail, expire, or cancel semantics.
rationale: D301 says complete emits attempt-completed plus work-completed for the current active lease/attempt, while D299 keeps workQueue generic and outside WorkItem/Executor-specific surfaces. D239 reserves WorkItem mutation for explicit domain action application, D270 defines artifact/ref boundaries, and D293 defines shared size-capacity evidence. Without a completion boundary, workQueue would collapse into a result bus or domain workflow engine. Keeping complete as queue-terminal success preserves replay honesty, lets domain layers consume completion evidence explicitly, and prevents large or sensitive worker outputs from bloating graph facts.

layer: L6 / workQueue lease renewal and voluntary release
question: How should workQueue renew leases and release work voluntarily without hidden heartbeats, private worker registries, or conflating release with fail/complete?
decision: workQueue treats renew-lease and release as explicit lifecycle commands over the current active lease/attempt. renew-lease requires stable workId, leaseId, attempt, workerId, commandId, explicit graph-local clock facts, and policy refs. An accepted renewal emits lease-renewed with previousLeaseExpiresAtMs, leaseExpiresAtMs, renewedAtMs or clock refs, worker or heartbeat evidence refs when supplied, and policy refs. Renewal may extend only the current lease ownership window; it must not change workId, attempt, workerId, payload, priority, queue binding, claim policy, completion evidence, retry disposition, or domain state. Renewal cannot resurrect expired, released, completed, failed-disposed, canceled, or dead-lettered work. If explicit clock/deadline facts show the lease has already expired, the command must not renew it; it may materialize lease-expired according to D314 and emit stale or expired DataIssue/status. Renewal is policy-bounded by max lease duration, max extension, queue shutdown or cancel policy, worker validity evidence, and capacity policy where configured; missing, stale, unsupported, or invalid renewal evidence emits visible issue/status rather than assuming an always-live worker. release requires the current active lease/attempt and emits work-released with workId, leaseId, attempt, workerId, commandId, releasedAtMs or clock refs, reason, policy refs, and optional evidence refs. Release ends worker ownership without emitting attempt-completed, attempt-failed, retry-scheduled, work-completed, or work-dead-lettered. Released work becomes ready by default; explicit release policy may instead emit visible scheduling material such as work-scheduled or notBeforeMs before it is claimable. Release does not ack messageBus cursors, dispatch another worker, mutate worker facts privately, or decrement or credit worker capacity through a hidden registry; worker availability and capacity are derived from records plus explicit worker/capacity facts per D313. Duplicate renew/release command handling reuses lifecycle idempotency and must never append a second lease-renewed or work-released record for the same accepted command.
rationale: D301 defines renew-lease and release as current-active-lease transitions, D314 makes expiration explicit and non-timer-based, D313 rejects private worker registries, and D315/D316 separate release from failed and completed attempt outcomes. Without this boundary, heartbeat could become a hidden liveness runtime and release could be misused as failure, retry, or scheduler dispatch. Keeping renew/release as visible lifecycle records preserves replay honesty, worker ownership auditability, and the invariant that claim creates leases, fail/complete close attempts with outcomes, and release merely gives ownership back to the queue.

layer: L6 / workQueue scheduling and delayed eligibility
question: How should workQueue support fixed-time scheduled work, BullMQ-style delayed jobs, and manual delay without hidden timers, private delayed queues, or conflating manual schedule with retry backoff?
decision: workQueue treats schedule as an explicit lifecycle command or policy result that records delayed eligibility for nonterminal work. An accepted schedule emits work-scheduled with stable workId, commandId, scheduleId or idempotency key where applicable, scheduledAtMs or clock refs, optional scheduleAtMs/runAtMs fixed-time intent, notBeforeMs eligibility lower bound, optional deadlineMs, reason, policy refs, source refs, and issue/audit refs. scheduleAtMs or runAtMs captures the user-facing fixed-time meaning such as run at 2026-06-16T09:00:00-07:00; notBeforeMs is the queue eligibility lower bound used by derived state and claim policy, normally equal to scheduleAtMs for fixed-time jobs but open to policy translation such as delayMs, windows, calendars, jitter, or timezone normalization. schedule may target admitted ready work, released work, or other nonterminal work allowed by queue policy, but it must not target completed, canceled, dead-lettered, unknown, or otherwise terminal work. schedule does not claim work, create a lease, create an attempt, ack messageBus cursors, publish messages, run timers, enqueue into a private delayed heap, or dispatch workers. Scheduled work becomes claim-eligible only when explicit graph-local clock/deadline facts make notBeforeMs eligible and claim policy admits it; available() may show scheduled, soon-eligible, or overdue candidates but must not mutate scheduling state. Manual work-scheduled and retry-scheduled are separate record families: retry-scheduled is produced by failure disposition under D315 and carries failed-attempt/backoff refs, while work-scheduled records explicit scheduling command or policy material. If both scheduling and retry material exist for the same work, derived eligibility uses the visible policy-defined effective time, normally the most restrictive eligible-at value unless policy says otherwise, and emits status/issues for conflicts. schedule may reschedule only under explicit policy; duplicate or stale schedule commands reuse lifecycle idempotency and must not append conflicting hidden timers. Canceling or completing work makes later schedule material stale or terminal but does not erase historical schedule records. No background sweeper, private delayed queue, or wall-clock read is the source of truth; eligibility is derived from records plus explicit clock/deadline and policy facts.
rationale: D301 defines scheduled and retry-wait states and requires scheduled/retry work to become available only through visible clock/deadline inputs. D312 keeps available() read-only, D315 separates retry-scheduled from worker failure disposition, D317 lets release policy optionally schedule released work, and the user explicitly wants BullMQ-like fixed-time scheduled jobs without losing the clean-slate visibility floor. Separating scheduleAtMs/runAtMs user intent from notBeforeMs queue eligibility supports fixed-time scheduling, delayMs translation, calendars, and policy windows while preserving replay honesty. Keeping schedule as visible records plus explicit clock facts avoids a private timer heap or delayed queue and preserves the invariant that claim alone reserves work.

layer: L6 / workQueue cancellation terminal boundary
question: How should workQueue cancel work without treating cancellation as fail/complete, deleting history, or pretending to abort external execution?
decision: workQueue treats cancel as a terminal queue lifecycle command for nonterminal work. An accepted cancel emits work-canceled with stable workId, commandId, canceledAtMs or clock refs, reason, policy refs, source refs, actor or request refs when available, optional canceledLeaseId and attempt refs, and issue/audit refs. cancel may target scheduled, ready, leased, retry-wait, or otherwise nonterminal work according to queue policy, but it must reject unknown, completed, already canceled, dead-lettered, or terminal work with visible DataIssue/status. If work is actively leased, cancel invalidates the active lease/attempt for queue purposes: later renew-lease, release, complete, fail, lease-expire, or duplicate lifecycle commands for that lease/attempt emit stale or canceled DataIssue/status rather than mutating state. cancel does not emit attempt-completed, attempt-failed, retry-scheduled, work-completed, work-dead-lettered, work-released, or lease-expired unless an explicit reviewed policy later adds separate audit material; cancellation is not success, failure, retry, or voluntary release. cancel must not delete historical records, erase schedule/retry/admission material, rewind messageBus cursors, ack messageBus messages, publish messages, dispatch workers, or mutate WorkItems/domain state. workQueue cancel does not by itself abort external worker processes, provider calls, tool execution, browser actions, subprocesses, or side effects. Cooperative or best-effort external cancellation is a separate graph-visible adapter/executor/domain flow such as cancel-requested, cancel-sent, cancel-acknowledged, cancel-unsupported, timeout-expired, or reconcile-needed under D275, correlated back to work-canceled when composed. If an external worker later reports complete/fail/release/renew after cancellation, workQueue treats it as stale or canceled issue/status, while adapter/domain layers may separately record external cleanup or reconcile evidence. Duplicate cancel command handling reuses lifecycle idempotency and must not append a second work-canceled record for the same accepted command.
rationale: D301 says cancel emits work-canceled for nonterminal work and invalidates active leases, while D315, D316, and D317 separate fail, complete, and release from cancellation. D275 keeps external cancellation and timeout as best-effort adapter evidence rather than protocol TEARDOWN or guaranteed undo. D299 keeps workQueue generic and outside WorkItem/Executor surfaces, and D307 separates messageBus ack from queue lifecycle. A terminal cancel record preserves replay honesty and lets queues stop future claim and worker mutation without pretending that side effects outside the queue were undone.

layer: L6 / workQueue pull projections and page params
question: How should workQueue expose available work, per-work inspection, dead-letter pages, and projection pagination without read-side mutation or opaque cursor state?
decision: workQueue projections are pull/read-only snapshots derived from records plus explicit policy and clock/deadline facts. The v0 projections are available(), work(workId), and deadLetter(), each with output-named pull ids such as availablePullId, workSnapshotPullId, and deadLetterSnapshotPullId. Projection pulls may accept explicit params, but params must not encode hidden mutable cursor state or grant mutation authority. available() returns claim candidates only: by default ready and currently claim-eligible work under the supplied or current explicit clock/policy facts. It does not reserve, claim, ack, seek, admit, reject, complete, fail, cancel, renew, release, schedule, expire leases, recover dead letters, or mutate queue state. available params may include limit, maxBytes or sizeLimit evidence when supported by D293, afterWorkId or afterAdmissionSeq for stable page continuation, workerId, policyRef, capability/capacity refs, priority/tag/requirement filters, nowMs or clockRef, includeIssues, and sort/order policy refs. available pages return items, nextAfterWorkId or nextAfterAdmissionSeq, hasMore, asOfRecordSeq or highWater, clock refs, policy refs, and issues/status; candidate entries carry workId, state, admission refs, priority/tags/requirements, notBeforeMs/retryAtMs/deadlineMs where relevant, capacity/size evidence, source refs, and claim policy evidence. scheduled, soon-eligible, leased, completed, canceled, and dead-lettered work are not included in default available() unless explicit inspection filters request non-default candidate classes; even then the projection remains read-only and must label non-claimable entries. work(workId) returns a per-work snapshot including current derived state, lifecycle record refs, admission/source refs, active lease/attempt if any, schedule/retry/deadline facts, terminal records, issues/status/audit refs, and optional bounded recent history. work(workId) must not mutate, refresh, renew, expire, or recover the work. deadLetter() returns pages over work-dead-lettered records, not messageBus dead-letter entries. deadLetter params may include limit, maxBytes or sizeLimit evidence, afterDeadLetterSeq or afterWorkId, code/reason filters, topic/source filters, includeIssues, and clock/policy refs. deadLetter pages return entries, nextAfterDeadLetterSeq or nextAfterWorkId, hasMore, asOfRecordSeq, policy refs, and issues/status. Projection page coordinates are stable explicit fields, not opaque page tokens; count bounds are required for list pages, and byte/size limits use D293 vocabulary when implemented. Projection snapshots may be stale by the time a later claim/command runs; commands must re-evaluate current derived state and emit stale-candidate or policy issues rather than trusting pages as reservations.
rationale: D299 defines available(), work(workId), and deadLetter() as on-demand projections, D307 forbids projections from admission, ack, seek, claim, or completion, D312 makes available() a read-only possibly stale candidate view, and D285 locks explicit page coordinates for messageBus projections. D318 adds scheduled/soon-eligible visibility and D319 adds terminal canceled state, so projection boundaries need a stable naming and pagination shape before implementation. Keeping pull projections read-only and page coordinates explicit preserves replay honesty, avoids hidden cursor state, and keeps claim as the only reservation operation.

layer: L6 / WorkQueueCommand public discriminated union shape
question: What public WorkQueueCommand shape should v0 use so submit, claim, lease, completion, failure, cancellation, and schedule commands are stable data facts without hidden handles or command-specific envelope drift?
decision: WorkQueueCommand v0 is a provider-neutral discriminated union of DATA facts with a shared command envelope plus kind-specific fields. Every command carries kind, commandId, queueId when the bundle cannot infer it structurally, optional idempotencyKey, correlationId, causationId, sourceRefs, policyRefs, actorRefs, auditRefs, and optional clock material such as nowMs or clockRef when the transition needs graph-local time. commandId is the lifecycle command identity used for duplicate command handling; idempotencyKey is an optional policy-level duplicate key and must not replace workId, leaseId, attempt, or messageBus commandId semantics. The v0 command kinds are submit, claim, renew-lease, release, complete, fail, cancel, schedule, and expire-leases. submit is publish/admission intent material: it may carry payload or payload/artifact refs, provided workId or idempotencyKey under dedupe policy, priority, tags, requirements, cost/size evidence, notBeforeMs, deadlineMs, and admission policy refs, but public submit helpers still publish to the bound messageBus topic rather than appending work records directly. claim carries workerId, requestedWorkIds or next/batch selection params, limit/maxBatch, claim policy refs, capability/capacity evidence refs, and lease policy material such as leaseDurationMs; it creates reservation only if accepted as work-claimed. renew-lease, release, complete, and fail require workId, leaseId, attempt, workerId, commandId, and clock/policy refs; complete carries bounded completion evidence/result refs, fail carries failure evidence and retryable/nonretryable hints, release carries reason/evidence, and renew carries requested extension or leaseExpiresAtMs policy material. cancel requires workId plus reason/policy/source refs and may include actor/request refs; schedule requires workId plus scheduleId or idempotency key, scheduleAtMs or runAtMs intent, notBeforeMs, optional deadlineMs, reason, and policy refs. expire-leases is an explicit maintenance/materialization command over requested work/lease ids or bounded scan params plus clock/policy refs; it may only materialize lease-expired according to D314 and must not claim, fail, complete, cancel, or schedule work. Commands are ordinary facts; helpers may construct and publish them, but commands do not carry live Node handles, worker objects, executor/provider handles, AbortControllers, callbacks, functions, promises, messageBus cursors, mutable registries, or runtime-private SDK/session/process objects. Malformed, missing-coordinate, unauthorized, stale, duplicate, unsupported, unknown-kind, policy-mismatched, or terminal-state commands emit DataIssue/status rather than protocol ERROR and never mutate hidden state. Runtime implementations may add language-local builder helpers, but the public fact contract remains this discriminated union shape.
rationale: D299 defines the v0 command kinds and requires commands to be graph-visible facts; D310 keeps submit on the messageBus-backed admission path; D311 separates commandId, workId, idempotencyKey, and messageBus identity; D312-D320 define claim, lifecycle, scheduling, cancellation, and projection boundaries. Existing TS surfaces show both generic command envelopes and discriminated command unions; workQueue needs the discriminated form because lease/attempt/schedule/failure/result coordinates differ by command, while a shared envelope prevents idempotency, policy, source, and clock refs from drifting. Keeping commands pure data facts preserves replay honesty, testability, and the no hidden worker/runtime handle boundary.
