layer: L6 / WorkQueueRecord common envelope and record family fields
question: What public WorkQueueRecord shape should v0 use so the append-only queue ledger can drive projections, status, retry, lease ownership, and audit without record-family drift or hidden runtime state?
decision: WorkQueueRecord v0 is a provider-neutral discriminated union of append-only ordered DATA facts with a shared record envelope plus family-specific fields. Every record carries kind, recordSeq, queueId, workId when a work item exists, optional commandId, optional idempotencyKey, correlationId, causationId, sourceRefs, policyRefs, actorRefs, auditRefs, issues refs, and graph-local time material such as recordedAtMs or clockRef. recordSeq is the queue-local monotonic ledger coordinate used for projection high-water and stable pagination; it is not a messageBus topic seq, subscription cursor, attempt number, or command id. Records may reference commandId and source command material, but records are facts, not commands: they do not authorize future mutation, carry live handles, or encode projection cursor state. v0 record families include work-admitted, work-rejected or admission-rejected, work-scheduled, work-claimed, lease-renewed, work-released, lease-expired, attempt-completed, attempt-failed, retry-scheduled, work-completed, work-canceled, work-dead-lettered, admission-deduped or equivalent dedupe status material, and lifecycle-rejected/status material where policy chooses durable rejection records. work-admitted carries messageBus source coordinates when admitted from the bound subscription, payload or artifact refs, workId, admission metadata, priority/tags/requirements, cost/size evidence, notBeforeMs/deadlineMs when admitted, and admission policy refs. work-rejected/admission-rejected carries stable source coordinates, rejection code/reason, existingWorkId when duplicate-related, DataIssue refs, and whether the rejection is deterministic enough to allow ingestion ack under D307. work-scheduled carries scheduleId or source command refs, scheduleAtMs/runAtMs intent, notBeforeMs, optional deadlineMs, reason, and schedule policy refs. work-claimed carries leaseId, attempt, workerId, claimedAtMs, leaseExpiresAtMs, selected-by policy refs, and capacity/capability evidence refs. lease-renewed carries leaseId, attempt, workerId, previousLeaseExpiresAtMs, leaseExpiresAtMs, renewedAtMs, and renewal policy/evidence refs. work-released carries leaseId, attempt, workerId, releasedAtMs, reason, and release policy refs. lease-expired carries leaseId, attempt, workerId, leaseExpiresAtMs, expiredAtMs or clock refs, expiration policy refs, and next-state policy refs. attempt-completed and work-completed are distinct records emitted together for accepted completion: attempt-completed carries lease/attempt/worker completion evidence, while work-completed carries terminal queue completion evidence/result refs and size/redaction refs. attempt-failed plus retry-scheduled or work-dead-lettered are emitted according to D315; attempt-failed carries failure evidence, retryable hints, and issue refs, retry-scheduled carries retryAtMs/delayMs/backoff refs, and work-dead-lettered carries terminal reason/exhausted policy/source refs. work-canceled carries cancel reason, canceledAtMs, actor/request/source refs, optional canceledLeaseId/attempt refs, and cancellation policy refs. Rejection/status records may be emitted for malformed, stale, duplicate, unauthorized, policy-rejected, terminal-state, capacity, or missing-coordinate inputs, but they must remain DATA-level issue/status facts and not protocol ERROR. Projection state such as current ready/leased/dead-lettered maps, available pages, deadLetter pages, cursor high-water, and worker capacity summaries is derived from records and explicit policy/clock facts, not stored as authoritative record fields. Records are immutable once emitted; corrections or recovery are new records/status facts, never in-place edits or history deletion.
rationale: D299 makes records the append-only lifecycle ledger and source of truth for derived queue state; D307 requires durable admission outcomes; D311 separates work identity, dedupe identity, and message identity; D314-D319 lock lease expiration, retry/dead-letter, completion, renewal/release, scheduling, and cancellation records; and D320 requires projections to page over explicit record coordinates. Existing CQRS and messaging surfaces use seq/cursor/timestamp envelopes for ordered facts, but workQueue needs queue-specific record families because lifecycle coordinates differ by transition. A shared record envelope plus family-specific fields preserves replay honesty, projection simplicity, auditability, and the no hidden mutable job map/worker registry boundary.

layer: L6 / workQueue status and DataIssue taxonomy
question: How should workQueue expose command, admission, projection, maintenance, and policy problems without turning status or issues into a second lifecycle ledger or protocol ERROR channel?
decision: workQueue status and issues are explanatory DATA facts over command/admission/projection/maintenance outcomes; lifecycle truth remains in WorkQueueRecord. The core bundle exposes status: Node<WorkQueueStatus> and issues: Node<DataIssue>, not errors. WorkQueueStatus is a provider-neutral status fact family with a small progress/outcome vocabulary such as command-accepted, command-rejected, admission-accepted, admission-rejected, admission-retryable, projection-ready, projection-partial, projection-stale, maintenance-applied, maintenance-noop, and policy-warning. Status facts may carry queueId, optional workId, commandId, idempotencyKey, recordSeq or record refs, sourceRefs, policyRefs, actorRefs, auditRefs, issue refs, asOfRecordSeq or high-water, and graph-local clock material, but they do not authorize mutation, reserve work, advance messageBus cursors, create leases, complete attempts, or replace required lifecycle records. Accepted lifecycle transitions must emit the required WorkQueueRecord family from D322; status may summarize or reference those records but is not the source of derived queue state. Rejected, stale, duplicate, malformed, unauthorized, policy-rejected, capacity-rejected, missing-coordinate, or terminal-state inputs may emit only DataIssue/status when no durable lifecycle record is required; admission outcomes that gate messageBus ack still follow D307 and must produce durable work-admitted or work-rejected/admission-rejected material before cursor advance. workQueue extends the shared D184 DataIssue base with queue-specific codes including malformed-command, unknown-command-kind, missing-coordinate, unknown-work, terminal-work, stale-candidate, not-ready, already-leased, stale-lease, lease-expired, lease-not-current, attempt-mismatch, worker-mismatch, duplicate-command, idempotency-conflict, policy-rejected, capacity-exceeded, capability-mismatch, clock-required, clock-stale, schedule-conflict, retry-policy-missing, disposition-undetermined, admission-rejected, transient-admission-failure, projection-stale, retention-gap-source, source-cursor-stale, and unauthorized. Codes remain open extension strings for domain/policy adapters, but shared helpers should prefer the common vocabulary before inventing new names. Issues carry stable subject coordinates such as queueId, workId, commandId, leaseId, attempt, workerId, recordSeq, messageBus topic/seq/subscriptionId, projection name, pull id, and policy refs where applicable. Retryable/transient flags on issues are evidence for policy and do not directly retry, ack, seek, claim, or dead-letter. Projection issues explain stale pages, bounded truncation, missing clock/policy refs, retention gaps, and partial views; they never mutate projection state or become opaque cursor tokens. Protocol ERROR remains reserved for substrate fn/protocol failures; ordinary queue validation, stale worker callbacks, policy rejection, admission rejection, and projection partiality are DATA-level issues/status.
rationale: D184 establishes DataIssue as the cross-library DATA-level issue vocabulary, D299 exposes status and issues as part of the workQueue core, D307 requires durable admission outcomes before messageBus cursor advance, D312-D320 separate read projections from mutation, and D322 makes records the authoritative lifecycle ledger. Without a hard taxonomy boundary, status could become a hidden second queue state machine, or every stale command could be misreported as protocol ERROR. Keeping status explanatory and issue codes shared gives implementers and UIs enough observability while preserving replay honesty, graph-visible lifecycle records, and the no hidden mutation boundary.

layer: L6 / workQueue public factory and TS/Rust implementation target
question: What public workQueue factory and package/module shape should TS and Rust implement so workQueue stays an independent messageBus-backed application-infrastructure primitive rather than becoming orchestration, a runtime object, or a second messaging implementation?
decision: workQueue is an independent reusable application-infrastructure surface layered above messageBus and below orchestration, patterns, and solutions. In TypeScript it lives under @graphrefly/ts/work-queue, not @graphrefly/ts/orchestration; in Rust it lives in a corresponding self-contained work_queue module. The public shape is a free graph-authoring helper such as workQueue<T>(graph, options) that returns a graph-visible bundle, not a Graph method, runtime object, reducer owner, worker registry, scheduler, or compatibility facade. Options identify the queue and its messageBus admission binding, including queueId, bus or bus refs, topic, subscriptionId, admission source coordinates, and explicit policies or policy refs for admission, claim, lease, retry/backoff, scheduling, dedupe, capacity/cost, clock/deadline, redaction/size, and status/audit where supported. The returned bundle exposes commands: Node<WorkQueueCommand<T>>, records: Node<WorkQueueRecord<T>>, status: Node<WorkQueueStatus>, and issues: Node<DataIssue>, plus convenience helpers submit, claim, renewLease, release, complete, fail, cancel, schedule, and expireLeases, and on-demand pull projections available(), work(workId), and deadLetter(). Helper methods are boundary sugar that construct and publish graph-visible command facts or messageBus publish facts and may return correlation material; they must not directly append records, mutate derived state, reserve work, advance cursors, dispatch workers, run timers, or call hidden runtime handles. submit remains messageBus-backed: public submit helpers publish to the bound messageBus topic, and accepted work appears only after the admission path consumes the retained message and emits a durable workQueue admission outcome under D307. The queue admission path depends on the messageBus retained log and independent subscription cursor substrate; ack means durable admission outcome and cursor advance, not work completion. Projections are read-only pull bundles from D320 and must not claim, ack, seek, admit, complete, fail, cancel, renew, release, schedule, expire leases, or recover dead letters. workQueue may reuse shared library policies and orchestration infrastructure such as RetryPolicy, BackoffPolicy, token-bucket/capacity helpers, rate limits, circuit breakers, deadline/retention utilities, DataIssue, DataResult, artifacts, and audit vocabulary through explicit policy facts/options, but workQueue must not depend on orchestration-owned WorkItem, EffectRun, AgentRequest, ExecutorOutcome, ProcessBundle, or worker/executor registries. Orchestration, WorkItem, and effectRun recipes may compose over workQueue records/projections later, but they do not own the queue core. TS and Rust should share the command, record, status, issue, admission, claim, lifecycle, projection, and policy-observable behavior even when language-idiomatic helper signatures differ; cross-runtime checks should use behavioral conformance scenarios rather than structural API parity. Implementation order should preserve the dependency chain: first messageBus PULL/subscription/cursor semantics, then workQueue facts/reducer/projections, then orchestration or WorkItem recipes over workQueue.
rationale: D125 places messaging, orchestration, and CQRS as reusable application-infrastructure subpaths; D279 defines messageBus as the retained topic-log plus independent subscription cursor substrate and keeps job queue semantics above it; D294 names workQueue as the generic queue primitive; D299-D323 lock workQueue core nodes, admission, identity, claim, lifecycle, projections, record fields, and status/issues. The user explicitly corrected job queue to workQueue and asked for a clean dependency chain independent of orchestration while still built on messaging. A free bundle factory preserves graph-first inspectability, keeps helpers as sugar over facts, prevents a hidden runtime/job map/worker registry from becoming public semantics, and gives TS/Rust a concrete implementation target without requiring structural parity. Keeping orchestration and WorkItem recipes above workQueue lets richer agent/process behavior reuse the queue without making the queue depend on those domains.

layer: L6 / messageBus-to-workQueue implementation handoff and dependency-order gate
question: What implementation order and acceptance gate should TS and Rust follow after the messageBus/workQueue redesign so implementation does not recreate old dynamicHub, hide cursor semantics, or make orchestration own queue behavior?
decision: The implementation handoff is locked as a three-stage dependency gate. Stage 1 is messageBus first: retire the old dynamicHub public surface with no thin alias or compatibility facade; reshape messageBus to the D279/D282/D284/D285/D276 surface with commands, messages, status, issues, strict topic policy by default, reused retention/dedupe policy, explicit page params, and output-named pull ids. RESUME must not be used for demand; retained/read demand uses PULL({pullId, params?}) according to D269/D272. Topic catalog, deadLetter, topic(topic), and subscription available views are on-demand pull projections. Subscription cursor movement is driven only by explicit command facts such as ack, seek, and close according to D266/D279; availablePullId is read-only and must not move cursor. Stage 2 is workQueue second: add the independent @graphrefly/ts/work-queue and Rust work_queue surfaces from D324, backed by messageBus subscription admission rather than direct payload-to-record mutation. Implement D299-D323 as graph-visible commands, records, status, issues, durable admission/ack boundary, work identity/dedupe identity separation, claim/lease/renew/release/expiration, retry/dead-letter disposition, completion, cancellation, scheduling, projections, record families, and status/issue taxonomy. workQueue must reuse shared retry/backoff, capacity/token-bucket, rate-limit/circuit-breaker, deadline/retention, DataIssue/DataResult, artifact, size/redaction, and audit vocabulary through explicit policy/options/facts instead of inventing hidden engines. Stage 3 is recipes last: orchestration, WorkItem, effectRun, agent, process, or solution recipes may compose over workQueue records/projections only after the queue core exists; workQueue must not import or depend on WorkItem, EffectRun, AgentRequest, ExecutorOutcome, ProcessBundle, executor bindings, or worker registries. The acceptance gate for TS includes tests that dynamicHub is absent, messageBus PULL/subscription/cursor behavior is correct, projections are read-only, strict topic policy and retention-gap behavior are visible, and workQueue admission, claim races, lease lifecycle, retry/dead-letter, completion, cancellation, scheduling, status/issues, and projections follow the locked decisions. Rust must cover the same behavior in its self-contained module. Cross-runtime validation is behavioral conformance over messageBus/workQueue scenarios, not symbol-set parity or exact helper-signature matching. Any protocol-message/tier/ctx behavior discovered during implementation routes through spec-amend before code; ordinary API polish that does not change protocol may remain per-language but must not violate the locked dependency order.
rationale: D269/D272 changed demand from overloaded RESUME to explicit PULL; D279-D285 lock the new messageBus retained-log/subscription-cursor substrate and retire dynamicHub compatibility; D299-D324 lock workQueue as messageBus-backed, independent from orchestration, and graph-visible through facts and projections. The implementation risk is high because the old code still contains messageBus/dynamicHub shapes and because workQueue could accidentally recreate its own hidden cursor, scheduler, or worker runtime if implemented before messageBus is corrected. A staged gate preserves the dependency chain messaging -> workQueue -> orchestration/recipes, keeps TS/Rust aligned by behavior rather than structural parity, and gives the next dev-dispatch session a concrete stop/go checklist.

layer: L6 / eventFlow source boundary after messageBus and workQueue redesign / CSP-8 Layer A
question: How should eventFlow simplify after messageBus owns retained topics/subscription cursors and workQueue owns claimable/retryable work lifecycle, without collapsing event projection into messaging or queue execution?
decision: eventFlow v0 consumes EventMessage or MessageEnvelope<EventMessage> facts from declared graph sources, normally messageBus retained message streams or subscription/read projections, and focuses only on normalizing event-flow records and materializing projections, status, DataIssue, audit, and projector high-water facts. eventFlow must not own topics, retained logs, topic lifecycle, subscription cursors, ack, seek, close, messageBus deadLetter, retention, dedupe, poison-message admission, work claim, lease, retry, schedule, queue dead-letter, worker capacity, or work completion semantics. messageBus remains the source for retained topic-log and independent subscription-cursor behavior under D279/D282/D284/D285/D287, while workQueue remains the source for admitted work records, claim/lease/retry/schedule/dead-letter/completion under D294/D299/D307/D324. eventFlow cursor or high-water means projector processing progress over source coordinates such as topic, seq, message id, source refs, or record refs; it is not a messageBus subscription cursor, storage replay offset, workQueue recordSeq, or ack authority. eventFlow may expose source refs and retention-gap/stale-source issues when its input stream has gaps, but it reports them as projection issues rather than repairing cursors or seeking subscriptions. Work that needs competing workers, visibility timeout, retry, delayed eligibility, dead-letter disposition, or durable completion evidence must be modeled through workQueue or a recipe over workQueue, not by adding queue lifecycle to eventFlow. Domain reducers/projectors, WorkItem projections, and FSM policies remain above messageBus/workQueue in eventFlow or solution layers; messageBus and workQueue do not run domain reducers, apply WorkItem actions, emit AgentDecision facts, dispatch executors, or mutate domain projections.
rationale: D182 defines Layer A as horizontal event-flow, Layer B as WorkItem solution, and Layer C as executor bridge; D183 makes EventMessage passive messaging vocabulary; D185 defines eventFlow as projector-family pattern with pattern-owned processing cursors; D279 locks messageBus as retained topic-log plus subscription cursor substrate; D294/D299/D307/D324 lock workQueue as the independent messageBus-backed work lifecycle layer. The new messaging/workQueue redesign lets eventFlow shed duplicated cursor, dead-letter, retention, dedupe, and queue semantics while preserving its core value: graph-visible event-to-view projection. This keeps the layering simple, avoids messageBus becoming a workflow engine, avoids eventFlow becoming a queue runtime, and gives WorkItem/Executor recipes a clean choice between projection via eventFlow and claimable work via workQueue.

layer: L6 / WorkItem async-work recipe over workQueue / CSP-8 Layer B-C boundary
question: How should WorkItem verification, approval, external sync, spawn review, placement review, and other asynchronous domain work use workQueue without making workQueue a WorkItem mutator or duplicating executor/request lifecycle?
decision: WorkItem async-work is an orchestration or solution recipe over workQueue, not a workQueue core responsibility and not a replacement for WorkItem domain events, AgentRequest, ExecutorBridge, or AgentDecision. WorkItem projectors or effect recipes may lower explicit WorkItem effect/request/proposal facts into workQueue submit commands when the work needs durable admission, claim, lease, visibility timeout, retry, delayed eligibility, capacity matching, cancellation, or dead-letter disposition. Common candidates include verification tasks, approval/review tasks, external sync tasks, spawn review or spawn emission tasks, placement/lane review tasks, scheduled follow-ups, SLA checks, and background evidence collection. The workQueue payload carries secret-free WorkItem and effect coordinates such as workItemId, effectRunId, sourceEventId or sourceDecisionId, requested action/proposal kind, policyRefs, sourceRefs, context refs, artifact refs, priority/deadline/size/capacity hints, and idempotency material; it must not carry WorkItem mutators, Graph handles, ExecutorBinding objects, provider clients, credentials, UI callbacks, or hidden runner state. Claiming or completing workQueue work does not mutate WorkItems, append WorkItemEvents, apply domain actions, emit ExecutorOutcome, or satisfy AgentRequest by itself. Accepted completion, failure, cancellation, dead-letter, or timeout records become evidence/status/issues/audit that a WorkItem recipe may map into WorkItem evidence events, domain action proposals, approval decisions, verification results, placement decisions, or DataIssue facts through explicit policy. WorkItem close, resolve, approve, verify, patch, spawn, re-lane, and similar mutations remain subject to D239 action admission/application and append-only WorkItemEvent projection. A WorkItem-specific queue recipe may expose convenience helpers and views, but those helpers construct messageBus/workQueue command facts and projections; they do not own the queue core, bypass messageBus admission, or treat workQueue completion as domain truth. eventFlow consumes resulting EventMessage/WorkItem facts for projections under D326, while workQueue remains the durable work lifecycle substrate underneath the recipe.
rationale: D182 separates Layer A eventFlow, Layer B WorkItem solutions, and Layer C executor/harness execution; D189 makes work-item effects graph-visible request projections; D239 reserves WorkItem mutation for explicit domain action application; D294/D299/D307/D324 define workQueue as a generic messageBus-backed claim/lease/retry work lifecycle layer independent of WorkItem and Executor types; D326 trims eventFlow back to event projection. Some WorkItem-related tasks need queue semantics such as competing workers, leases, retries, delayed eligibility, and dead-lettering, but embedding those semantics in WorkItem lanes or eventFlow would duplicate workQueue and blur domain projection with execution lifecycle. A recipe over workQueue reuses the general queue layer while preserving WorkItem evidence/proposal/application boundaries and keeping workQueue reusable outside issue tracking.

layer: L6 / executor durable dispatch recipe over workQueue / CSP-8 Layer C
question: How should durable or claimable LLM, tool, human, browser, CLI, MCP, or external executor work use workQueue without making workQueue an ExecutorBridge, ExecutorBinding, AgentRequest ledger, or hidden worker runtime?
decision: Durable executor dispatch is an optional orchestration or executor recipe over workQueue, not a workQueue core behavior and not a replacement for AgentRequest, ExecutorBridge, ExecutorBinding, AgentDecision, or ExecutorOutcome. AgentDecision lowerers, executor admission policy, or solution recipes may submit workQueue commands for execution work that needs durable admission, competing worker claim, lease/visibility timeout, retry/dead-letter disposition, delayed eligibility, worker capacity matching, or offline worker handoff. The workQueue payload carries secret-free executor coordinates such as requestId, operationId, parentRequestId, sourceDecisionId, intentId, inputId, toolCallSeriesId, routeId, profileId, executorId, effectRunId, promptBundle refs, ToolDefinition refs, policyRefs, budgetRefs, permission/sandbox refs, sourceRefs, artifact refs, idempotency keys, priority, deadline, size/capacity hints, and required capability material. It must not carry ExecutorBinding objects, SDK clients, credentials, headers, AbortControllers, subprocess handles, browser sessions, Graph/Ctx/Node handles, callbacks, promises, or provider request bodies as canonical facts. Claiming workQueue work only reserves the right for a worker recipe to issue or continue an AgentRequest/ExecutorBridge attempt under the existing visible gates; it does not execute providers or tools by itself. ExecutorBridge remains the boundary that dispatches to runtime-private ExecutorBinding implementations after graph-visible request issuance, route/profile compatibility, permission, pressure, budget, and authorization have admitted the attempt. ExecutorBinding remains the boundary that talks to LLM/tool/human/browser/CLI/MCP/HTTP/SDK substrates and emits ExecutorStreamEvent, ExecutorOutcome, DataIssue, status, and audit material. workQueue completion records may summarize durable work handling or worker handoff, but they are not ExecutorOutcome and must not drive prompt continuation, AgentDecision, WorkItem mutation, retry/fallback, or tool-result joins unless explicit lowerers/projectors consume both queue and executor facts under policy. If a claimed work item cannot be dispatched because route, binding, credentials, permission, budget, sandbox, or provider availability fails, the worker recipe emits visible workQueue failure/retry/dead-letter material plus executor status/issues as appropriate; it must not silently requeue or fabricate ExecutorOutcome. Cancellation, timeout, reconcile, stale callbacks, duplicate terminal outcomes, and side-effect uncertainty remain governed by D274-D275/D286 at the executor layer, with queue cancellation/lease expiry used only for durable work ownership and scheduling.
rationale: D251 and D252 define ExecutorBinding and ExecutorBridge as the runtime-private dispatch boundary and graph-visible execution bundle; D274-D275 define executor idempotency, reconcile, cancellation, and timeout; D286 defines request/outcome vocabulary; D294/D299/D307/D324 define workQueue as generic messageBus-backed work lifecycle independent of executor types; D302-D304 define AgentDecision intents and lowerers; D327 defines the analogous WorkItem recipe. Some executor work needs queue semantics such as worker claiming, leases, retries, delayed dispatch, and dead-lettering, but putting provider dispatch into workQueue would create a hidden executor runtime and collapse queue lifecycle with execution outcome. A recipe over workQueue lets durable dispatch reuse the general queue substrate while preserving AgentRequest, ExecutorBridge, ExecutorBinding, ExecutorOutcome, and tool/LLM continuation boundaries.

layer: L6 / messaging generalization boundary after eventFlow and workQueue split / messaging application infrastructure
question: Which general application responsibilities should be owned by messageBus after the eventFlow/workQueue redesign, and which responsibilities must remain above messaging so messageBus does not become a workflow, queue, or executor runtime?
decision: messageBus owns the reusable retained messaging substrate and passive event vocabulary only. General responsibilities that may live in messaging include EventMessage and MessageEnvelope vocabulary; topic catalog and topic lifecycle command facts such as ensure-topic and close-topic; retained per-topic message streams with stable seq coordinates; publish command admission; subscription creation; independent subscription cursors; ack, seek, and close cursor commands; on-demand read projections such as topic(topic), catalog(), deadLetter(), and subscription.available(); strict topic policy by default with explicit opt-in auto-create policy; retained-log retention and command dedupe using shared policy vocabulary; status facts for accepted messaging operations; DataIssue facts for malformed, unknown-topic, closed-topic, duplicate, retention-gap, invalid-cursor, or policy-rejected messaging operations; and source coordinates suitable for eventFlow, workQueue, adapters, storage, and observability. messageBus must not own reducers, FSMs, projector execution, eventFlow high-water, WorkItem lifecycle, WorkItem action admission/application, approval or verification policy, queue claim/lease/retry/schedule/dead-letter/work completion, worker registries, AgentDecision, AgentRequest, ExecutorBridge, ExecutorBinding, provider lowering, tool execution, human inbox semantics, storage hydration, Canvas views, or domain solution commands. Schema validation in messaging remains explicit helper or policy evidence; messageBus does not silently reject or transform domain payloads unless the command/topic policy explicitly says so and emits visible issue/status material. messageBus may provide conventions, helper builders, and sourceRefs that make eventFlow and workQueue easier to compose, but those helpers emit or read messaging facts only and do not run domain projection, queue lifecycle, or executor dispatch. If a feature needs retained delivery and cursor movement only, it belongs in messageBus; if it needs projection semantics, it belongs in eventFlow/patterns; if it needs claim/lease/retry/work completion, it belongs in workQueue; if it needs domain mutation, it belongs in the domain solution; if it needs side-effecting execution, it belongs in executor/adapters.
rationale: D183 gives messaging passive EventMessage vocabulary, D259/D279 define messageBus as the single retained topic-log plus independent subscription-cursor substrate, D282/D284/D285/D287 lock topic policy, retention/dedupe, page params, and status taxonomy, D326 trims eventFlow back to projection, and D294/D299/D307/D324 place workQueue above messageBus for claimable work lifecycle. The redesign creates an opportunity to move generic delivery/cursor/retention/dedupe concerns down into messaging, but moving reducers, queues, domain actions, or executor behavior down would recreate the exact layering collapse D182 was designed to prevent. This boundary keeps messaging widely reusable while preserving eventFlow, workQueue, WorkItem, and Executor as distinct graph-visible layers.

layer: L6 / workQueue generalization boundary after eventFlow and executor split / workQueue application infrastructure
question: Which general application responsibilities should workQueue own after the eventFlow/messageBus/executor split, and which responsibilities must stay above it so workQueue does not become WorkItem, AgentDecision, ExecutorBridge, or domain workflow runtime?
decision: workQueue owns generic durable work lifecycle above messageBus and below orchestration, patterns, solutions, and executors. General responsibilities that may live in workQueue include messageBus-backed admission; deterministic accepted or rejected admission outcomes for poison-message handling; stable work identity and dedupe/idempotency policy; submit, claim, renew-lease, release, complete, fail, cancel, schedule, and expire-leases command facts; append-only WorkQueueRecord lifecycle facts; available/work/deadLetter read projections; claim ordering and replaceable claim policy; worker identity/capability/capacity evidence; lease/visibility timeout materialization from graph-local clock/deadline facts; retry/backoff and dead-letter disposition; delayed eligibility and scheduling; terminal queue completion/cancellation/dead-letter records; queue status and DataIssue taxonomy; page params and projection high-water over workQueue recordSeq; and reusable policy hooks for bounded-flow, size-capacity, retention, idempotency, redaction, audit, capacity, and rate-limit evidence. workQueue must not own EventMessage vocabulary, topic retained logs, subscription cursors, ack/seek semantics, eventFlow projectors, WorkItem lifecycle or action application, approval/verification domain semantics, AgentDecision, AgentDecision intents or lowerers, AgentRequest ledger truth, ExecutorBridge dispatch, ExecutorBinding execution, ExecutorOutcome terminal truth, provider/tool/human/browser/CLI/MCP execution, prompt continuation, Canvas/WorkspaceGraph UI state, storage hydration, or domain-specific workflow reducers. workQueue completion means queue work terminal disposition or worker handoff evidence, not business success, WorkItem mutation, executor result, prompt continuation, messageBus ack, or eventFlow projection update. Recipes may map WorkItem or executor facts into workQueue commands and map workQueue records back into evidence, proposals, statuses, or follow-up requests, but those recipes live above workQueue and must be explicit graph-visible projectors/lowerers. If a feature needs retained delivery and cursor movement, it belongs in messageBus; if it needs event-to-view projection, it belongs in eventFlow; if it needs durable claim/lease/retry/work ownership, it belongs in workQueue; if it needs domain mutation, it belongs in WorkItem/domain application; if it needs side-effecting execution and outcomes, it belongs in executor/adapters.
rationale: D294 names workQueue as generic queue substrate, D299 defines its command/record/status/issues core, D307 defines messageBus-backed admission, D311-D323 lock identity, claim, capacity, leases, retries, completion, cancellation, projections, command/record envelopes, and issue taxonomy, D324 makes workQueue an independent package/module, D327 maps WorkItem async-work onto workQueue recipes, D328 maps durable executor dispatch onto workQueue recipes, and D329 keeps messageBus limited to delivery/cursor substrate. This boundary captures the useful generalization: many layers need durable work ownership, leases, retries, scheduling, and dead-lettering. It also prevents the tempting but harmful collapse where queue completion becomes WorkItem mutation, ExecutorOutcome, prompt continuation, or domain success. Keeping workQueue generic makes it reusable while preserving graph-visible layering and single-source-of-truth responsibilities.

layer: L6 / eventFlow-workQueue recipe package surface and implementation order / CSP-8-CSP-9
question: Where should eventFlow, WorkItem-over-workQueue, and executor-over-workQueue recipes live in the package surface, and what implementation order should preserve the messageBus/workQueue dependency chain without mixing recipes into core infrastructure?
decision: GraphReFly keeps the optimized messageBus/workQueue/eventFlow/recipe split as focused static package surfaces. @graphrefly/ts/messaging owns messageBus plus EventMessage and MessageEnvelope vocabulary. @graphrefly/ts/work-queue owns the generic workQueue core, factory, commands, records, status, issues, and read projections. The reusable eventFlow projector-family pattern lives under a patterns/event-flow style subpath or equivalent pattern surface that consumes messaging facts and does not own messageBus or workQueue. WorkItem-over-workQueue recipes live under orchestration/work-item or solution-focused subpaths that consume eventFlow, messaging, and workQueue contracts; they must not be imported by workQueue core. Durable executor-over-workQueue recipes live under executors recipe subpaths or orchestration recipe subpaths that consume @graphrefly/ts/executors and @graphrefly/ts/work-queue; they must not be imported by workQueue core, messageBus core, or provider-neutral executor facts. Provider helpers and concrete adapters remain in focused adapter/helper subpaths, and Canvas/WorkspaceGraph UI renderers remain solution/framework/app consumers. No root export, monolithic agent module, dynamic plugin registry, or compatibility facade should combine messaging, workQueue, eventFlow, WorkItem recipes, executor recipes, provider bindings, and UI renderers into one public surface. Implementation order is: first messageBus according to D325 stage 1; second generic workQueue according to D325 stage 2 and D324; third eventFlow simplification according to D326 so it consumes messageBus without duplicate cursor/dead-letter/retention/queue semantics; fourth WorkItem async-work recipes over workQueue according to D327; fifth executor durable dispatch recipes over workQueue according to D328; and only after those, solution-level WorkspaceGraph/Canvas integrations may compose the recipes. Tests and examples should mirror that layering: messaging tests prove retained delivery/cursors; workQueue tests prove generic work lifecycle; eventFlow tests prove projection high-water over messaging sources; WorkItem recipe tests prove evidence/proposal mapping without mutation; executor recipe tests prove queue ownership plus ExecutorBridge/ExecutorOutcome separation. Any implementation pressure to move recipe-specific types into messageBus or workQueue core requires a new design review rather than quiet import-cycle or barrel-export drift.
rationale: D125 requires focused package subpaths and dependency direction; D283 and D309 define executor and AgentDecision package surfaces; D324 and D325 define workQueue package target and messageBus-to-workQueue implementation order; D326-D330 lock eventFlow simplification plus WorkItem/executor recipes and messageBus/workQueue generalization boundaries. The remaining risk is implementation convenience: recipes could be placed in the same module as workQueue or exported from the root, recreating the layering collapse the redesign just avoided. A package and implementation-order lock gives dev-dispatch a concrete sequencing target while preserving tree-shaking, optional provider dependencies, graph-visible composition, and clean ownership between infrastructure, patterns, orchestration recipes, executors, and UI solutions.

layer: L6 / workQueue admission ack command wiring / messageBus command-source boundary
question: How should workQueue emit messageBus ack commands after durable admission outcomes without cache peeking, imperative side channels, or expanding the messageBus public API surface?
decision: workQueue admission ack is derived from durable workQueue admission outcome records. Accepted or deterministic rejected admissions emit workQueue records first; a graph-visible admissionAckCommands node derives messageBus ack command facts from those records and attaches to the bound messageBus command stream through package-internal command-source/sink wiring. Acyclic sources may attach as internal command sources; the workQueue admission ack path uses a boundary-deferred command sink when direct composition would feed back into the same messageBus command stream. submit helpers only publish to the bound messageBus topic and never ack, append records, or move cursors. messageBus public API remains the D279 surface; no public transactional admit/ack API, dynamicHub facade, or queue-aware messageBus method is added. Boundary-deferred ack is an implementation mechanism for cyclic admission-ack topology after the durable record fact exists, not a second public ack API or hidden reducer-side cursor mutation.
rationale: D307 requires a durable workQueue-visible admission outcome before cursor advance, while D310 forbids submit/admission shortcuts and D279 keeps messageBus as a retained log plus independent subscription-cursor substrate. Deriving ack from records preserves replay honesty, describe-visible topology, and messageBus cursor ownership: record facts explain why a retained message was accepted or rejected, and ack remains an ordinary messageBus command fact. Keeping the command-source/sink attachment package-internal avoids expanding the messageBus public surface while still letting workQueue and messaging sugar compose through declared graph edges. Deferring on the cyclic workQueue admission-ack path avoids same-wave feedback/re-entry without normalizing reducer-side imperative ack calls or hidden cache reads.

layer: L6 / WorkItem authoring data surface / CSP-8 Layer B
question: How should human-created and LLM-spawned WorkItems carry summary, detail, acceptance criteria, verification steps, and pre-execution edits so product UIs and agent workflows share one explicit authoring contract?
decision: WorkItem authoring uses a shared WorkItemDraft data shape for human/API creation, human edits, LLM spawn proposals, and LLM patch proposals. The draft carries summary, detail or detail refs, acceptanceCriteria, verificationSteps or verificationPlan, and ordinary product fields such as kind, priority, tags, owner or assignee, deadline, custom fields, sourceRefs, and metadata. These fields are explicit message/event payload data, not metadata-only, prompt-only, executor-private state, workQueue payload truth, or hidden runner configuration. Human creation requests and LLM propose-work-spawn intents may both carry WorkItemDraft material, but LLM output remains a proposal. Human and LLM authors may propose changes to detail, acceptance criteria, verification steps, and other draft-owned fields for any WorkItem while the relevant WorkItem revision has not yet been admitted for execution, claimed as durable work, or otherwise used as execution input; authorization, concurrency, and allowed-field checks remain explicit apply policy. After execution starts for a revision, edits must be represented as a new revision or explicit WorkItem patch that triggers visible policy for re-verification, rescheduling, cancellation, requeue, or review rather than silently mutating already-executed work. Accepted application lowers draft or patch material into append-only WorkItem facts such as WorkItemCreated, WorkItemPatched, AcceptanceCriteriaChanged, VerificationPlanChanged, SpawnEmitted, and SpawnLinked under explicit apply policy. Verification steps may later be projected into WorkItemEffectRequested facts for human, tool, LLM, or workQueue execution, but the steps themselves are authoring data and do not execute, close, verify, spawn, patch, schedule, dispatch, or mutate WorkItems by themselves. Spawned children own their copied or transformed draft facts; parent provenance is represented by sourceRefs, spawnedFrom, and SpawnLinked rather than hidden inheritance. Downstream prioritization, dispatch, and scheduling policies may read the resulting WorkItem properties and metadata as ordinary graph-visible data, but those policies live in replaceable nodes or recipes above WorkItem authoring and workQueue core.
rationale: Power users building Linear/Jira-like products need ordinary users and agents to author the same inspectable WorkItem data, including detail, acceptance criteria, and verification steps. They also need human and LLM authors to revise unexecuted work before it is dispatched, without creating hidden imperative mutation paths or stale execution inputs. D182 already places summary, detail, acceptance criteria, and verification in the Layer B WorkItem solution; D188 requires explicit WorkItem fact names and spawn phases; D189/D217/D235 keep execution and result mapping evidence-first; D239 requires domain mutation through admitted action application; D327 keeps workQueue from becoming a WorkItem mutator. A shared draft payload gives good DX while preserving append-only WorkItem facts, graph-visible provenance, policy-controlled spawn/application, revision-aware editing, and a clean separation between authoring data, verification requests, execution outcomes, scheduling policy, and domain mutation.

layer: L6 / WorkItem prioritization dispatch and scheduling policy / CSP-8 Layer B-C
question: How can power users replace WorkItem prioritization, dispatch, and scheduling logic based on WorkItem metadata or properties without moving workflow policy into WorkItem core, workQueue, or executors?
decision: WorkItem prioritization, next-work selection, placement, dispatch preparation, and scheduling are replaceable graph-visible policy/projector nodes over WorkItem projections, metadata, properties, status, evidence, acceptance criteria, verification plans, deadlines, placement lanes, dependency state, queue availability, executor availability, capacity, and explicit policy facts. These policy nodes may emit placement decisions, schedule facts, WorkItemEffectRequested facts, WorkItem domain action proposals, workQueue submit command facts through WorkItem-over-workQueue recipes, or executor/request proposals through existing lowerers. They must not mutate WorkItems directly, append WorkItemEvents directly except through admitted action application, bypass WorkItem apply policy, bypass workQueue admission, claim work imperatively, dispatch ExecutorBindings, fabricate ExecutorOutcome, or hide scheduling loops/timers outside graph-visible facts. workQueue remains the generic durable work lifecycle substrate; executor recipes remain dispatch/outcome boundaries; product-specific priority, lane selection, next-work choice, and scheduling policy live above them as replaceable composition nodes. Default helpers may provide simple priority/deadline/metadata policies, but they are conveniences over the same fact contracts and may be replaced by power-user nodes.
rationale: Power users building Linear/Jira-like systems need to rank and route work using arbitrary WorkItem data, metadata, deadlines, capacity, executor availability, and product policy. D182 places WorkItem lifecycle and default views in Layer B; D188 allows custom projectors; D192 requires narrow indexes and explicit policy; D239 reserves mutation for action application; D327 maps WorkItem async work onto workQueue recipes; D328 keeps executor dispatch separate; D330 keeps workQueue generic; and D333 makes WorkItem authoring data explicit. Locking prioritization, dispatch preparation, and scheduling as replaceable policy nodes preserves GraphReFly's graph-visible composition model while avoiding a hidden workflow engine in WorkItem, workQueue, or executors.

layer: L6 / WorkItem scheduling policy output vocabulary / CSP-8 Layer B-C
question: What graph-visible output facts should replaceable WorkItem priority, placement, dispatch, and scheduling policies emit so downstream recipes can schedule work without hiding stale-input or mutation behavior?
decision: Replaceable WorkItem scheduling policies emit narrow policy facts such as WorkItemPriorityAssessment, WorkItemPlacementDecision, WorkItemScheduleDecision, and WorkItemDispatchIntent. These facts carry workItemId, revision or source event refs, policy refs, source refs, reason or audit material, priority or rank material when applicable, placement lane or target material when applicable, and scheduling material such as notBefore, deadline, requirements, and capacity hints. They are not WorkItemEvents and do not mutate WorkItems. Lowerers and recipes consume these policy facts plus current WorkItem projections to emit admitted WorkItem domain action proposals, WorkItemEffectRequested facts, workQueue submit commands, or executor/request proposals. All execution-producing outputs must be revision/source-ref aware so edits to detail, acceptance criteria, verification steps, or other execution inputs before claim or execution can stale, cancel, reschedule, requeue, or require review through visible policy rather than silently running old input. Policies may be replaced by power users and may use arbitrary WorkItem metadata/properties, but workQueue must receive only generic queue payload/options and must not import WorkItem projections to make domain priority decisions.
rationale: D333 makes WorkItem authoring data explicit and revision-sensitive, while D334 places priority, dispatch, and scheduling in replaceable policy nodes above WorkItem and workQueue. A small output vocabulary gives downstream recipes stable contracts without creating a hidden scheduler or overloading workQueue claim policy with domain metadata. Revision/source-ref awareness preserves stale-input safety when humans or LLMs edit unexecuted work. Keeping lowerers responsible for WorkItem actions, effect requests, queue commands, and executor proposals preserves D239, D327, D328, and D330 boundaries.

layer: L6 / WorkItem scheduling lowerers and stale-input policy / CSP-8 Layer B-C
question: How should WorkItem priority, placement, schedule, and dispatch policy facts lower into domain actions, effect requests, workQueue commands, or executor proposals without running stale input or hiding workflow behavior?
decision: WorkItem scheduling lowerers are explicit graph-visible projector nodes that consume D335 policy facts plus current WorkItem projections, revision or source refs, dependency state, queue and executor availability, and lowerer policy facts. Priority assessments are advisory facts for views, indexes, and downstream ranking and do not execute work by themselves. Placement decisions lower to WorkItem domain action proposals such as place or re-lane and remain subject to D239 admission/application. Schedule decisions lower to WorkItemEffectRequested facts, workQueue schedule or submit command facts through WorkItem-over-workQueue recipes, or visible status/audit facts according to explicit policy. Dispatch intents lower to WorkItemEffectRequested facts for verification, approval, human review, external sync, spawn review, or background evidence collection, or to executor/request proposals through existing AgentDecision/AgentRequest lowerers when the target is executor work. Lowerers must validate workItemId, revision or source event refs, idempotency material, policy refs, allowed target kind, placement lane, timing fields, requirements, capacity hints, and current WorkItem lifecycle/dependency state. If the referenced revision or execution input is stale because detail, acceptance criteria, verification steps, dependencies, placement, or other execution-relevant facts changed before claim or execution, the lowerer emits visible DataIssue/status/audit and follows explicit stale policy such as cancel, reschedule, requeue, emit replacement intent, or require review. Lowerers must not mutate WorkItems directly, append WorkItemEvents except through admitted action application, claim work, dispatch ExecutorBindings, fabricate ExecutorOutcome, or silently execute stale input.
rationale: D333 makes WorkItem authoring revision-sensitive, D334 makes prioritization, dispatch, and scheduling replaceable policy, and D335 defines narrow output facts. A separate lowerer boundary keeps policy choice, domain mutation, queue lifecycle, and executor dispatch distinct. Stale-input validation is necessary because humans and LLMs may edit detail, acceptance criteria, and verification steps before execution. Requiring explicit lowerers and stale policy preserves D239 domain action application, D327 WorkItem-over-workQueue recipes, D328 executor dispatch separation, and D330 workQueue genericity while giving product builders a safe way to customize next-work routing.

layer: L6 / WorkItem scheduling recipe package surface / CSP-8 Layer B-C
question: Where should WorkItem prioritization, placement, scheduling, dispatch-intent vocabulary, default policy helpers, and lowerers live in the package surface so product builders can replace policy without importing workQueue or executor semantics into WorkItem core?
decision: WorkItem scheduling vocabulary and recipes live under a solution-focused WorkItem subpath such as @graphrefly/ts/solutions/work-item/scheduling, not in workQueue core, executor core, messageBus, eventFlow, or the root export. The surface may export narrow policy fact types such as WorkItemPriorityAssessment, WorkItemPlacementDecision, WorkItemScheduleDecision, and WorkItemDispatchIntent; lowerer bundles that consume those facts plus current WorkItem projections and emit WorkItem domain action proposals, WorkItemEffectRequested facts, workQueue command facts through WorkItem-over-workQueue recipe wiring, executor/request proposals through existing lowerers, status, issues, and audit; and optional default policy helpers for common priority, deadline, placement, metadata, dependency, and verification-plan cases. Default policy helpers are replaceable conveniences only. Power users may supply their own policy/projector nodes that emit the same fact vocabulary. The scheduling recipe must not be imported by WorkItem core, workQueue core, executor core, messageBus, or eventFlow. It must not own queue admission, queue claim, executor dispatch, domain mutation, WorkItem event application, hidden timers, worker registries, or product-specific workflow engines. Any scheduling that needs durable delayed eligibility must lower to explicit workQueue schedule/submit commands or graph-visible time/clock facts through recipes rather than private timers.
rationale: D331 places WorkItem-over-workQueue recipes in solution-focused subpaths and keeps workQueue/executor recipes out of core infrastructure. D333-D336 now define WorkItem authoring data, replaceable scheduling policy, policy output vocabulary, and lowerer/stale-input behavior. A focused scheduling subpath gives product builders a usable Linear/Jira-like extension point while preserving dependency direction: WorkItem core owns domain facts and projections; scheduling policy lives above as replaceable composition; workQueue owns durable lifecycle; executors own dispatch/outcome boundaries. Keeping default helpers optional avoids baking one team's workflow into the reusable solution while still providing a practical starter path.

layer: L6 / WorkItem revision and execution-input identity / CSP-8 Layer B-C
question: How should WorkItem projections expose revision identity so scheduling lowerers, workQueue recipes, and executor recipes can detect stale detail, acceptance criteria, verification steps, or other execution inputs without treating every metadata change as execution-stale?
decision: WorkItem projections expose explicit revision coordinates derived from append-only WorkItem facts, including at least an authoringRevision and an executionInputRevision. Revisions are graph-visible projection data, not substrate protocol versions, global clocks, hidden mutable counters, or executor/workQueue state. authoringRevision advances when accepted WorkItem authoring facts change the WorkItem draft/projection. executionInputRevision advances when execution-relevant inputs change, including detail or detail refs, acceptance criteria, verification steps or verification plans, and dependency/source facts declared execution-relevant by policy. Product metadata or custom fields advance executionInputRevision only when explicit WorkItem policy marks them execution-relevant; otherwise they may still advance authoringRevision without staling already-prepared execution. WorkItem scheduling policy facts, dispatch intents, WorkItemEffectRequested facts, workQueue payloads, and executor/request proposals that may execute work must carry the relevant revision coordinate or source event refs. Lowerers compare carried revision/source refs against current WorkItem projections and emit visible issue/status/audit plus explicit stale policy when they no longer match. Spawned children own their own initial revision coordinates from accepted child WorkItem facts; parent changes stale child work only through explicit dependency/source policy, not hidden inheritance.
rationale: D333 makes detail, acceptance criteria, and verification steps explicit authoring data and allows pre-execution edits. D335 requires execution-producing outputs to be revision/source-ref aware, and D336 requires stale-input validation. A dedicated revision projection keeps this check cheap and explainable while avoiding over-invalidation from harmless metadata edits. Keeping revisions as projection data preserves eventFlow/WorkItem ownership, keeps workQueue generic under D330, and lets executor/workQueue recipes detect stale execution inputs without importing WorkItem reducers or reading hidden state.

layer: L6 / WorkItem authoring event vocabulary v0 / CSP-8 Layer B
question: What minimal WorkItem authoring facts should represent WorkItemDraft creation, edits, acceptance criteria, verification plans, and revision advancement without creating per-field event sprawl or hiding execution-stale changes?
decision: WorkItem authoring v0 uses a small bounded event vocabulary over explicit payload data. WorkItemCreated records an accepted WorkItemDraft initial state, including summary, detail or detail refs, kind, priority, tags, owner or assignee, deadline, custom fields, source refs, metadata, optional initial acceptance criteria, and optional initial verification plan. WorkItemPatched records accepted generic draft/projection changes through PatchSpec-style data for summary, detail refs, ordinary product fields, metadata, and custom fields. AcceptanceCriteriaChanged records replacement or patch material for acceptance criteria as a first-class fact. VerificationPlanChanged records replacement or patch material for verification steps/plans as a first-class fact. Helper request/proposal facts such as WorkItemCreateRequested or LLM spawn proposal payloads may carry WorkItemDraft, but accepted domain state is derived only from recorded WorkItem facts emitted through apply policy. Revision advancement is projection/status output derived from these facts, not a user-authored event required for correctness. The vocabulary must not expand into one public event type per arbitrary product field; product-specific fields use WorkItemPatched/custom fields plus policy-declared execution relevance when needed.
rationale: D188 already requires bounded WorkItem event names and cites WorkItemCreated, WorkItemPatched, AcceptanceCriteriaChanged, and VerificationResultRecorded. D193 rejects per-field/per-dimension event sprawl. D333 adds shared WorkItemDraft authoring data, and D338 requires projection-level authoringRevision and executionInputRevision. A small event vocabulary keeps the Linear/Jira-like API ergonomic while making AC and verification plans first-class because they drive verification and stale-input behavior. Keeping revisions derived preserves a single source of truth in append-only facts and avoids user-authored revision counters.

layer: L6 / VerificationPlan to WorkItemEffectRequested lowerer / CSP-8 Layer B-C
question: How should accepted WorkItem verification plans and acceptance criteria become executable verification requests without treating verification steps as hidden runners or direct WorkItem mutations?
decision: Verification execution is driven by an explicit graph-visible lowerer from current WorkItem projections and accepted verification plan facts to WorkItemEffectRequested facts. VerificationPlanChanged facts and initial verification plans in WorkItemCreated are authoring data; they do not execute by themselves. The verification-request lowerer consumes current WorkItem projection, acceptance criteria, verification plan or steps, executionInputRevision, dependency state, policy facts, prior verification evidence/results, and optional queue/executor availability. It emits WorkItemEffectRequested facts with effectKind:"verification" or narrower verification subkind, stable requestId/effectRunId/idempotencyKey, workItemId, executionInputRevision or source refs, step ids, AC refs, policy refs, limits, context refs, and source/audit refs. Each emitted request is an execution proposal/input fact only; WorkItem verification state changes still require evidence/result mapping and domain action application. If no verification plan exists, a step is manual-only, prerequisites are unmet, policy disallows auto-run, prior equivalent evidence is still valid, or the referenced execution input is stale, the lowerer emits visible status/DataIssue/audit such as needs-human-review, verification-unplanned, blocked-prerequisite, duplicate-suppressed, or stale-verification-input instead of silently running or closing work. Spawned WorkItems use the same lowerer after their accepted child WorkItem facts create their own projection and executionInputRevision; parent LLM output may propose a child verification plan, but only accepted child facts can drive verification requests.
rationale: D333 makes verification steps explicit WorkItem authoring data, D338 gives lowerers revision identity, and D339 makes VerificationPlanChanged a first-class recorded fact. D189 requires work-item effects to be graph-visible request projections rather than imperative runners, D217/D235 keep effect results evidence-first, D239 reserves verification state mutation for admitted action application, and D327 allows WorkItem verification tasks to use workQueue only through recipes. A dedicated lowerer keeps authoring, scheduling, execution, evidence, and mutation separate while giving both human-created and LLM-spawned WorkItems a uniform path from AC/verification steps to executable verification.

layer: L6 / Verification evidence and result mapping / CSP-8 Layer B-C
question: How should completed verification effects become WorkItem verification results, domain action proposals, human-review needs, or lifecycle changes without letting executor/workQueue completion mutate WorkItems directly?
decision: Verification outcomes return evidence-first. EffectRunResult facts, executor outcomes, or terminal workQueue records from verification work map first to WorkItemEvidenceRecorded with effectRunId, requestId, workItemId, executionInputRevision or source refs, verification step refs, acceptance-criteria refs, status, output/error/needs, issues, and audit refs. A separate verification-result mapper consumes WorkItemEvidenceRecorded plus current WorkItem projection, verification plan, acceptance criteria, executionInputRevision, prior verification results, and explicit verification mapping policy. It may emit VerificationResultRecorded facts, WorkItemDomainActionProposal facts such as mark-verified, mark-failed, require-review, close, reopen, patch, or relane, status, DataIssue, and audit. VerificationResultRecorded records the interpreted domain verification result for specific AC/step/revision coordinates; it is not raw executor output and does not itself mutate lifecycle unless later admitted/applied by D239 action application. Completed verification does not globally imply close, resolve, approve, verify, spawn, patch, or placement changes. Stale revision, missing policy, ambiguous AC coverage, partial step completion, failed required step, manual-review need, duplicate evidence, malformed output, policy mismatch, or unverifiable output emits visible issue/status/audit rather than best-effort mutation. Human review may be represented as verification result status or domain action proposal, but must remain graph-visible and policy-controlled.
rationale: D217/D235 make the default WorkItem effect result path evidence-first and conservative. D239 requires domain mutation through admitted action application. D333-D340 define authoring data, execution-input revision, verification plans, and verification request lowering. A dedicated verification-result mapper separates raw execution evidence from domain interpretation, keeps executor/workQueue completion from becoming business truth, and lets product builders decide whether verification evidence means verified, failed, needs review, blocked, close-ready, or evidence-only.

layer: L6 / AcceptanceCriteria and VerificationPlan data shape v0 / CSP-8 Layer B-C
question: What minimal data shape should WorkItem acceptance criteria and verification plans use so humans and LLMs can author them, policies can schedule them, and lowerers can execute them without turning them into prompt-only text or hidden runner configuration?
decision: Acceptance criteria and verification plans use compact data-first shapes inside WorkItemDraft, WorkItemCreated, AcceptanceCriteriaChanged, and VerificationPlanChanged payloads. AcceptanceCriterion v0 carries a stable criterionId, human-readable statement, optional required flag, optional sourceRefs, and metadata. VerificationPlan v0 carries stable plan identity or revision material and a list of VerificationStep values. VerificationStep v0 carries stepId, optional title/description, verifiesCriteriaIds, mode such as auto, manual, or hybrid, optional effectKind or verification subkind, optional goal/input material for WorkItemEffectRequested lowering, optional context refs, requirements/capacity hints, dependsOnStepIds, policyRefs, sourceRefs, and metadata. These shapes are authoring and policy data, not executable callbacks, provider prompts, tool bindings, queue payload truth, or domain mutations. Step ids and criterion ids are the stable coordinates used by verification request lowerers, evidence mapping, stale-input checks, and VerificationResultRecorded coverage. Missing ids, duplicate ids, dangling verifiesCriteriaIds, cyclic step dependencies, unsupported mode/effectKind, oversized inline data, or policy-incompatible goal material emit visible DataIssue/status/audit at validation or lowering boundaries rather than executing best-effort. Products may extend with metadata/custom fields, but execution relevance and scheduling behavior must be declared through policy rather than inferred from arbitrary metadata.
rationale: D333 makes AC and verification steps explicit WorkItem authoring data, D339 makes AcceptanceCriteriaChanged and VerificationPlanChanged first-class facts, D340 lowers verification plans to WorkItemEffectRequested, and D341 maps verification evidence back to interpreted results. A small data-first schema gives human and LLM authors a shared contract while preserving graph-visible validation, source refs, revision/stale tracking, and policy-based execution. Keeping callbacks, provider clients, prompt rendering, and runner handles out of these shapes preserves D189, D327, D328, and D330 boundaries.

layer: L6 / WorkItem authoring and verification validation status taxonomy / CSP-8 Layer B-C
question: How should WorkItem authoring, acceptance criteria, verification plans, scheduling policy facts, and verification lowerers report malformed, stale, missing, or policy-incompatible data without throwing protocol errors or silently skipping work?
decision: WorkItem authoring and verification validation problems are reported as graph-visible DataIssue/status/audit facts, not protocol ERROR, hidden exceptions, silent no-ops, or best-effort execution. The v0 taxonomy should cover malformed-draft, missing-required-field, invalid-patch, duplicate-id, dangling-ref, cyclic-dependency, unsupported-mode, unsupported-effect-kind, oversized-inline-data, policy-mismatch, missing-policy, stale-revision, stale-execution-input, blocked-prerequisite, verification-unplanned, manual-review-required, duplicate-suppressed, ambiguous-coverage, partial-coverage, unverifiable-output, unauthorized-author, unauthorized-target, and invalid-schedule. Status facts may classify these as rejected, deferred, blocked, needs-human-review, validation-warning, stale, duplicate, or policy-rejected. Constructors may throw only for programmer-invalid static helper configuration; runtime WorkItem facts, LLM proposals, human edits, queue records, executor outcomes, and policy facts should produce DataIssue/status/audit so the graph remains inspectable and recoverable. Validation status must carry workItemId when known, revision/source refs when relevant, policy refs when relevant, and offending field/path/step/criterion ids when available.
rationale: D184 establishes DataIssue/DataResult as passive DATA-level issue vocabulary distinct from protocol ERROR. D188/D193 require bounded WorkItem fact vocabulary; D333-D342 define authoring data, revisions, scheduling policy facts, verification lowerers, evidence mapping, and AC/verification shapes. A small validation/status taxonomy prevents runtime user/LLM data errors from becoming protocol failures and gives product builders visible hooks for human review, repair, reschedule, or rejection.

layer: L6 / A2UI durable schema boundary / React reference UI and Canvas product integration
question: If GraphReFly adds a durable Agent-to-UI JSON/schema/registry contract beyond the React-local AutoPanel widget catalog, what shape should it follow and where should the schema, catalog, renderer registry, boundary lowering, and capability metadata live?
decision: Durable GraphReFly A2UI work must align with the A2UI-style surface lifecycle, catalog, and data-model separation rather than promoting the React AutoPanel widget catalog into a long-term JSON standard. The recommended durable shape is a versioned stream of surface messages such as createSurface, updateComponents, updateDataModel, and deleteSurface, with component structure validated against a versioned catalogId and live values supplied through a separate JSON-Pointer-addressed data model. Catalog schemas and renderer registries are UI/product-layer contracts owned by React, Canvas, solution, or product packages; renderer registries map trusted component keys to local implementations and must not be supplied as arbitrary executable code by an agent. @graphrefly/ts boundaryManifest remains framework-neutral boundary inspection owned by the TS package under D238 and may be used only as an input to explicit lowering into A2UI data bindings or initial surface structure. BoundaryManifest must not grow product widget semantics, design-system component names, A2UI catalog vocabulary, OAuth/config presentation metadata, renderer registry material, or agent-generated UI instructions without a separate design review. GraphReFly should prefer a fixed-schema path first, where product-authored surfaces consume GraphReFly data-model updates, and treat dynamic agent-generated component trees as a later layer that requires catalog negotiation, schema validation, safe fallbacks, and client/server error reporting. A2UI capabilities and metadata belong to transport, product initialization, or solution-level negotiation, not the generic boundaryManifest vocabulary, unless a later BS-4 capability decision explicitly locks a narrow TS-owned generic capability taxonomy. The existing @graphrefly/react AutoPanel widgetCatalog/resolver remains a React-local trusted reference UI affordance, not the durable cross-agent schema contract.
rationale: The current @graphrefly/react BS-5 catalog is intentionally local reference UI: it proves trusted caller-supplied widgets without changing hook semantics, substrate behavior, or TS-owned boundary metadata. External A2UI v0.9.1 practice separates UI surface lifecycle, component catalog schema, data model updates, and transport capabilities; promoting a static widgets array or resolver keys into GraphReFly's durable schema would lose streaming/update semantics and blur data/render ownership. D238 keeps framework-neutral boundaryManifest in @graphrefly/ts while React owns live hooks and presentation. D240 and the Canvas/product split keep workspace UI state and renderer choices above the generic boundary layer. Keeping catalog/schema/renderer registry above boundaryManifest preserves single source of truth, avoids putting product/widget metadata into generic graph inspection, keeps agent output validateable and non-executable, and leaves a safe path for both fixed-schema production surfaces and later dynamic generated UI.

layer: L6 / boundary capability references / D238 boundaryManifest extension guard
question: How may boundary nodes expose capability requirements such as auth, permissions, config, or external resources without pushing OAuth flows, widget semantics, or product presentation metadata into the generic boundaryManifest vocabulary?
decision: Boundary capability metadata may enter the TS-owned @graphrefly/ts/inspection/boundary surface only as narrow generic capability references. A future boundary node extension may expose capabilities as data such as {id, kind, required, sourceRefs?}, where kind is a bounded generic category such as auth, permission, config, or resource and id is an opaque stable reference understood by a product or solution registry. The generic boundary layer must not own OAuth provider flows, credential material, config form schemas, widget selection, palette grouping, one-click-config copy, icons, design-system component names, or product-specific capability semantics. Boundary role inference remains structural under D238: writable source nodes are candidate inputs, unconsumed sinks are candidate outputs, and capability refs do not change input/output classification. React, Canvas, WorkspaceGraph, or product packages may map capability refs to OAuth flows, permission prompts, setup wizards, disabled states, or palette affordances through trusted registries. Capability refs may be derived from node meta only when the meta is strict-data and framework-neutral; richer product metadata stays in product registries or graph-visible solution facts above boundary inspection. Missing or unsatisfied capability is not a protocol ERROR and does not add a tier/message; it is surfaced as product status, DataIssue, or admission/setup policy at the consuming layer.
rationale: D238 deliberately keeps boundaryManifest structural and warns that capability, OAuth, config, widget, or product metadata requires later design review before extending BoundaryNode. BS-4 needs a fork half for OAuth and one-click config, but putting provider flows or widget instructions into the generic manifest would make @graphrefly/ts own presentation and app semantics. A small opaque reference vocabulary gives Canvas and React enough information to request setup while preserving TS ownership of only framework-neutral boundary inspection. Keeping capability satisfaction outside protocol ERROR/tier semantics preserves F-NO-IMPL-DEFINED and avoids turning boundary metadata into hidden execution policy. Product registries can evolve rapidly without freezing OAuth/config UI into the cross-runtime graph boundary contract.

layer: L6 / dynamic A2UI schema generation and catalog negotiation / product pipeline boundary
question: Where should dynamic A2UI component-tree generation, catalog negotiation, validation, AI-output lowering, and renderer registry ownership live after the fixed-schema A2UI data-model path was locked?
decision: Dynamic A2UI generation is a product or solution-layer pipeline above @graphrefly/react and @graphrefly/ts, not a generic boundaryManifest behavior, not a substrate feature, and not a root React binding primitive. The durable pipeline shape is: product-owned prompt or authoring input produces candidate A2UI surface messages; agent output is validated against the selected catalog schema before rendering; client capabilities and supported catalogIds are negotiated through transport/product initialization metadata; trusted renderer registries map catalog component keys to local UI implementations; validation/runtime failures emit visible error/status material and may fall back to text or fixed-schema surfaces. Dynamic component trees may consume GraphReFly boundary data-model lowering and capability refs, but they must not mutate boundaryManifest, import arbitrary React components from JSON, execute agent-supplied code, or embed secrets/credentials. Catalog schemas, schema managers, examples, validators, and repair loops may live in product, Canvas, or a focused optional subpath only after a concrete API review; the @graphrefly/react root remains the lightweight live binding/reference UI surface. Fixed-schema A2UI data-model lowering remains the safe first path; dynamic schema generation is a later layer that must prove catalog negotiation, validation, fallback, and error reporting before public API hardening.
rationale: D347 locks the A2UI-compatible surface/catalog/data-model separation and prefers fixed-schema surfaces first. External A2UI practice also separates catalog schemas, data model updates, and transport capabilities. Dynamic agent-generated UI adds a trust boundary: malformed JSON, unsupported catalogs, unknown components, schema mismatch, and arbitrary-code risk. Keeping this above boundaryManifest and outside the root React SDK preserves D238, keeps agent output validateable and non-executable, and lets product UX evolve without forcing @graphrefly/ts or @graphrefly/react to own full generative UI orchestration. A focused optional surface can be reviewed later when the validator/catalog/transport shape is concrete.

layer: L6 / WorkspaceGraph and Canvas durable public API boundary / D240 hardening
question: What should be locked before WorkspaceGraph or Canvas grows a durable public API for selection, layout, workspace placement, value/status overlays, React Flow or ELK rendering, and root exports?
decision: Durable WorkspaceGraph and Canvas APIs remain solution/product-layer surfaces over ordinary GraphReFly topology and graph-visible facts. WorkspaceGraph is a bundle or factory over an existing graph, not a Graph subclass, hidden runtime owner, storage owner, executor, or Canvas-owned graph. Canvas consumes WorkspaceGraph projections, boundary data, status, issues, audit, topology snapshots, and optional A2UI/capability facts; it may emit graph-visible command, proposal, policy, selection, placement, or input facts, but must not mutate WorkItems directly, claim workQueue records, dispatch ExecutorBindings, own generic boundary vocabulary, or hide topology changes through imperative side channels. Layout engines, React Flow, ELK, value/status overlays, viewport, selection, and workspace placement are renderer/product concerns and should live in Canvas/product packages or focused optional subpaths with explicit peer dependencies. Shared workspace state that must survive collaboration or replay should be modeled as graph-visible product facts or solution projections, while ephemeral viewport/UI affordances may stay local UI state. No root export, monolithic Canvas runtime, or reusable WorkItem/core import should mix Canvas renderer state with WorkItem, workQueue, executor, messageBus, or boundaryManifest core semantics. Any concrete public WorkspaceGraph/Canvas API must expose named handles/views/status/issues/extension slots and run a focused design review before long-term export.
rationale: D240 already locks WorkspaceGraph as a solution-level bundle and Canvas as a consumer, while D182/D204 keep renderer-like functionality downstream from reusable event-flow/work-item/context kernels. The next risk is implementation convenience: selection, layout, overlays, and placement could become a hidden Canvas runtime or push product nouns into generic WorkItem, boundary, or graph layers. Explicitly keeping heavy rendering dependencies and workspace UI state in product/focused optional surfaces preserves graph-first composition, tree-shaking, and inspectability. It also lets React Flow/ELK be swapped without changing substrate or boundary semantics.

layer: L6 / @graphrefly/react package surface and productionization policy / BS-8
