D379-D381 make persistent snapshot facts, revision acceptance, and conflict material explicit, while D382 makes CanvasScopeResolution the canonical output. Splitting input nodes preserves explainable topology, lets storage/router/product code remain caller-owned, and prevents a single setter from becoming an implicit controller for UI navigation, reload restore, conflict repair, and current scope mutation. An explicit precedence/mode avoids hidden race or arrival-order semantics when requested and persisted scope material coexist.

layer: L6 / tool provider adapter runtime retention concrete API shape / CSP-8 Layer C
question: What concrete TypeScript retention API shape should ToolProviderAdapterRuntime use so bounded runtime-private indexes reuse GraphReFly's shared policy vocabulary while preserving D362 visible run/attempt semantics?
decision: ToolProviderAdapterRuntime retention uses GraphReFly's D80 shared policy vocabulary over explicit runtime-private index categories rather than tool-provider-specific max-field dialects. The retention option exposes per-index policies for adapterInputs, runRequests, executions, runStatuses, and runIssues. Each index policy may use FIFO capacity via CapacityPolicy<'fifo'> or score-based retention via RetentionPolicy<Entry>, where maxSize remains ReactiveOpt<number> and score callbacks receive only exported bounded public lifecycle entry shapes for that index. Static maxSize values become constant graph-visible policy config; Node-valued maxSize values must be declared deps through a graph-owned runtime retention policy reader. Implementations may reuse D70 PolicyInputs/PolicyReader, trimHeadOverflow, and selectRetentionVictims, while each runtime index still owns trimming, gap detection, status/issues/audit emission, and execution safety. Execution retention-gap safety is preserved by treating adapterInputId plus monotonic attempt as the bounded replay coordinate: if a trimmed or missing execution proof covers an equal-or-lower attempt, replay emits retention-gap DataIssue/status and must not execute provider bindings. Runtime maintenance statuses use a separate ToolProviderAdapterRuntimeStatus fact for retention-trimmed, retention-gap, and invalid-retention-policy; run-scoped retention gaps may also emit ToolProviderAdapterRunStatus. Invalid policies or invalid scorer results keep the last-known-good effective policy, emit visible status/DataIssue/audit, and do not fall back silently, delete emitted graph facts, or protocol ERROR.
rationale: D371 locks tool-provider runtime retention as a Layer C runtime-index policy reusing D284 rather than a bespoke retention dialect. D80 already exposes shared ReactiveOpt, CapacityPolicy, RetentionPolicy, and ViewCachePolicy vocabulary, and D70 provides internal policy reader and victim-selection helpers while preserving structure-owned mutation. Reusing those shapes keeps the tool runtime aligned with existing @graphrefly/ts library policy surfaces, supports simple FIFO and custom score-based ordering, and avoids premature maxBytes/TTL semantics deferred under D293. Bounded public lifecycle entry shapes prevent retention scorers from observing provider raw output, runtime bindings, secrets, large artifacts, or sanitized text internals. The per-input monotonic attempt high-water rule preserves D362's visible retry model and prevents bounded retention from turning replay into hidden repeated execution.

layer: L6 / Canvas scope focused subpath public symbol list / D368-D386 follow-up
question: Which Canvas scope/navigation symbols should become the first durable public surface of the focused @graphrefly/canvas/scope-style subpath, and which current scaffold symbols should remain private?
decision: The first durable Canvas scope subpath exports only the focused scope/navigation contract: CanvasScopeModel, WorkGraphScopeModel, WorkspaceGraphScopeModel, CanvasScopeKind, WorkGraphSelectionKind, WorkGraphSelectionRef, WorkspaceSelectionReturnRef, CanvasReturnContext, WorkGraphReturnContext, WorkspaceGraphReturnContext, ScopeUnresolvedReference, ScopeActionIntent, CanvasScopeResolution and its conflict/status supporting data, PersistentCanvasScopeSnapshot, normalized snapshot key and sequence revision types, pure snapshot acceptance/conflict helpers, and pure transition/reconcile helpers for opening Workspace issues from WorkGraph selections, opening WorkGraphs from Workspace refs, returning to context, and validating/reconciling scope references. The subpath may also export a migrated durable Canvas scope bundle adapter only after it follows D382/D386 by exposing CanvasScopeResolution as canonical output, separate accepted/current scope, and distinct workspace/requestedScope/snapshotCandidates inputs. The current root-barrel workspace-scope re-exports, WorkspaceScopeBundle/WorkspaceScopeBundleOptions, createWorkspaceScopeBundle, fixtures, WorkspaceGraph UI/layout/panel symbols, React bindings, storage/router helpers, executor/work-item mutation helpers, and scaffold-only names remain private or non-durable until separately reviewed. Root exports may continue as private scaffold but must not be documented as the durable API.
rationale: D368 chooses a focused scope subpath and keeps root exports private scaffold; D370 splits pure model/transitions from the narrow bundle adapter; D372-D381 define resolution, snapshot, revision, conflict, and unresolved semantics; D382/D386 make the durable adapter shape incompatible with the current scope-only scaffold bundle. A focused minimum gives callers enough stable data and pure helpers to avoid copying restore logic while preventing Canvas scope from absorbing React, storage, routing, WorkspaceGraph mutation, executor behavior, or current scaffold convenience APIs.

layer: L6 / tool provider adapter runtime retention evidence horizon / CSP-8 Layer C
question: How should ToolProviderAdapterRuntime bound runtime-private retention proof evidence without allowing hidden replay or inventing a new retention dialect?
decision: Add an explicit bounded retentionEvidence horizon to ToolProviderAdapterRuntime retention. The horizon reuses D80 CapacityPolicy and RetentionPolicy vocabulary and is read through the graph-owned runtime retention policy reader like the existing D387 indexes. Evidence entries contain only bounded public lifecycle proof material such as adapterInputId, sequence, occurredAtMs, evidenceKind, and attemptHighWater. Trimming evidence never deletes emitted graph facts and never permits hidden execution. If execution proof evidence for an adapterInputId is evicted, the runtime must fail closed by removing or closing any retained executable adapter input for that coordinate; later requests that cannot be proven fresh emit visible retention-gap status, DataIssue, and audit material rather than executing bindings. RuntimeStatus continues to use retention-trimmed and retention-gap; horizon-specific meaning is carried by issue and audit codes plus bounded metadata.
rationale: D387 bounds lifecycle indexes but replay safety requires proof evidence such as adapter-input tombstones and per-input execution high-water. Leaving that evidence unbounded weakens the runtime-private memory-retention story, while silently evicting it would violate D362 and D387 by allowing old adapterInputId plus attempt coordinates to execute again. A bounded, fail-closed evidence horizon preserves D80/D284 policy reuse, keeps graph facts append-only, and makes the liveness tradeoff visible through ordinary Layer C status/issues/audit material.

layer: L6 / Canvas WorkspaceGraph topology projection focused surface / D240-D345 follow-up
question: What durable Canvas public surface should expose WorkspaceGraph issue/work-control topology projection without turning WorkspaceGraph into runtime topology, renderer ownership, or a hidden Canvas graph owner?
decision: WorkspaceGraph topology projection is a pure Canvas product-layer selector over WorkspaceGraph facts. The durable surface may extend @graphrefly/canvas/workspace-graph with WorkspaceTopologyNodeKind, WorkspaceTopologyEdgeKind, WorkspaceTopologyTone, WorkspaceTopologyNode, WorkspaceTopologyEdge, WorkspaceTopologyModel, WorkspaceTopologyOptions, and deriveWorkspaceTopology. These nodes and edges represent WorkspaceGraph issue/work-control projection only; they are not GraphReFly runtime nodes, substrate edges, execution status, renderer layout, storage, routing, executor behavior, or WorkItem mutation. The projection may map issues, queues, input gates, WorkGraphRefs, verification summaries, artifacts, memory, and regression/reference relationships into renderer-independent topology data, but React/UI components, layout/measurement bundles, fixtures, scope/card-feed bundles, and mutation helpers remain outside the focused durable surface.
rationale: D240 and D345 keep Canvas as a product/solution layer over ordinary GraphReFly topology and forbid hidden runtime ownership. The Workspace Graph handoff identifies the P0 missing slice as a pure topology model for issue/work-control semantics, while existing focused subpaths already separate WorkspaceGraph data selectors, card-feed projection, scope navigation, and Topology Lens interaction. Locking a pure projection surface prevents future renderers from inventing incompatible node/edge vocabularies or misusing GraphReFly runtime status, while avoiding a new React/layout/runtime owner.

layer: L6 / Canvas topology-to-scope entry helper / D368-D390 follow-up
question: Should Canvas expose a durable helper that resolves WorkspaceGraph topology projection nodes into Canvas scope-entry data?
decision: Canvas may expose resolveWorkspaceTopologyScopeEntry from the focused @graphrefly/canvas/scope subpath as a pure data-only adapter from WorkspaceGraph topology projection nodes or node ids plus a WorkspaceGraph snapshot into explicit Canvas scope-entry results. The helper must validate topology node ids against the current derived WorkspaceGraph topology, may return open-workspace-issue, open-work-graph, or unavailable results, and must preserve missing-node, missing-target, dangling-owner, unsupported-node-kind, and workspace-mismatch states as explicit unresolved/unavailable data. It must not live in or be exported from the focused @graphrefly/canvas/workspace-graph projection surface, must not create/load/route workspaces, mutate WorkItems or WorkspaceGraph facts, own storage/router/executor behavior, invoke React, or add renderer/layout semantics. Root package exports remain private scaffold.
rationale: D390 keeps WorkspaceGraph topology projection pure, while D368/D388 place durable Canvas scope/navigation in @graphrefly/canvas/scope. P1 Lens scope entry needs a single reusable reference-safe bridge from projected Lens nodes to existing CanvasScopeModel transitions without making topology nodes runtime authority or forcing UI/renderers to duplicate fallback logic. A focused scope export preserves single source of truth and keeps WorkspaceGraph projection, scope navigation, renderer/layout, storage, executor, and mutation boundaries separate.

layer: L6 / graph-visible public material boundary / CSP-8 Layer C
question: Should ToolProviderAdapterRuntime and adjacent AgentRequest ledgers expose separate sanitizer/evidence/status dialects, a public sanitizer API, or a locked internal graph-visible public-material contract?
decision: Layer C agent/tool runtime graph-visible material uses a canonical internal public-material boundary, not a public sanitizer API and not protocol behavior. The boundary owns provider-aware metadata/details/text sanitization, canonical SourceRef copying, DataIssue preservation plus details redaction, bounded runtimeStatus/audit metadata, and request material cloning/freezing before facts enter graph-visible ledgers. RuntimeStatus, DataIssue, audit, retentionEvidence, and run/request status facts share one evidence grammar: sourceRefs identify public proof coordinates, metadata carries bounded explanatory scalar/record material, issueCode links status/audit to DataIssue, and raw provider/runtime material is omitted or represented by D270 summary/ref artifact envelopes. Retention gaps, missing input, and evidence-horizon closure remain distinct DATA-level status/issue/audit material; they never become protocol ERROR and never permit hidden provider execution.
rationale: D360 and D362 keep provider runtime clients, raw responses, secrets, and large provider material out of graph DATA while allowing bounded public lifecycle text. D371, D387, and D389 require retention trimming and replay-proof loss to be graph-visible, fail-closed, and based on shared policy vocabulary. A single internal boundary prevents sanitizer/status/evidence drift across AgentRequest ledgers, adapter-input replay, runtimeStatus, audit, DataIssue, and retentionEvidence without making sanitizer helpers a misleading security boundary or expanding public API during CSP-8/CSP-9.

layer: L6 / tool provider adapter runtime public evidence coordinate / CSP-8 Layer C
question: Should ToolProviderAdapterRuntime expose runtime-private retention index keys as public status coordinates, omit keys entirely, or define a bounded public evidence coordinate shape?
decision: ToolProviderAdapterRuntime public evidence coordinates are typed DATA-level diagnostic coordinates, not runtime-private index keys. RuntimeStatus, DataIssue details, audit metadata, and retention evidence material should use sourceRefs plus typed fields such as index, adapterInputId, runId, attempt, issueCode, evidenceKind, and gapKind as the public coordinate. The optional status key and metadata key are diagnostic display material only: they must be bounded public text, must not be required for replay correctness, and should use a stable opaque summary for long or potentially private internal keys rather than exposing raw runtime-private key strings. Trimming, missing proof, invalid policy, and evidence-horizon closure continue to surface through retention-trimmed, retention-gap, invalid-retention-policy, DataIssue, and audit facts; they never become protocol ERROR and never permit hidden execution.
rationale: D371 and D387 make retention indexes runtime-private and visible statuses explanatory. D389 requires evidence loss to fail closed while keeping emitted graph facts append-only. D392 locks a canonical public-material boundary and shared evidence grammar. Treating sourceRefs and typed coordinate fields as authoritative avoids leaking or over-promising internal Map keys, while retaining a bounded diagnostic key keeps debugging useful without expanding public API or changing protocol behavior.

layer: L6 / tool provider adapter runtime absence and retention-gap taxonomy / CSP-9 Layer C
question: How should ToolProviderAdapterRuntime distinguish ordinary missing input, request-admission failures, retention gaps, and closed retention-evidence horizon without expanding public status kinds?
decision: ToolProviderAdapterRuntime locks absence and retention-gap taxonomy over the existing public status vocabulary. missing-input means an adapter input is currently absent and the runtime has no retained proof that the absence is caused by retention trimming, execution high-water evidence, or a closed retention-evidence horizon; later graph-visible input may repair it. retention-gap means the runtime has retained evidence that the required adapter input, request, execution proof, or retention evidence cannot safely prove freshness or replayability because bounded retention removed needed material or the retention-evidence horizon is closed; provider execution must fail closed. Closed retention-evidence horizon is represented as a retention-gap subtype through issue code, sourceRefs, and bounded metadata such as gapKind, not as a new run status or runtimeStatus kind. missing-request, stale-request, and mismatched-request remain request-admission, readiness, or identity-shape outcomes and must not be used as retention evidence substitutes. runtimeStatus remains runtime-maintenance diagnostic material, while runStatus remains run-scoped admission/execution material; neither becomes protocol ERROR for these Layer C conditions.
rationale: D362 requires real retries and repeated executions to be explicit run/attempt facts rather than hidden adapter behavior. D371, D387, and D389 make retention trimming, replay proof loss, and evidence-horizon closure graph-visible and fail-closed while keeping runtime indexes private. D392 and D393 establish a shared public evidence grammar using sourceRefs, typed coordinates, issue codes, and bounded metadata. Locking the taxonomy prevents future runtime paths from downgrading retention proof loss into ordinary missing input, inventing new public status strings for each gap subtype, or conflating request-shape failures with retention evidence.

layer: L6 / dashboard-private Workbench session ledger and projection lifetime / CSP-8
question: How should CSP-8 Workbench model session ledger lifetime, projection index updates, and dashboard-private persistence without creating a public Canvas, WorkspaceGraph, runtime, storage, or protocol contract?
decision: CSP-8 Workbench uses a dashboard-private append-only session ledger for emitted WorkbenchCommand, CommandResult, ProjectorRun, ViewProjection, provenance, action, run, issue, audit, and bounded material-ref facts. Already emitted session facts are not deleted or rewritten. The Workbench may maintain a dashboard-private active projection index that selects the latest applicable ViewProjection for Queue, Execution, Ledger, filters, disabled reasons, and triage views; updating that index is projection selection, not graph fact deletion or runtime retention. Projection index updates must derive only from graph-visible dashboard facts plus dashboard-private Workbench policy facts, and any visible index/compaction event must itself append bounded dashboard-private facts. Workbench may persist a bounded dashboard-private local/session snapshot for UI continuity, but that snapshot restores only Workbench session/UI facts and active projection index material. It must not claim Graph restore/hydration, WorkspaceGraph ownership, Canvas public API, provider execution replay, hidden retry, or retention-gap repair; reload from a snapshot cannot execute provider bindings or convert missing/stale/mismatched/request-admission material into retention evidence.
rationale: This preserves the useful operations-panel shape while respecting D359-D394: runtime-private provider material stays out of graph DATA, retry/attempt lifecycle stays visible, retention evidence gaps remain fail-closed and distinct from missing/stale/mismatched request states, and emitted graph-visible facts remain append-only. Separating session ledger, active projection index, and bounded dashboard-private snapshot persistence prevents projection compaction from becoming deletion of graph facts, a durable runtime ledger, WorkspaceGraph ownership, Canvas API, or provider replay mechanism.

layer: L6 / dashboard-private Workbench operation catalog and triage / CSP-8
question: How should CSP-8 Workbench derive command availability, disabled reasons, and triage actions without scattering UI handler rules or creating a public command/runtime API?
decision: CSP-8 Workbench uses dashboard-private WorkbenchOperationPolicy and TriageProjection facts to derive command availability, disabled reasons, idempotency/no-op/terminal states, generated fact kinds, and issue-code triage actions. Operation policies are internal dashboard trace/policy material only; they are not public Canvas commands, WorkspaceGraph APIs, provider runtimes, WorkItem mutators, or protocol behavior. Triage keeps policy-denied, approval-needed, retention-gap, missing-input, stale-request, mismatched-request, failed, timeout, and canceled as distinct visible classes. retention-gap is inspect-only/fail-closed and must not enable retry repair; missing-input may request input but must not substitute for retention evidence; policy-denied cannot be bypassed by UI approval. Queue, Execution, Ledger, buttons, and disabled reasons must derive from visible dashboard facts plus these dashboard-private policy facts.
rationale: The current Workbench already appends visible command/result/projector/provenance facts, but command grammar and triage semantics are still partly encoded in UI handlers. Centralizing them as dashboard-private facts keeps the internal operations panel inspectable and product-like while preserving D359-D395 boundaries: no runtime-private material in graph DATA, no hidden retry/fallback, no WorkItem/domain direct mutation, no retention taxonomy collapse, no public Canvas/WorkspaceGraph/runtime surface, and no protocol/spec change.

layer: L6 / WorkItem spawn proposal and creation admission / CSP-8 Layer B
question: What should be the canonical proposal path for manual, LLM-assisted, linked, and policy-generated WorkItem creation?
decision: WorkItemSpawnProposed is the canonical create proposal for WorkItems. It covers top-level manual creation, LLM-assisted intake, linked or child creation, and policy/helper-generated repair or follow-up work. WorkItemDomainActionProposal with spawn-proposed or spawn-child remains an action over an existing WorkItem and may lower into WorkItemSpawnProposed after admission; it is not the canonical representation for top-level create because top-level create has no existing target WorkItem. Accepted creation lowers through explicit admission/application into WorkItemCreated and, when needed, relationship/link facts. Canvas may emit or display WorkItemSpawnProposed material but must not directly mutate WorkItems or introduce a Canvas-private create proposal API.
rationale: This preserves D333's shared WorkItemDraft authoring contract, D188/D193's bounded WorkItem vocabulary, D358's proposal/admission boundary for repair spawning, and D240/D345's Canvas no-mutation boundary. It avoids fake workspace target ids in WorkItemDomainActionProposal and prevents Canvas from becoming a separate WorkItem creation authority. It also gives manual Side Panel intake, later LLM-assisted classification, linked WorkItem creation, and failure-to-repair helpers one reusable proposal path without changing the wave protocol or spec.

layer: L6 / Canvas Workspace WorkItem type catalog and policy customization / CSP-8 Layer B
question: How should Canvas Workspace support user-customizable WorkItem types and policies without hardcoding issue enums or creating a Canvas-private WorkItem authority?
decision: Canvas Workspace represents WorkItem type customization as a workspace-level type catalog and policy profile over the existing WorkItemDraft.kind string and customFields shape. Default user-facing seed types are Task, Spike, and Review, but they are not a closed enum and may be renamed, hidden, reordered, or extended by workspace/project policy. Runtime/status taxonomies such as missing-input, retention-gap, stale, mismatched, and policy-denied are not default WorkItem types; they remain visible issue/status/actionability reasons that projections may map into attention, recommended actions, evidence, and debug sections. Canvas projections may consume type catalog and policy facts to derive attention dashboard groups, side-panel cards, action availability, required fields, and LLM-assisted draft classification, but Canvas must not directly mutate WorkItems, bypass WorkItemSpawnProposed/admission/application, or import dashboard-private OperationPolicy/TriageProjection as public API.
rationale: @graphrefly/ts already exposes WorkItemDraft.kind and customFields as open authoring data, so a Canvas-specific enum would duplicate truth and block Linear/Jira-style customization. D397 makes WorkItemSpawnProposed the canonical creation proposal and keeps Canvas out of direct mutation. D390 keeps WorkspaceGraph as a pure projection surface, while D395-D396 keep dashboard Workbench policy/triage private. A data-first catalog/profile gives Canvas usable defaults while preserving user customization, graph-visible explainability, and admission boundaries without changing protocol behavior.

layer: L6 / Canvas Workspace Side Panel card and section model / CSP-8 Layer B
question: How should Canvas Workspace structure Side Panel information without turning it into fixed regions, scattered cards, or a dashboard-private inspector?
decision: Canvas Workspace Side Panel uses a sticky Selection Card plus one consolidated WorkItem Details Card whose content is organized as collapsible sections. Section kinds are stable rendering/component slots, not fixed panel positions and not a closed dashboard-private information architecture. Required input, blockers, and highest-priority recommended actions may auto-expand by default; evidence, context, linked WorkGraph, artifacts, policy/admission, recent activity, and debug material default collapsed unless user preference or immediate attention policy expands them. User collapse/expand preference is UI preference data keyed by actor/workspace/card or section identity and must not become WorkItem truth. Debug material appears only in an explicit Debug section/card path and is opened by deliberate Debug interaction; raw runtime/private/provider/client/subprocess/credential material still must not enter graph-visible data. Side Panel actions emit proposal/action-intent/admission-facing facts and never directly mutate WorkItems, WorkspaceGraph facts, runtime state, provider execution, or Canvas topology.
rationale: The existing Canvas scaffold proves that a reactive card feed is easy to compose, but many independent cards recreate a dashboard cockpit and raise information load. The Workspace product goal is to compress graph/runtime/verification facts into the few things the user must act on, with Why/Evidence and Debug available on demand inside the Side Panel. A consolidated details card preserves a stable component vocabulary while letting policy, WorkItem type, selected object, evidence, and user preference determine visibility and ordering. This respects D397 WorkItem creation/admission boundaries, D398 user-customizable type/policy, D390 pure WorkspaceGraph projection, and D395-D396 dashboard Workbench privacy boundaries without changing protocol behavior.

layer: L6 / Canvas Workspace Attention Dashboard projection / CSP-8 Layer B
question: How should Canvas Workspace organize the default WorkItem surface without hardcoding board lanes or exposing dashboard-private triage as product IA?
decision: Canvas Workspace default surface is an Attention Dashboard projection over WorkItems, visible status/issues/evidence, workspace type catalog, workspace policy profile, and actor/filter preferences. Default groups are Needs me, Review, Waiting, and Recent, but they are configurable projection groups, not WorkItem lifecycle states, queue truth, fixed board lanes, or a closed enum. A WorkItem may match multiple groups; projection policy owns ordering, dedupe, and whether an item appears in its highest-priority group or multiple filtered groups. All WorkItems remains a secondary list/board/search surface for finding and organizing work, while Topology Lens remains an overlay for graph/trust/debug inspection rather than a separate default page. Existing Canvas WorkspaceIssueBoard/queue scaffold and dashboard Workbench TriageProjection may inform default actionability rules, but dashboard-private fixtures, OperationPolicy, and TriageProjection must not become public Canvas API or main workspace data.
rationale: The Workspace product goal is attention reduction: users should first see what needs action, review, waiting awareness, or recent context, while graph/runtime/verification details stay compressed into WorkItem projections and Side Panel sections. Existing board/queue scaffold is useful as a secondary organizational view, but making it the default would recreate a dense dashboard cockpit and conflict with D398 user-customizable type/policy. D399 places details, evidence, and debug in the Side Panel; D390 keeps WorkspaceGraph topology as projection; D395-D396 keep Workbench private. A configurable Attention Dashboard gives Canvas a simple default without freezing Linear/Jira-like customization or changing protocol behavior.

layer: L6 / Canvas Workspace WorkItem spawn admission and application / CSP-8 Layer B
question: How should Side Panel, manual, LLM-assisted, and linked WorkItem creation become WorkItemCreated without Canvas mutation, fake parent WorkItems, or direct runtime authority?
decision: WorkItemSpawnProposed remains the canonical proposal fact for WorkItem creation, while accepted creation flows through an explicit spawn admission/application path before emitting WorkItemCreated. Manual Side Panel intake, LLM-assisted classification, policy/helper follow-up, and existing-WorkItem child or linked creation may produce WorkItemSpawnProposed material; none may directly emit WorkItemCreated, mutate WorkItems, bypass admission, or use a fake workspace/parent WorkItem to satisfy an action API. Spawn admission consumes the proposal plus workspace type catalog, workspace policy profile, actor/capability evidence, user confirmation when required, idempotency material, and current visible WorkItem projections to admit, reject, defer, merge, or mark duplicate creation. Spawn application consumes only admitted proposals, validates draft/type-policy/idempotency/proposedWorkItemId/duplicate constraints, and emits WorkItemCreated plus explicit relationship/link facts only through a separately reviewed relationship vocabulary. Until that link vocabulary is locked, parentWorkItemId and sourceRefs on a proposal are creation intent/provenance, not durable relationship truth. WorkItemDomainActionProposal spawn actions remain actions over an existing WorkItem and may lower into this same spawn proposal/admission/application path; they are not the top-level create representation.
rationale: D397 already makes WorkItemSpawnProposed the canonical create proposal, while the existing @graphrefly/ts WorkItemDomainActionProposal path requires an existing target WorkItem and is therefore the wrong top-level create authority. D398 requires user-customizable type catalog and policy profiles, D399 requires Side Panel actions to emit proposal/admission-facing facts instead of mutation, and D400 keeps the Workspace surface projection-based. Separating proposal, admission, and application lets manual creation and later LLM-assisted intake share one path, preserves idempotency and policy visibility, avoids Canvas-private create APIs and fake parent ids, and keeps linked WorkItem relationship truth out of metadata until the relationship model is explicitly designed.

layer: L6 / WorkItem relationship facts and link projection / CSP-8 Layer B
question: How should WorkItem relationships such as parent-child, blocking, related, duplicate, and spawned-from be represented without hiding truth in metadata or Canvas topology edges?
decision: Durable WorkItem relationship truth is represented by explicit append-only WorkItem link facts such as WorkItemLinked and WorkItemUnlinked plus a derived WorkItemLink projection. Link facts carry fromWorkItemId, toWorkItemId, an open linkKind string, direction or inverse semantics, sourceRefs, bounded metadata, and idempotency/provenance coordinates where needed. linkKind is interpreted through a workspace-level link type catalog and policy profile; default seed kinds may include parent-child, blocks, related, duplicate, and spawned-from, but these are not a closed enum and may be renamed, hidden, extended, or policy-mapped by the workspace. Structural rollup, dependency/blocking, duplicate identity, related context, and spawn provenance are distinct relationship semantics and must not substitute for one another. parentWorkItemId, childWorkItemId, linkParent, and sourceRefs in spawn/create proposals are intent, policy input, or provenance until admitted application emits explicit link facts. Canvas Side Panel, Attention Dashboard, All WorkItems, and Topology Lens consume WorkItemLink projections and may display or filter by relationship semantics, but Canvas does not own link truth or mutate links directly. Invalid endpoints, duplicate links, dangling refs, unauthorized links, policy mismatch, unsupported linkKind, and disallowed cycles emit graph-visible status/DataIssue/audit material rather than protocol ERROR.
rationale: D188/D193 bound WorkItem event vocabulary while allowing relation kinds in payload data, and D239 requires links to be produced by admitted action application rather than hidden mutation. D397-D401 route creation through WorkItemSpawnProposed and explicit admission/application, but they leave relationship truth intentionally unmodeled. Keeping links as explicit facts and projections prevents metadata fields from becoming unqueryable truth, prevents Canvas topology edges from becoming domain state, preserves the difference between parent structure, dependency, duplicate, related context, and provenance, and lets Workspace policy shape how relationships affect attention without changing the wave protocol or introducing dashboard-private APIs.

layer: L6 / Workspace link type catalog and attention projection policy / CSP-8 Layer B
question: How should WorkItem link kinds affect the Attention Dashboard and Side Panel without making every relationship noisy or hardcoding Canvas link enums?
decision: Workspace link behavior is governed by a workspace-level link type catalog and projection policy over open WorkItemLink linkKind strings. The catalog owns display labels, inverse labels, directionality, default visibility, default collapse behavior, allowed endpoint constraints, cycle policy when relevant, and projection effects such as attention-needs-me, attention-waiting, attention-review, side-panel-context, topology-edge, provenance-only, duplicate-suppression, or navigation-rollup. Default seed link kinds may include parent-child, blocks, related, duplicate, and spawned-from, but these are configurable seeds rather than closed enums. By default, blocker/waiting relationships, duplicate/merge confirmation, relationship policy review, dangling refs, conflicts, and unsupported or unauthorized links may affect Attention Dashboard groups; parent-child navigation, related context, spawned-from provenance, historical provenance, weak references, and source/evidence references default to Side Panel or Topology Lens context rather than attention. Unknown custom link kinds default to context-only unless workspace policy explicitly grants stronger projection effects. Dashboard Workbench triage rules may inform defaults, but dashboard-private OperationPolicy/TriageProjection and fixture scenarios must not become Canvas link policy or public API.
rationale: D400 makes Attention Dashboard a configurable projection rather than a fixed board, and D402 makes link truth explicit while keeping linkKind open and workspace-customizable. Without a separate catalog/policy layer, product code would either hardcode blocks/duplicate/parent semantics or flood users with every relationship. Separating relationship identity from projection effect lets Canvas stay useful out of the box while allowing Linear/Jira-like customization, preserving the Side Panel as the place for contextual relationships, and keeping Topology Lens as an overlay rather than relationship truth or inbox logic.

layer: L6 / Canvas Side Panel WorkItem Details section priority and collapse policy / CSP-8 Layer B
question: How should Canvas Side Panel prioritize WorkItem information without turning every information type into a fixed card or dashboard cockpit?
decision: Canvas Workspace Side Panel uses a sticky Selection Card plus one primary WorkItem Details Card whose contents are section render slots ordered and expanded by projection policy. Sections are stable component slots, not fixed positions, fixed panel regions, or a closed information architecture. Section visibility, ordering, tone, and default expansion derive from attention reason, workspace policy, WorkItem type catalog, link type policy, selected object, actor preference, and user collapse/expand preference. Required input, primary recommended action, current blocker/waiting reason, duplicate/merge confirmation, relationship conflict, and currently blocking policy/admission reason may auto-expand. Summary/detail, status, type/owner/priority, acceptance criteria, relevant links, artifacts, verification summary, recent activity, Why/Evidence, and policy/admission material are available as sections but default to collapsed unless they are needed for the current action. Debug material is deliberate-open only, defaults collapsed, and must not enter the default workflow. User collapse/expand preference is UI preference data, not WorkItem truth, and must not delete, rewrite, or hide graph-visible facts from projections. Existing WorkspaceCardKind/card-feed scaffold may inform section components, but it should migrate away from many fixed peer cards as the durable Side Panel IA.
rationale: D399 already consolidated the Side Panel into Selection plus WorkItem Details, while D400-D403 make attention, type, and link behavior policy-driven and customizable. The current Canvas card-feed scaffold proves useful render components but its fixed peer-card order risks reproducing the paused dashboard Workbench cockpit and overloading users with context. A section priority/collapse policy keeps the user focused on what requires action, preserves Why/Evidence and Debug on demand, remembers UI preference without corrupting WorkItem facts, and lets custom WorkItem/link policy change the Side Panel without creating a new Canvas mutation authority or public dashboard API.

layer: L6 / Canvas Side Panel input drafts and proposal lowering / CSP-8 Layer B
question: How should Side Panel user input, console interaction, and later LLM assistance enter Workspace facts without direct mutation or runtime authority?
decision: Canvas Side Panel is a user-facing input and console surface, not an executor, runtime binding, WorkItem mutator, or hidden command bus. Side Panel interactions first produce local or graph-visible input drafts and action intents, then lower on explicit submit into graph-visible proposal/intake facts such as WorkItemSpawnProposed, WorkItemDomainActionProposal, WorkItem link proposals, required-input response proposals, or other reviewed domain-specific proposal facts. Drafts are editable, cancelable, and may be enriched or classified by LLM helpers; drafts become graph-visible only when collaboration, recovery, audit, or policy requires it. Submitted proposals, admission decisions, and application outputs are graph-visible and append-only. LLM helpers may classify, fill, summarize, suggest links, suggest WorkItem kinds, or propose actions from Side Panel context, but they must not directly emit WorkItemCreated, WorkItemPatched, WorkItemLinked, input-response truth, admission, or application facts, and they must not bypass policy, capability, user confirmation, or admission. Side Panel actions such as provide-input, request-input, create WorkItem, patch fields, add link, mark duplicate, or trigger recommended action lower into proposal/admission/application paths rather than callback mutation. Side Panel must not connect directly to real provider, MCP, CLI, bash, file-edit, URL, credentials, SDK, subprocess, or transport runtime, and must not silently select fake/demo fixture data for the main Canvas workspace.
rationale: D397-D401 establish WorkItem creation and mutation through proposal/admission/application, D402-D403 route relationship truth through link facts and link policy, and D404 makes Side Panel the focused place for action and context. The existing Canvas Side Panel callback/actions scaffold is useful UI plumbing but is not a durable domain boundary. A draft-to-proposal model gives the current manual product a simple path while allowing later LLM-assisted classification and filing without making the LLM or Canvas UI an authority. It preserves visible causality, supports collaboration/recovery only when needed, keeps fake fixtures out of the main workspace, and maintains the hard boundary between product input, domain facts, admission, application, and runtime/provider execution.

layer: L6 / Workspace Required Input gate and response admission / CSP-8 Layer B
question: How should Canvas Workspace represent required user input without conflating missing-input, retention gaps, human-task execution, WorkItem patches, or UI callbacks?
decision: Required Input is a graph-visible Workspace/WorkItem input gate with explicit request, response proposal, admission/application, and satisfied or rejected status facts. It is not a plain WorkItem field, not a dashboard triage category, not a human-task executor request by itself, not an AgentNeed by itself, and not a Side Panel callback mutation. Required input requests may be projected from WorkItem type required fields, workspace policy, AgentNeed/effect evidence, verification results, link policy, or other visible status facts. Side Panel user forms, human executor outcomes, LLM suggestions, artifacts, or evidence may produce required-input response proposals, but they do not satisfy the gate directly. Admission/application consumes the request, response proposal, current WorkItem projection, policy, actor/capability evidence, sourceRefs/evidenceRefs/artifact refs, and stale/revision coordinates, then emits a satisfied response fact or visible rejection/status/DataIssue/audit material. Responses may carry bounded inline values or summary/ref material under size/redaction policy. Ordinary missing-input gates may be satisfied by admitted responses; retention-gap, closed evidence horizon, stale request identity, mismatched request, and request-admission failures remain distinct and cannot be repaired by an ordinary input response unless a separately visible evidence recovery or request repair path proves the needed material. Required Input sections in the Side Panel may auto-expand, while Why/Evidence and Debug material about the gate stays collapsible inside the WorkItem Details Card.
rationale: D394 keeps missing-input, retention-gap, stale, mismatched, and request admission distinct. D217/D235 map effect results to evidence by default, D230 models human work as executor requests, D333 keeps WorkItem authoring fields separate from execution, D343 requires visible validation/status for malformed user data, and D405 routes Side Panel input through drafts and proposals. A dedicated input gate lets Canvas give users a simple form for missing information while preserving graph-visible causality, admission, replayability, evidence boundaries, and the fail-closed retention taxonomy. It also lets human-task outcomes and LLM suggestions contribute responses without making either one the source of domain truth.

layer: L6 / Canvas Recommended Action views and Side Panel action intent lowering / CSP-8 Layer B
question: How should Canvas Workspace recommend and trigger user actions without turning UI buttons into commands, hardcoded enums, or runtime executors?
decision: Canvas Recommended Actions are projection/view material derived from visible WorkItem projections, Required Input gates, WorkItemLink projections, evidence/status/DataIssue facts, workspace type/link/action policy, actor/capability context, and user preferences. A RecommendedActionView may carry label, description, tone, priority/rank, disabled reason, confirmation requirement, form schema or draft seed, target refs, and lowering hints, but it is not a command, executor binding, mutation, or admission. User clicks or form submissions in the Side Panel produce a local or graph-visible SidePanelActionIntent or equivalent draft/intent fact, which then lowers through explicit domain paths such as WorkItemSpawnProposed, WorkItemDomainActionProposalIntake, required-input response proposal, WorkItem link proposal, admission decision proposal, or UI navigation intent. UI navigation actions such as opening evidence, topology, references, or artifacts may remain UI-local unless collaboration, recovery, or audit requires graph-visible intent. Domain mutation, input satisfaction, link truth, create, patch, review/approval, merge/defer/reject, and verification changes require proposal/admission/application and must not be performed by the RecommendedActionView or button handler. LLM helpers may suggest, rank, summarize, or prefill recommended actions, but they must not execute, admit, apply, bypass policy, or connect runtime providers. Existing Canvas WorkspaceActionId and dashboard Workbench OperationPolicy/TriageProjection may inform default seeds, labels, and disabled-reason language, but they are not durable closed Canvas enums, public policy APIs, runtime commands, or main workspace fixture data.
rationale: D399-D406 make Canvas Workspace attention, Side Panel details, input, creation, and relationships projection-driven and admission-bound. The existing Canvas WorkspaceAction callback scaffold is useful for mockups, but keeping action availability and effects in UI handlers would recreate the paused dashboard cockpit and bypass graph-visible causality. A view-to-intent-to-proposal path keeps the product ergonomic while preserving user customization, policy visibility, LLM non-authority, and separation between UI navigation, domain mutation, input response, admission decisions, and runtime/provider execution.

layer: L6 / Canvas fixture, demo, and Workbench isolation / CSP-8 Layer B
question: How should Canvas Workspace keep fake/demo/fixture and dashboard Workbench material useful for tests without letting users confuse it with main workspace data?
decision: Main Canvas Workspace must never silently consume fake, demo, fixture, mockup, screenshot, dashboard Workbench session, or dry-run/mock executor data as production workspace facts. Fixture scenarios live only in explicitly named testing, demo, fixture, story, dev-harness, or app-local mockup entrypoints and must not be root/default exports, production fallbacks, persistence restore inputs, or invisible data sources. Empty, missing, inaccessible, or not-yet-connected production workspace data shows an empty/setup/unresolved state or action intent, not a fixture fallback. Demo, fixture, dry-run, and debug surfaces must visibly label themselves as demo, test, mock, dry-run, or debug when rendered. Dashboard Workbench remains an internal fixture lab/debug/test material surface; its session ledger, local/session snapshot, OperationPolicy, TriageProjection, fake runs, generated workbench-* facts, and dashboard-private active projection index are not Canvas Workspace persistence, policy, runtime, main data, action API, or public WorkspaceGraph API. Fake executor outcomes and fakeExecutor* helpers remain test/dry-run fixtures only and must be marked dry-run/mock if rendered. Main Canvas Workspace cannot mix real and fake facts unless an explicit dev/test harness boundary owns the whole mixed scenario and labels it as such.
rationale: The product goal is that users never need to distinguish real from fake data in the main workspace. D395-D396 keep CSP-8 dashboard Workbench private, D400-D407 define Canvas Workspace as a projection/admission-driven user surface, and D298/D308 reserve dry-run/mock fixtures for testing. Existing Canvas workspaceGraphFixtures and dashboard fake Workbench scenarios are useful for tests, screenshots, and internal debugging, but without an isolation lock they would naturally become convenient fallbacks or product seeds. Explicit fixture entrypoints and visible demo labeling preserve test velocity while preventing fake scenarios, fake executor outcomes, dashboard snapshots, or Workbench policy from becoming Canvas truth.

layer: L6 / Canvas Side Panel Why-Evidence and Debug section boundary / CSP-8 Layer B-C
question: How should Canvas Workspace expose Why/Evidence and Debug material without overwhelming users, leaking runtime-private data, or making debug flow part of the default workspace experience?
decision: Canvas Side Panel WorkItem Details Card separates user-facing Why/Evidence sections from deliberate-open Debug sections. Why/Evidence sections explain the selected WorkItem and current recommended action using bounded summaries, sourceRefs, evidenceRefs, artifact refs, verification summaries, user-readable DataIssue/status summaries, policy reasons, and bounded output/error/needs material. Debug sections are for developer or advanced diagnostic inspection of projection paths, policy/admission details, audit/status ledgers, trace envelopes, dry-run/mock labels, retention diagnostic coordinates, and malformed/stale/duplicate/unsupported internals. Why summary may be visible when needed for action, while evidence details, artifacts, policy/admission details, recent activity, and debug default collapsed unless current policy or user preference expands them; Debug is always deliberate-open and must not enter the default action flow. All displayed material must obey the D270 artifact/ref boundary, D277 redaction/audit boundary, D293 size-capacity vocabulary, D392 public-material boundary, and D393 public evidence coordinate boundary. Runtime-private provider/client/SDK/subprocess/transport/credential state, raw provider requests/responses, unbounded logs/stdout/stderr, filesystem/browser/session private material, and raw retention index internals must not enter graph DATA or Canvas display. Missing, unsupported, redacted, summarized, external-only, dry-run/mock, demo, or fixture evidence must be visibly represented as status/DataIssue/label material rather than pretending complete production evidence is available.
rationale: D399 and D404 put Why/Evidence and Debug inside the Side Panel Details Card while keeping Debug deliberate and collapsed. D270, D277, D293, D392, and D393 define the public-material, ref/summary, redaction, size, and evidence-coordinate boundaries for agent/tool/runtime material. D408 prevents fixture or dry-run material from being confused with production facts. A clear section boundary lets Canvas lower information load for users while preserving explainability for verification and debugging, without turning debug/audit traces into product workflow truth or leaking runtime-private material.

layer: L6 / Canvas Side Panel intent lowering and Workspace projection interface / CSP-8 Layer B
question: How should Canvas lower SidePanelActionIntent and Attention Dashboard actions into Workspace proposal/admission flows without becoming a command bus or Workspace domain authority?
decision: Canvas SidePanelActionIntent is an open, data-only UI intent envelope. It never admits, applies, mutates WorkItems, executes runtime/provider actions, or satisfies input gates. A reviewed lowering adapter may translate intents into Workspace-owned proposal families such as WorkItemSpawnProposed, WorkItemDomainActionProposalIntake, RequiredInputResponseProposed, WorkItem link proposals, admission-decision proposals, or UI-local navigation. Canvas may render form schemas and perform shallow client validation, but Workspace logic owns schema semantics, actor/capability policy, idempotency, stale-ref handling, duplicate/merge decisions, admission, and application. Unknown lowering kinds produce unsupported-lowering preview/status material and never execute. Attention Dashboard groups remain policy-driven projections over WorkItem/actionability/link/evidence/status material and actor preferences, not lifecycle state, queue truth, or board lanes. Hidden, snoozed, and dismissed attention entries are actor/workspace projection preferences unless a later Workspace logic decision introduces explicit projection facts; they are not WorkItem state.
rationale: D397-D407 already lock Canvas to proposal/admission boundaries and RecommendedActionView as view material, but the implementation now needs a concrete interface between UI intents, attention projections, and Workspace logic. This decision prevents the intent envelope from becoming a hidden command bus, keeps Canvas out of domain mutation and runtime execution, preserves configurable attention policy, and lets Canvas consume existing Workspace proposal/admission/application families instead of creating a parallel Canvas authority.

layer: L6 / Canvas Side Panel lowering preview interface / CSP-8 Layer B
question: What concrete boundary should Canvas use between SidePanelActionIntent and Workspace proposal/admission facts?
decision: Canvas introduces a lowering-preview boundary that translates SidePanelActionIntent into UI-local navigation, required draft or confirmation states, unsupported-lowering/status material, or Workspace-owned proposal drafts. The preview boundary may validate shallow client requirements such as serializability, missing target refs, confirmation requirement, and visible form completeness, but it must not admit, apply, mutate WorkItems, satisfy Required Input, create durable relationship truth, execute providers, or invent canonical proposal/admission ids when Workspace logic has not supplied them. Proposal drafts lower only into reviewed Workspace proposal families: WorkItemSpawnProposed, WorkItemDomainActionProposalIntake, RequiredInputResponseProposed, WorkItem link proposal, admission-decision proposal, or UI-local navigation. Unknown lowering kinds and unsupported target-ref shapes produce explicit unsupported/invalid preview statuses rather than fallback execution.
rationale: D410 locks the high-level intent boundary. A concrete preview layer gives Canvas an implementable next slice while preserving D397-D407 proposal/admission/application ownership. It lets Side Panel and Attention Dashboard show confirmation, draft-required, invalid-target, unsupported-lowering, and proposal-ready states without making React callbacks or Canvas adapters into a hidden command bus or Workspace domain authority.

layer: L6 / Canvas WorkItem projection and Attention policy interface / CSP-8 Layer B
question: What projection shape should Canvas consume for WorkItem details and Attention Dashboard grouping without deriving Workspace truth from board/card scaffolds?
decision: Canvas consumes a WorkItem projection bundle from Workspace logic rather than deriving durable attention or Side Panel truth from board/card scaffolds. The bundle centers on a WorkItem projection plus optional required-input gates, recommended actions, link projections, bounded material sections, and attention reasons. Attention reasons are source/projection material explaining why a WorkItem needs visibility or action; Attention Dashboard groups are configurable projection policy over those reasons, actor/workspace preferences, and visible status/evidence/link material. Default groups such as Needs me, Review, Waiting, and Recent are seed policies, not closed enums, lifecycle states, queue truth, or board lanes. Hidden, snoozed, and dismissed attention entries are actor/workspace projection preferences unless a later Workspace logic decision introduces explicit projection facts; they are not WorkItem state. Canvas may render, sort, dedupe, and preserve UI preferences, but Workspace logic owns reason derivation, type/link policy interpretation, required-input gate truth, recommended-action availability, and durable WorkItem/link/evidence facts.
rationale: D400 locks the Attention Dashboard as a configurable projection, D404 locks Side Panel sections as policy-ordered render slots, and D410-D411 lock action intents as UI envelopes that lower through Workspace-owned proposal/admission paths. A shared WorkItem projection bundle prevents Canvas from hardcoding board queue semantics or duplicating Workspace logic while still giving the UI enough structured material to render attention groups, details sections, recommended actions, and Why/Evidence consistently. It also provides a clean migration path away from the current WorkItem board/card compatibility adapter without promoting Workbench, fixtures, or IssueBoard into public Canvas truth.

layer: L6 / Canvas Workspace focused package surfaces / CSP-8 Layer B
question: How should @graphrefly/canvas expose Workspace-related APIs without promoting Workbench, fixtures, issue-board scaffolds, or runtime execution into public product surface?
decision: Canvas Workspace APIs are exposed through focused subpaths rather than a broad durable root. The workspace-graph surface is data/projection only: WorkItem projection bundles, attention reason/policy types, Side Panel intent data, lowering-preview data, topology projection data, constants, and pure helpers. React components live in focused UI subpaths such as workspace-side-panel or workspace-attention only after their props consume projection/intention surfaces rather than fixture/card-feed compatibility scaffolds. The package root may remain a private scaffold while @graphrefly/canvas is private; before public hardening it must either become minimal or re-export only reviewed focused surfaces. Workbench, fixtures, demo harnesses, IssueBoard scaffolds, dashboard-private OperationPolicy/TriageProjection, fake provider/runtime helpers, storage/router/executor bindings, and mutation/application helpers are not public default exports and must not be production fallbacks. Any dev/test/demo subpath must be explicitly named and visibly labeled as such when rendered.
rationale: D368 and D388 already require focused Canvas scope surfaces, while D408 prevents fixture and Workbench material from becoming production truth. D410-D412 introduce new Workspace intent, projection, and attention interfaces that need package boundaries before implementation hardens them. Focused subpaths keep pure data/projection contracts separate from React UI and internal dev harnesses, prevent root-export drift, and allow Canvas to evolve pre-1.0 without accidentally freezing board/workbench/demo scaffolds as durable public API.

layer: L6 / Canvas Trusted Data Query pack boundary / CSP-8 Layer B
question: How should Canvas introduce a Trusted Data Query pack without rebuilding semantic/query runtimes, executing providers from Canvas, or creating Canvas-private verification truth?
decision: Canvas Trusted Data Query is a product pack over existing Workspace, WorkItem, evidence, verification, and executor/result projection surfaces. The pack may provide WorkItem draft templates, metric/query-oriented WorkItem kinds or catalog seeds, required-input request seeds, acceptance criteria, verification-plan recipes, bounded evidence/material section projections, and recommended-action seeds. It must not directly execute SQL, semantic queries, warehouse calls, provider/MCP/CLI/bash/file-edit/URL runtimes, or LLM/tool adapters from Canvas. Query execution and external work remain routed through existing EffectRun/executor/provider paths; evidence and verification results remain mapped through Workspace/WorkItem evidence and verification projectors. Trusted Data Query projections may summarize metric/query state, freshness, source refs, verification status, confidence, and evidence gaps for Attention Dashboard and Side Panel, but they do not create WorkItem truth, verification truth, relationship truth, or runtime truth. Demo graphs and sample query scenarios live only behind explicit fixture/demo/dev-harness boundaries with visible labels and must never be production fallbacks.
rationale: CS-4 needs a concrete Canvas product pack, but D405-D413 keep Canvas out of runtime execution, WorkItem mutation, and private fixture truth. Existing @graphrefly/ts WorkItem scheduling, evidence, and verification surfaces already provide draft, EffectRun, evidence, verification plan, result mapping, status, issue, and audit paths. Treating Trusted Data Query as templates and projections over those paths gives Canvas a useful metric/query workflow while preserving proposal/admission/application, public evidence boundaries, fixture isolation, and provider/runtime privacy. It also prevents the pack from becoming a parallel query engine or dashboard Workbench reincarnation.

layer: L6 / Rust native host binding boundary / CSP-10 and CSP-7
question: How should Rust, TypeScript, and Python divide ownership now that Python and future non-TS hosts need native bindings without reopening structural parity or a second Python wave core?
decision: TypeScript remains a self-contained complete package. Rust is the native shared engine and reusable graph-infrastructure library for Python and future non-TS host-language packages. Python and other host packages own their idiomatic public API, typing/decorators/context managers, value registry and host-object lifetime policy, exception mapping, async/runtime integration, ecosystem adapters, and vertical/product recipes. Rust may expose a PyO3/native foundation over the clean-slate Rust graph engine with opaque graph/node/subscription handles, graph-local synchronous core entry points, stable describe/observe/status/cache surfaces, graph-infrastructure DTOs, and host callback entry points that go through the dispatcher. Rust must not structurally copy the TypeScript package surface, revive the old Impl/facade/port/binding-boundary model, make TypeScript depend on Rust, make host callbacks bypass the dispatcher, or change protocol tiers/messages/ctx semantics for binding convenience. Cross-runtime graph collaboration remains the coarse wire bridge; in-process Python bindings are host-language access to the Rust graph engine, not hidden distributed same-wave semantics.
rationale: D32 keeps language packages self-contained and rejects cross-language peer dependencies, while D24 makes parity behavioral conformance rather than structural symbol matching. Rust has become the practical native engine for slow or FFI-friendly hosts, but TypeScript still needs native JS/browser/V8 completeness. Putting Python idioms, lifetime policy, exception taxonomy, asyncio integration, and product recipes in the Python host package preserves language-native ergonomics and prevents Rust from turning into a monolithic vertical runtime. Keeping Rust responsible for the synchronous graph engine and reusable infrastructure gives CSP-7 a native substrate without reimplementing a separate Python wave core, while preserving F-SYNC-CORE, F-DISPATCH-ALL, D22 graph-domain boundaries, and spec-first protocol discipline.

layer: L6 / async tool-provider adapter runtime boundary / CSP-9
question: How should async tool-provider adapters such as HTTP execute without weakening the synchronous ToolProviderAdapterBinding contract or hiding retry, approval, or artifact lifecycle?
decision: Synchronous ToolProviderAdapterBinding remains sync-only and continues to reject thenables. Async tool providers such as HTTP use separate Layer C runtime helpers that consume graph-visible ToolProviderAdapterInput plus ToolProviderAdapterRunRequested facts and publish provider-neutral ExecutorOutcome, ToolProviderAdapterRunStatus, AgentRequestStatusChanged, DataIssue, and audit material. Async runtime helpers may hold runtime-private drivers, AbortControllers, clients, transports, credentials, response streams, and cancellation state, but none of that state becomes graph DATA, policy material, WorkItem truth, or AgentRequest truth. Retry and repeated execution of an unchanged input remain explicit ToolProviderAdapterRunRequested facts carrying runId, adapterInputId, attempt, reason, retry provenance, policyRefs, and sourceRefs; hidden adapter retry, hidden fallback, and adapter-private repeated execution are forbidden. Approval-required work is represented as visible blocked/needs/status/audit material, and a later approval path must produce a new visible run request rather than resume a private callback. Large, raw, sensitive, or streaming response material, including response bodies beyond inline policy, headers, provider raw responses, traces, stdout/stderr-style logs, files, and binary/media material, must use D270 summary/ref artifact material with D293 size/redaction evidence. Async helpers may offer auto-run attempt 1 for ready inputs, but this is just a visible run-request producer over the existing D362 run coordinate, not a hidden execution loop or protocol change.
rationale: D359-D362 already split provider-neutral graph facts from runtime-private bindings, require visible run/attempt identity, and forbid hidden retry/fallback. The first concrete adapter pack intentionally deferred HTTP because fetch-style work cannot honestly fit the sync ToolProviderAdapterBinding contract. A separate async helper preserves F-SYNC-CORE by keeping async at a Layer C adapter/runtime boundary, preserves D360 by treating policy as descriptive graph material while enforcement remains adapter-owned, preserves D270/D293 by keeping large outputs as refs/summaries, and avoids reopening protocol tiers/messages/ctx semantics. Reusing ToolProviderAdapterRunRequested keeps retry, approval, and attempt lifecycle inspectable instead of inventing a parallel HTTP-only execution coordinate.

layer: L6 / Canvas generated component binding contract / CSP-8 Layer B
question: How should Canvas bind generated or pasted components to Workspace, WorkItem, graph-node, and boundary-input data without creating a command bus, runtime executor, or mutation authority?
decision: Canvas component binding is a slot-addressed render contract over supplied projection snapshots. Components read only reviewed slots such as WorkItem projection, attention item, projection bundle, recommended action, required input, material section, graph-node output projection, and boundary-input draft descriptors. Slot paths are bounded inside those DTOs and are not arbitrary graph/cache/runtime access. Component events emit typed data-only event intents such as UI navigation, SidePanelActionIntent, required-input draft proposal, domain-action draft proposal, WorkItem spawn/link proposal draft, or boundary-input draft preview. The binding layer may preview props, validation diagnostics, and lowering status, but must not execute code, providers, SQL, URLs, MCP/CLI/bash/file edits, mutate WorkItems, satisfy input gates, write graph state, admit, apply, or emit truth facts. Pasted/generated component source is inert manifest material unless a later sandbox/runtime decision explicitly admits rendering behavior.
rationale: D410-D414 keep Canvas on projection, preview, static pack, and package-surface boundaries. Generated component binding needs enough structure to wire UI props and user events, but raw paths or callback commands would recreate hidden mutation/runtime authority. Slot-addressed projection reads plus typed event-intent previews let generated components be useful while preserving Workspace ownership of truth, admission, application, graph input writes, and runtime execution.

layer: L6 / Workspace proposal intake boundary from Canvas previews / CSP-8 Layer B-C
question: How should Canvas SidePanelActionIntent previews enter real Workspace proposal/admission without making Canvas an authority?
decision: Real proposal/admission is Workspace-owned. Canvas may emit SidePanelActionIntent and pure lowering preview material, but canonical proposal facts are created only by a Workspace proposal intake boundary that consumes a proposal-ready preview plus Workspace-supplied ids, actor/capability context, idempotency material, visible projection bundle, and policy. Admission and application remain separate append-only Workspace stages. Canvas must not generate canonical proposal/admission/application ids, admit proposals, apply domain facts, mutate WorkItems, satisfy input gates, execute runtime/provider actions, or promote SidePanelActionIntent into durable graph truth.
rationale: D410-D411 keep Canvas action intents UI-local and preview-only, while D397-D407 require WorkItem creation, input satisfaction, links, and mutations to flow through proposal/admission/application. A Workspace-owned intake boundary lets UI previews become real proposal material without turning Canvas into a command bus, callback executor, or duplicate domain authority.

layer: L6 / tool-provider run admission and approval path / CSP-9
question: How should high-risk tool-provider runs require visible approval or admission without hiding execution, retry, or route selection inside adapter runtimes?
decision: Tool-provider approval is modeled as a graph-visible run-admission gate before adapter runtime execution. Candidate ToolProviderAdapterRunRequested facts are consumed by a provider-neutral admission projector together with ToolProviderAdapterInput and ToolProviderExecutionPolicy approval material. Candidate run requests are not executable until admitted when a policy requires approval. The projector emits proposal, admission, status, issues, audit, and view facts; only approved or admitted work becomes a new visible ToolProviderAdapterRunRequested fact for runtime consumption. Approval-required work must not resume a private callback or mutate an existing run request; it produces a later run request with sourceRefs to the admission decision. Auto approval may pass through visibly, never/block policies emit blocked status/issues/audit, and defer/waiting states remain graph-visible. Adapter runtimes may still fail closed if approval evidence is absent, but they are not the owner of approval lifecycle, human UI, or policy decision state.
rationale: D360 exposes approval as data-only policy material, D362 and D416 require run/attempt lifecycle to be visible, and D213/D214 place authorization/admission before execution. A separate admission gate keeps high-risk tool execution inspectable, lets human or policy executors participate without becoming hidden callbacks, and preserves runtime-private bindings while avoiding protocol changes, hidden fallback, hidden retry, WorkItem mutation, or AgentRequest mutation.

layer: L6 / Canvas generated component renderer admission boundary / CSP-8 Layer B
question: How should Canvas render generated or pasted components after D417 without executing untrusted source, creating callback command buses, or making renderers mutation/runtime authorities?
decision: Canvas generated component rendering is admitted through a renderer manifest and host-owned renderer registry, not by executing raw pasted/generated source inside the main Canvas package. A render request consumes a D417 WorkspaceComponentBindingPreview plus a WorkspaceComponentRendererManifest and produces render-ready or blocked preview material: resolved serializable props, rendererRef, event port declarations, diagnostics, and capability policy status. The first supported renderer kind is host-registered: callers may map rendererId to a trusted React/component implementation outside the pure binding surface. Pasted/generated source remains inert artifact/source material until a later explicit sandbox/build/admission decision produces an admitted renderer manifest. Renderer event ports may only emit typed D417 event intents and downstream D411/D418 previews; they must not expose arbitrary callbacks that mutate WorkItems, write graph state, satisfy input gates, admit/apply proposals, execute providers/runtimes, access credentials, or emit truth facts. Any iframe/worker/dynamic-source sandbox is a separate future runtime decision with explicit capability, origin, asset, dependency, and postMessage boundaries.
rationale: D417 deliberately stops at inert binding preview, while D410-D414 and D418 keep Canvas out of mutation, admission, application, and runtime execution. Rendering is useful for generated components, but raw source execution would collapse the binding boundary into a hidden runtime and callback command bus. A host-registered renderer admission step lets Canvas connect resolved props and typed event ports to trusted product components while preserving package-surface purity, testability, and future room for a separately designed sandbox runtime.

layer: L6 / Canvas Side Panel intent envelope validation / CSP-8 Layer B
question: How should Canvas lowering previews represent malformed SidePanelActionIntent envelope material such as non-data metadata without conflating it with draft, target, lowering, or admission failures?
decision: Canvas SidePanelActionIntent preview uses an explicit invalid-intent status with reason kinds such as malformed-metadata for non-data envelope material. Invalid intent material fails closed as UI/projection status material and never lowers to proposal-ready, admission, application, runtime execution, or durable graph truth. Draft-specific malformed material remains draft-required/malformed-draft, target-specific failures remain invalid-target, and unsupported lowering kinds remain unsupported-lowering.
rationale: D410 makes SidePanelActionIntent a data-only UI intent envelope, and D411 makes lowering preview the fail-closed boundary before Workspace-owned proposal/admission. Metadata is envelope material rather than domain draft, target ref, or lowering family, so reusing those statuses would blur remediation and make UI handling ambiguous. A separate invalid-intent status preserves D410-D411 boundaries while keeping validation pure and local to Canvas preview material.

layer: L6 / tool-provider graph-visible retry orchestration / CSP-9
question: How should provider-neutral tool-provider retry and delayed attempt readiness be represented without hidden adapter/runtime retry loops?
decision: Tool-provider retry is a provider-neutral graph-visible projector over ToolProviderAdapterInput, terminal ExecutorOutcome or run-status material, retry policy material, and optional graph-visible clock/readiness facts. It emits retry proposal, scheduled/pending status, issues, audit, and views, and emits the next ToolProviderAdapterRunRequested only when policy permits and the attempt is immediate-ready or a visible readiness/now fact makes a scheduled retry eligible. Delayed/backoff retry is represented as graph-visible scheduled/pending material with bounded provenance, retryAtMs/delayMs, next attempt, policyRefs, and sourceRefs; it never uses hidden setTimeout, sleep, or runtime-private loops. High-risk retry candidates still pass through D419 admission before runtime execution. Runtime/private adapter bindings remain one-shot executors and do not mutate WorkItem, ExecutorRoute, AgentRequestFact, or ToolProviderAdapterInput.
rationale: D362 and D416 require retries and repeated executions to be explicit ToolProviderAdapterRunRequested facts and forbid hidden retry. D419 requires admission before execution for approval-required tool work. Existing RetryPolicy and BackoffPolicy helpers provide retry math but intentionally do not schedule work. Locking the projector and scheduled/pending fact boundary preserves graph visibility, approval, artifact/ref limits, and runtime privacy without changing protocol semantics.

layer: L6 / Canvas host-registered renderer runtime bridge / CSP-8 Layer B
question: How should host-registered Canvas component renderers connect to real host runtime implementations without making Canvas own registries, callbacks, permissions, or Workspace mutation?
decision: Host-registered renderer runtime binding is caller-owned and runtime-private. Canvas may publish only renderer manifest/ref DTOs, render-admission previews, serializable props, event port declarations, diagnostics, preview-only capability status, and typed data envelopes derived from event ports. A host may map rendererId to a trusted implementation outside Canvas, but that registry, implementation object, lifecycle, teardown, framework adapter, and permission enforcement are not Canvas public package state. Renderer events cross back only as typed data envelopes derived from D417 event intents and D411/D418 preview material; they must not expose arbitrary callbacks, command buses, graph writes, WorkItem mutation, input-gate satisfaction, proposal admission/application, provider/runtime execution, credentials, browser/session handles, or truth facts. Capability policy in Canvas remains descriptive preview material; runtime enforcement belongs to the host/runtime or a separately designed Workspace policy/admission layer. Generated source execution, iframe/worker/postMessage sandboxing, dependency loading, remote asset loading, and compiler/bundler admission remain separate future decisions.
rationale: D417 keeps component binding inert, D418 keeps proposal/admission/application Workspace-owned, and D420 admits only host-registered renderer preview material. A separate runtime bridge lock prevents later slices from smuggling registry ownership, callbacks, permission enforcement, or sandbox execution into Canvas while still allowing product hosts to render trusted components through their own runtime-private implementations.

layer: L6 / graph-visible scheduled readiness / CSP-9-CSP-8 shared orchestration
question: How should delayed graph-visible work become ready without hidden timers, runtime-private scheduler loops, or protocol changes?
decision: Scheduled readiness is represented by a provider/domain-neutral graph-visible projector over explicit schedule facts and explicit graph-local clock/readiness facts. Schedule facts carry stable scheduleId, subject refs, readyAtMs or notBeforeMs eligibility, optional deadlineMs, policyRefs, sourceRefs, reason, and bounded metadata. The projector emits pending, ready, overdue, status, issues, audit, and views; it does not execute providers, claim work, mutate WorkItems, admit proposals, satisfy input gates, or append domain truth. Domain projectors such as tool-provider retry, workQueue claim/lease, and effect/workflow helpers may consume ready facts and emit their own ordinary domain facts through existing admission/runtime paths. Timer or sleep drivers may exist only as optional source/runtime helpers that publish graph-visible clock or wake facts; they are never the authority for readiness or execution. No protocol tier, message, ctx.up/down behavior, graph verb, or cross-language conformance rule changes.
rationale: D422 requires delayed tool-provider retry to wait on graph-visible clock/readiness facts; D314-D318 already lock workQueue lease expiration, retry wait, and delayed eligibility as visible clock/deadline material rather than hidden timers. D52 confines wall-clock timers to source composition, while RetryPolicy and BackoffPolicy provide retry math without scheduling. A shared scheduled-readiness projector prevents domain-specific drift, keeps delayed eligibility inspectable and replayable, preserves D419 admission before high-risk execution, and maintains F-SYNC-CORE/R-no-raw-async without changing the wave protocol.

layer: L6 / Workspace proposal spine durable fact boundary / CSP-8 Layer B-C
question: How should Workspace-owned proposal intake, admission, and application become durable graph-visible facts without turning Canvas previews into mutation authority or creating a universal apply blob?
decision: Workspace proposal/admission/application uses a generic append-only proposal spine plus family-specific application. The generic spine records WorkspaceProposalRecorded material from a proposal-ready Canvas preview or Workspace-owned ready request material, using only Workspace-supplied proposalId, actor/capability context, idempotency material, visible projection bundle refs, policy refs, sourceRefs, audit, target refs, proposal family, and bounded data-only draft material.
