Existing envelope metadata owns session ordering, sequence, cursor, idempotency, ack/nack, attempts, and request correlation. The wire-edge payload adds only tagged edge frames: dirty(edgeId,causeId) and data(edgeId,causeId,value). causeId is a bridge-local causal emission id, not a graph wave id. A v1 WireEdgeGroup is static, one in-flight cause at a time, and gates all DATA frames for a cause until every expected DIRTY frame in the group has arrived. Inbound edge adapters inject ordinary local DIRTY/DATA through the owning graph boundary; remote nodes, Ctx/Node handles, live topology, local pending/diamond accounting, function bodies, and remote COMPLETE/ERROR terminals never cross. TS and Rust implement self-contained idiomatic APIs over the shared semantic frame contract; Python exposes only an idiomatic facade over native/Rust-owned bridge semantics, not a Python wave core. B2 uses protobuf bytes as the canonical cross-runtime wire representation for bridge envelopes and wire-edge frames. Avro is not used for the C-1 bridge v1; future storage/log/analytics exports may review Avro separately if a real consumer appears.
rationale: D22/R-graph-domain require cross-domain delayed consistency with a two-phase wire gate, while D134/D140/D141 already lock ordered acknowledged bridge envelopes and forbid remote ordinary deps, distributed same-wave, and terminal leakage. C-1 needs edge identity and causal grouping beyond session seq/cursor, but not a new protocol message/tier or broad trace system. A minimal tagged frame payload preserves existing bridge metadata, keeps runtime packages self-contained under D32, and gives conformance one behavior to test across TS/Rust/Py without structural parity. Protobuf is already the authority direction in R-msg-format, D33, protocol.proto, and B2; using Avro here would be a separate architectural fork rather than an implementation detail.

layer: L6 / B2 canonical protobuf wire profile
question: How should GraphReFly define canonical protobuf bytes, validation, and golden vectors for B2/C-1 without turning value codecs or wire-edge adapters into new protocol semantics?
decision: B2 uses a canonical protobuf wire profile over spec/protocol.proto for bridge envelopes and wire-edge frames. A valid canonical byte sequence must decode to a semantic DTO, pass runtime validation, deterministically re-encode, and match the original bytes exactly. Unknown fields, duplicate singular fields, non-canonical ordering/default emission, missing required semantic fields, invalid oneof combinations, and invalid wire-edge kind/value combinations are rejected. Validator rules are part of the B2 contract because proto3 cannot express all GraphReFly semantics. Golden vectors live in the language-neutral authority repo and include positive and negative cases consumed by TS, Rust, and Python/native gates. Fixture value bytes for C-1 use a strict canonical JSON v1 profile only for tests/golden vectors; this is not a production value registry, storage codec, or analytics/export format. WireEdgeGroup remains the D496 graph/application adapter over the bridge envelope: static v1 group, one in-flight cause, DIRTY gate before DATA release, local injection through owning graph boundary, and no remote ordinary deps, distributed same-wave, raw Node/Ctx handles, live topology, functions, or terminal leakage.
rationale: D11/D33/D496 require protobuf as the cross-runtime wire representation, while D134/D140/D141/D496 keep bridge payloads as graph/application facts rather than protocol messages. Proto3 parsers are intentionally permissive and cannot encode all field-presence and cross-field semantics, so canonical bytes require an explicit validate-and-reencode profile plus shared golden vectors. Strict JSON fixture bytes give C-1 readable cross-language test values without prematurely creating a value codec registry or reopening storage/export design. Keeping WireEdgeGroup under D496 avoids a spec-amend because no tier, message, ctx, or wave semantics change.

layer: L6 / B2-C1 bridge adapter implementation surfaces
question: How should B2 protobuf byte integration, Python/native gates, and C-1 WireEdgeGroup public shape land without widening protocol semantics?
decision: B2 protobuf integration uses focused wireBridgeProtobuf adapter helpers over existing D134/D140/D141 semantic wireBridge bundles, not wireBridge core options and not a new protocol surface. The helper exposes graph-visible inbound byte decoding, outbound byte encoding, and decode/encode issue facts; malformed canonical protobuf bytes become bridge invalid/issue facts and never local protocol terminals. Python first consumes D497 golden vectors through a private/native validator gate over Rust-owned canonical protobuf validation, not a public raw wire facade. C-1 WireEdgeGroup is a static graph/application adapter over wireBridge that owns bridge-local cause ids, permits one in-flight cause at a time, gates inbound DATA until all expected DIRTY frames for that cause arrive, and returns local inbound edge source nodes plus status/issues; it never injects remote ordinary deps, remote Node/Ctx handles, live topology, distributed same-wave state, or remote COMPLETE/ERROR terminals.
rationale: D496/D497 already lock protobuf canonical bytes and WireEdgeGroup semantics while forbidding protocol/tier/message changes, Avro, value codec registry, remote ordinary deps, distributed same-wave, and Python wave-core duplication. Focused helpers preserve the existing transport-free wireBridge semantic surface, keep byte parsing inspectable through graph facts, allow Python/native conformance without public raw protocol escape hatches, and make C-1 composition explicit and describe-visible through local returned nodes rather than hidden target injection.

layer: L6 / TS adapter side-fact projector discipline / D498 follow-up
question: How should TypeScript adapter helpers expose side facts such as protobuf issues/status without hidden sibling writes while preserving wireBridgeProtobuf behavior?
decision: Adapter helpers that expose graph-visible side facts must route internal observations through declared event/result nodes and derive public issue/status/output nodes from those events with ordinary deps. wireBridgeProtobuf should use internal protobuf event/result lanes over inbound bytes and bridge outbound facts, derive inboundDecoded/outboundBytes/issues/status from those lanes, keep status in ctx.state, and keep malformed bytes as bridge invalid/issue facts rather than protocol terminals. Direct sibling .down() from one projector into another public side node is forbidden except for explicit external ingress/source nodes. The public bundle shape does not grow unless tests prove a subscription-order edge requires separate internal event lanes. This is not a protocol, tier, message, or ctx semantic change.
rationale: D39/D51 require describe-visible causal edges for graph facts, and D498 says protobuf helper issue facts are graph-visible. Existing wireBridge and remoteResponder precedent uses event nodes plus projectors. This keeps adapter facts inspectable without adding protocol behavior or hidden transport/session ownership.

layer: L6 / B2-C1 focused byte helper and adapter-driver boundary / D498 follow-up
question: How should the Rust B2 protobuf byte helper, C-1 WireEdgeGroup v1 API shape, and ack timeout/retry boundary be narrowed after D498 without moving byte or timer mechanics into core protocol semantics?
decision: Rust wireBridgeProtobuf lands as a focused byte-specific DTO/helper over the existing semantic D134/D140/D141 wireBridge envelope and D496 wire-edge frame bundle. The helper may decode canonical protobuf bytes into semantic bridge DTOs, encode semantic bridge DTOs into canonical protobuf bytes, and report byte validation issues/status, but it must not add wireBridge core options, protocol messages or tiers, a value codec registry, storage hydration, checkpoint replay, or Python-public raw wire facade. C-1 WireEdgeGroup v1 returns local inbound edge source nodes plus status/issues/release material, uses a static expected DIRTY set, permits one in-flight bridge-local causeId at a time, and fails closed on competing or malformed causes; causeId is never a graph wave id. Ack timeout/retry is a cross-runtime adapter-driver semantic contract over bridge metadata/status facts, not wave protocol or core graph behavior. Libraries may reuse passive timeout/retry/backoff math, but any timer, retry pump, sleep, retransmit, or wake driver lives only at the adapter/driver/source boundary and must surface graph-visible status/issues rather than hidden core mutation.
rationale: D496-D499 lock the bridge envelope, canonical protobuf profile, focused helper surface, and TypeScript side-fact discipline. The remaining implementation risk is boundary drift: Rust byte helpers could become a broad raw wire surface, WireEdgeGroup could smuggle remote ordinary deps or distributed same-wave state, and ack timeout/retry could look like protocol policy if timer pumps enter the sync core. A byte-specific helper over semantic DTOs, static one-cause WireEdgeGroup shape, and adapter-driver-only retry/timer boundary keep B2/C-1 inspectable and cross-runtime without changing R-msg-format, R-tier, R-ctx-up, R-sync-core, or D22 graph-domain semantics.

layer: L6 / C-1 WireEdgeGroup concrete adapter shape and ack-driver ingress / D500 follow-up
question: How should C-1 WireEdgeGroup and ack timeout/retry implementation shape become concrete without adding protocol behavior, value codecs, or hidden timer ownership?
decision: WireEdgeGroup v1 is a byte-valued static adapter over wireBridge. Public bundles return inbound edge nodes keyed by edgeId plus status/issues/release; outbound edge sources are declared in options, not hidden remote deps. Each cause uses a static expected edge set and must carry DIRTY and DATA for every expected edge; DIRTY frames gate release and DATA frames settle the local inbound edge nodes. Missing snapshots, unknown edges, duplicate frames, competing causes, malformed frames, and incomplete causes fail closed as issue/status facts, not protocol terminals. Internal event/gate/projector lanes derive public status/issues/inbound nodes through declared deps so describe can show the causal path. Ack timeout/retry uses passive retry math plus explicit graph-visible driver timeout ingress; timer, sleep, retry pump, and wake scheduling live only in adapter/driver/source helpers, never in core wave protocol or hidden bridge timers. Rust wireBridgeProtobuf remains a byte-specific semantic DTO helper and must not grow a raw wire facade, value codec registry, storage hydration, checkpoint replay, or Python-public raw wire surface.
rationale: D496-D500 already lock bridge envelope semantics, canonical protobuf bytes, side-fact discipline, and adapter-driver-only retry/timer boundaries. The remaining ambiguity is implementability: static cause completion must avoid remote inbound wedges, returned nodes must be describe-visible, and timeout retries must not be hidden captured-ctx timer mutation. Byte-valued groups and explicit driver ingress keep C-1 inspectable and cross-runtime without changing message/tier/ctx semantics.

layer: L6 / TypeScript wireBridge ack-driver exact API / D501 follow-up
question: What exact TypeScript API shape should replace hidden wireBridge ack timeout/retry timers under D501?
decision: TypeScript replaces wireBridge internal setTimeout/captured-ctx ack scheduling with an explicit graph-visible ack-timeout command ingress and a focused ack driver helper. WireBridgeCommand may grow a focused DATA command variant {kind:"ack-timeout", seq:number, attempt:number, observedAtMs?:number}; seq+attempt identify the pending outbound attempt, malformed timeout commands become invalid/issue facts, and well-formed stale or mismatched timeout commands are fail-closed no-ops that never emit retries or terminals. wireBridge remains the owner of pending seq/attempt/envelope state plus retry, exhausted, outbound, status, and error facts; the ack driver never mutates bridge state directly and never emits bridge outbound/status/error nodes by side effect. A public wireBridgeAckDriver(graph, bridge, {clock, timeoutMs, name?}) helper may consume graph-visible monotonic clock facts and declared bridge facts, derive ack-timeout command facts through ordinary deps, attach those commands to bridge.command using the existing command-source attachment/release discipline, and return commands/status/issues/release. ackTimeoutMs moves out of wireBridge internal scheduling responsibility; timeout policy for this explicit helper is helper input, while retry policy remains bridge metadata and passive retry math. This slice does not add EnvironmentDrivers timer expansion, hidden setTimeout fallback, protocol messages or tiers, core wave scheduler behavior, or WireEdgeGroup runtime.
rationale: D501 locks explicit graph-visible driver timeout ingress but does not choose the TypeScript API shape. The command-plus-driver shape keeps timeout wakeups inspectable as ordinary graph facts, preserves wireBridge as the semantic owner of retry/exhaustion decisions, prevents hidden captured-ctx mutation after release, and avoids widening the core graph scheduler or protocol. seq+attempt is the minimal stale-wake guard for retries without adding public timer tokens or a broader runtime driver abstraction.

layer: L6 / Canvas project settings authority model
question: How should Canvas model project settings authority without making Workbench a settings owner, opening a generic runtime registry, or leaking runtime-private configuration?
decision: Canvas may define a focused data-only project settings surface for known Canvas setting domains, effective setting display views, redacted runtime posture, and user setting-change intent DTOs. The surface may include a typed settings catalog, but the catalog is definition/view material only, not an executable registry or persistence owner. Workbench may own ephemeral session UI state such as open panels, temporary toggles, collapsed sections, and hover/follow display state, but it must not become the project settings authority, append setting events as lifecycle owner, or persist settings directly. Project-persistent settings are caller/project-owned material; hosts may pass already-derived effective settings views into Workbench and may receive data-only user setting-change intents, then decide admission, persistence, and audit outside Workbench. Runtime-private configuration remains outside Canvas setting values: secrets, provider tokens, env vars, runner bindings, storage handles, query handles, callbacks, registries, clients, opaque cursors, and runtime handles must not enter graph truth, display DTOs, tests, snapshots, or generated proposals except as explicitly redacted status/posture metadata. Future settings domains such as topology behavior, sandbox policy, runner posture, credential posture, and display preferences should be typed known domains, not open arbitrary setting plugins. Root package exports must not grow casually; any public Canvas settings API should live in a focused subpath and export only data-only types/builders/intents/status helpers.
rationale: The Canvas product needs visible project settings for topology behavior, sandbox policy, runner readiness, credential posture, and display preferences, but D413/D420/D423/D426/D485/D487/D491/D493 keep Workbench and focused surfaces out of lifecycle authority, runtime execution, provider/storage ownership, callbacks, selectors, and current-view owner/store internals. A constrained typed catalog gives the UI and hosts a stable vocabulary without reopening the forbidden generic selector/registry/provider API. Splitting ephemeral Workbench UI state from caller-owned project settings preserves replay and persistence authority, while redacted runtime posture lets users understand capability state without leaking secrets or handles into graph-visible material.

layer: L6 / Canvas sandbox runtime boundary
question: How should Canvas represent sandboxed generated or pasted UI runtime without owning iframe/postMessage execution, renderer registries, callbacks, credentials, or graph mutation authority?
decision: Canvas may define data-only sandbox request intents, admission/session descriptors, runtime status views, typed event-envelope material, bounded log displays, and bounded component error displays for generated, pasted, marketplace, host-registered, and trusted-built-in component sources. Workbench may emit sandbox request intents and display host-produced lifecycle/status/diagnostic material, but it must not create isolation hosts, wire postMessage, load assets, register renderers, enforce origin/sandbox/CSP/permission policy, own teardown, or hold runtime handles. Actual iframe, worker, dynamic-source, postMessage, origin, asset, lifecycle, and permission enforcement remain host-private runtime responsibilities. Hosts may map sandboxSessionId values to private iframe/runtime instances, but those handles must not enter graph truth, display DTOs, tests, snapshots, generated proposals, or public Canvas surfaces. Sandbox props are serializable data derived from the admitted render preview and declared input schema only; they must not include graph stores, credentials, filesystem paths, runner state, storage/query/provider handles, clients, callbacks, registries, opaque cursors, or runtime handles. Sandbox messages may lower only into validated typed event envelopes and existing event-lowering preview paths; payloads cannot override routing authority, action ids, target refs, lowering kind, policy, or permission material. Malformed, unknown, stale, or unauthorized sandbox messages fail closed as data-only status/diagnostic material, not protocol terminals, graph truth, Workspace mutation, proposal admission/application, provider execution, or raw command dispatch. Raw console output and runtime errors are normalized into bounded redacted log/error display records; component failures are sandbox/component status, not graph node ERROR facts. Promotion of generated or pasted UI into a trusted host-registered component pack is a separate reviewed host workflow that may change trust posture, but never graph semantics or automatic proposal/application authority.
rationale: D417, D420, D423, D426, and D451 lock Canvas component rendering as descriptor/DTO-oriented, with typed event previews and host-owned runtime bridges, while explicitly deferring iframe/worker/postMessage/dynamic-source sandboxing. D503 adds settings posture without making settings an enforcement owner. This decision closes that deferred sandbox boundary by allowing Canvas to name and display sandbox lifecycle material while keeping execution, registry, origin, permission, asset, and teardown authority in the host runtime. The split lets generated/pasted UI become interactive later without reopening callback buses, raw command refs, credential leakage, provider/runtime access, Workbench lifecycle ownership, or graph-visible mutation authority.

layer: L6 / Canvas runner and credentials boundary
question: How should Canvas expose runner and credential readiness without collecting secrets, launching raw commands, owning approvals, or crossing runtime-private execution boundaries?
decision: Canvas may define data-only runner capability views, credential posture views, credential setup intents, typed runner command intents, run status views, approval display material, audit display material, bounded log summaries, and artifact/evidence refs. Workbench may display runner and credential readiness and may emit user intents to start a caller-owned credential setup flow or request a typed runner command, but it must not collect secrets, tokens, passwords, OAuth codes, env vars, connection strings, private keys, filesystem paths, raw shell strings, raw SQL connection material, runner handles, clients, storage/query/provider handles, callbacks, registries, or opaque runtime cursors. Credential setup forms in Canvas accept only redacted metadata and setup intent coordinates such as profile kind, requested scopes, return target refs, actor refs, and policy refs; secret entry, OAuth exchange, vault writes, token refresh, and credential validation remain host/private-runner responsibilities. Runner launch intents must name typed command kinds over runner-scoped refs and bounded parameters, such as tests over repo refs, dbt over project refs and model selectors, SQL over warehouse profile refs and query-plan refs, or verification over issue/work graph refs. They must not carry raw shell, raw path, raw token, raw environment, arbitrary command argv, or direct filesystem/credential handles from the browser. The runner or host admission path owns workspace/repo authorization, filesystem and command allowlists, credential lookup, approval gates, runtime limits, execution, cancellation, artifact/log/evidence collection, and audit persistence. Workbench is not the approval lifecycle owner or audit writer; approval, status, issues, audit, logs, and evidence appear in Canvas only as already-derived data-only views or refs. Missing, expired, unauthorized, stale, denied, approval-required, or unsupported runner/credential cases fail closed as visible status/issues/audit material, not hidden execution, callback resume, graph truth mutation, proposal admission/application, provider execution, or WorkItem mutation.
rationale: Canvas needs a usable execution entry point for tests, dbt, SQL, verification, and local or hosted runners, but docs/plan.md already frames runner execution as a separate capability boundary and D359/D361/D416/D419 keep clients, secrets, subprocess access, transports, approval lifecycle, and adapter runtime execution outside graph-visible data and UI-owned state. D503 permits redacted runner and credential posture as settings/display material without making settings an enforcement authority. This decision gives Workbench enough vocabulary to show readiness and request typed runs while preserving host/private-runner ownership of secrets, authorization, allowlists, approvals, limits, artifacts, logs, evidence, and audit persistence. Requiring typed command refs prevents the browser from becoming a raw remote shell or credential transport and keeps execution material reviewable, replayable, and bounded.

layer: L6 / C-1 WireEdgeGroup residual directionality and tombstone retention
question: How should C-1 resolve mixed-direction WireEdgeGroup declarations, ack-timeout commands without observed time, and failed/released cause tombstone retention after the Rust QA slice?
decision: WireEdgeGroup v1 declarations are single-direction bundles: an instance may be inbound-only or outbound-only, but must not mix inbound-only and outbound edges. Callers that need bidirectional bridge composition must create separate inbound and outbound WireEdgeGroup bundles over the same wireBridge, so D501's static expected edge set and per-cause DIRTY+DATA-for-every-edge rule stay literal. Ack-timeout command ingress keeps D502 parity: when observedAtMs/observed_at_ms is absent, the explicit driver command is treated as the driver's assertion that the timeout is due now; delayed retry suppression only applies when a timestamp is present and is earlier than the stored retry due time. WireEdgeGroup failed and released cause tombstones are bounded recent-memory guards, not unbounded replay logs; recent replays fail closed as issue/status facts, while evicted very old cause ids are outside the v1 exact replay-detection guarantee. This does not add protocol messages, tiers, raw wire facades, production codec registries, storage/checkpoint replay, scheduler policy, or missed/catch-up timer semantics.
rationale: D501 requires every cause to carry DIRTY and DATA for every expected edge. A mixed inbound/outbound bundle would either wedge outbound causes on inbound-only snapshots or silently weaken the expected-edge rule, so splitting bundles preserves the locked semantics and keeps describe-visible topology simple. D502 already made ack timeout an explicit driver ingress; treating a missing observed time as due-now matches the TypeScript first cut and avoids inventing a Rust-only clock fallback. Bounded recent tombstones prevent a hostile or long-lived bridge from growing memory without limit while preserving fail-closed behavior for the practical late-replay window covered by C-1 tests.

layer: L6 / Canvas topology behavior persistence
question: How should Canvas persist topology lens behavior without letting hover, follow, minimap, or debug toggles hijack the canvas, become Workbench-owned project settings, or produce graph-visible policy material by default?
decision: Canvas topology behavior splits into Workbench session-only state, caller-owned project settings, and graph-visible policy material only when an external host explicitly creates it. Workbench may own ephemeral session-only topology UI state such as overlay open/closed, hovered topology node, selected topology node, temporary tracking override, minimap expanded/collapsed, debug panel open/closed, and pan/zoom viewport. These values are local presentation state and must not become project truth, graph truth, WorkItem truth, proposal/admission/application material, or durable audit by default. Caller-owned project settings may provide typed effective defaults under the D503 settings authority model, including default lens mode, default tracking mode, minimap default visibility, whether selection may follow pinned widgets, and whether inferred input UI is enabled. Persistence, admission, and audit for those project settings remain host/project-owned; Workbench may consume an already-derived effective topology behavior view and may emit data-only topology setting-change intents, but it must not persist settings directly or append setting events as lifecycle owner. Conservative defaults remain locked: Workbench starts with the topology overlay closed/off; when opened the lens mode defaults to focused-path, hover tracking defaults to none, pinned-node hover shows pinned state only, unpinned-node hover shows a ghost frame only, canvas pan on hover is disabled, minimap defaults hidden/collapsed unless enabled by an effective setting, and debug-protocol is session/dev-only rather than a project default. Topology behavior changes remain presentation preferences by default and must not synthesize graph-visible policy, mutate WorkItems, alter graph topology, execute runtime/provider work, or change proposal/application authority. If a host wants audit or durable project policy for a setting change, it must route the data-only intent through its own settings/admission/audit path outside Workbench.
rationale: AGENTS.md and the existing topology-lens surface already lock the product rule that topology hover must not hijack the canvas by default and that existing pinned UI shows pinned state unless the user enables stronger following. D390 keeps WorkspaceGraph topology projection as pure Canvas product-layer data rather than runtime/substrate truth, while D400 keeps Topology Lens as an overlay rather than the default page. D503 permits typed known settings domains but keeps Workbench out of project-settings authority. This decision makes the persistence split explicit: individual UI affordances stay session-local, durable defaults are caller-owned effective settings, and graph-visible policy appears only through a deliberate external host path. The result preserves user-pinned output authority, prevents hover/minimap/debug state from polluting project truth, and leaves future topology settings implementable as data-only effective views and change intents.

layer: L6 / Canvas generated component promotion boundary
question: How should Canvas represent promotion of generated, pasted, or marketplace UI into a trusted host-registered component pack without owning registries, installation, source execution, or graph/proposal semantics?
decision: Canvas may define data-only component promotion candidate views, review checklist views, promotion request intents, promotion status views, and installed renderer-manifest preview material for generated, pasted, marketplace, sandboxed, and host-registered component sources. Workbench may display whether a component is eligible for host review and may emit a data-only promotion request intent with candidate ids, target trust posture, actor refs, policy refs, evidence refs, and audit context, but it must not install component packs, assign renderer ids, write host registries, execute generated or pasted source, load dependencies, build packages, sign artifacts, mutate trust policy, or mark a component trusted by UI toggle. Host-private review and runtime infrastructure owns source storage, source retrieval, dependency audit, code/security review, build, signing, packaging, registry installation, rendererId assignment, trust-policy enforcement, rollback, uninstall, and runtime binding. Canvas promotion DTOs must use bounded summaries, manifest snapshots, source/artifact refs, fingerprints, sandbox evidence refs, review statuses, issues, and installed renderer manifest previews; they must not carry raw source code, package archives, dependency trees, build outputs, executable modules, registry objects, callback maps, clients, credentials, filesystem paths, provider/runtime handles, opaque cursors, or permission objects. Promotion is a reviewed trust transition for future rendering posture only: it may allow a future host-produced host-registered renderer manifest/ref after host admission, but it does not retroactively trust old sandbox sessions, change graph truth, expand event ports, bypass D417/D426 typed event envelopes, auto-admit/apply proposals, mutate WorkItems, satisfy input gates, execute providers/runners, or alter proposal/application authority. Rejected, blocked, stale, failed-review, unavailable-source, or install-failed cases remain visible as data-only promotion status/issues/audit refs and never fall back to direct source execution or silent host-preview trust.
rationale: D417, D420, D423, D426, D451, and D504 lock generated/component rendering as descriptor/DTO-oriented, host-owned, sandboxed when untrusted, and free of callback buses, registries, runtime handles, and graph mutation. D504 explicitly leaves promotion to a trusted component pack as a separate reviewed host workflow. This decision closes that workflow boundary by allowing Canvas to show candidates, request review, and display promotion status while keeping installation and trust authority in the host. Treating promotion as a future-rendering trust posture prevents a review outcome from becoming graph semantics, proposal admission, WorkItem mutation, or a shortcut around typed event lowering. Using refs/fingerprints/evidence instead of raw source or packages keeps Canvas public DTOs bounded and avoids turning Workbench into a source store, package manager, or component registry.

layer: L6 / Canvas component source intake material boundary
question: How should Canvas represent generated, pasted, or marketplace component source intake without becoming a source store, dependency parser, build owner, or implicit hydrate/execution authority?
decision: Canvas may define data-only component source intake views and review intents that expose only bounded source posture: component id, source kind, display name, source availability, source/artifact refs, source fingerprint or content hash, declared binding manifest snapshots, event-port summaries, sandbox posture, sandbox evidence refs, review status, and issue summaries. Workbench may display source posture and review readiness and may emit data-only source review or intake intents with component ids, source refs, requested review kinds, actor refs, policy refs, evidence refs, and audit context, but it must not store raw component source, parse source, load dependencies, build modules, hydrate refs, execute code, infer trust, install renderers, or derive binding/event manifests from raw source. Raw generated or pasted source code, uploaded files, package archives, dependency graphs or lockfiles, build outputs, executable modules, source maps, scanner raw logs, signing keys, registry objects, runtime handles, filesystem paths, clients, credentials, provider/storage/query handles, opaque cursors, and permission objects remain host-private or artifact-store-private material. Source refs, artifact refs, and fingerprints are evidence/address material only; they are not authority to hydrate, execute, install, promote, or bypass sandbox/admission. Source intake does not directly render or promote a component: it may feed binding/render preview, sandbox admission/status, and optional promotion review through explicit data-only requests and host-owned admission paths. Missing, restricted, stale, mismatched, unavailable, oversize, malformed, or unverifiable source material fails closed as visible source status/issues/audit refs and must not fall back to inline source DTOs, direct execution, host preview, proposal admission/application, WorkItem mutation, or generated truth facts.
rationale: D417 and D420 keep generated component binding/rendering descriptor-oriented and reject raw pasted/generated source execution in Canvas. D504 keeps sandbox runtime host-private and D508 keeps promotion installation/trust host-private. D270/D293 and the broader artifact policy pattern favor bounded summaries/refs over raw large or sensitive material. This decision fills the intake gap before promotion or sandbox work expands: Canvas can show enough source posture for review workflows while avoiding a public source store, dependency parser, package manager, build system, scanner log carrier, or hidden hydrate channel. Treating refs and fingerprints as evidence only preserves inspectability without granting execution or registry authority.

layer: L6 / Canvas sandbox log and error capture boundary
question: How should Canvas display sandbox logs and component errors without owning console capture, leaking raw stacks/source/secrets, or mapping component failures into graph truth?
decision: Canvas may define data-only sandbox log display records, sandbox error display records, diagnostic status views, redaction evidence summaries, artifact/log refs, and Side Panel console/debug display sections. Workbench may display host-produced bounded/redacted log and error records for selected sandboxed or generated components, but it must not subscribe directly to iframe console streams, read runtime error objects, inspect iframe handles, expand source maps, parse raw stacks, read raw source excerpts, store full log buffers, or perform redaction itself as runtime authority. Host-private sandbox/runtime infrastructure owns raw console capture, raw error capture, stack collection, source-map expansion, source excerpt handling, log buffering, redaction, truncation, retention, artifact storage, and correlation to private sandbox runtime handles. Canvas log/error DTOs must contain only bounded fields such as sandbox session refs, component ids, source kind, level, error kind, message summary, optional source label, optional occurredAtMs, redaction status, truncation/size evidence, issue summaries, and artifact/log refs. They must not carry raw console streams, full stack traces, raw Error objects, source-map-expanded frames, raw source excerpts, filesystem paths, tokens, secrets, env vars, credentials, connection strings, clients, provider/storage/query handles, runtime handles, iframe/window references, callback maps, opaque cursors, or permission objects. Component crashes and sandbox runtime failures are sandbox/component status and diagnostics, not GraphReFly protocol terminals, graph node ERROR facts, WorkItem lifecycle failures, proposal admission/application, repair triggers, promotion approval, provider/runner execution, or generated truth facts by default. If a host wants repair, review, or audit follow-up, it must route bounded log/error refs through an explicit host-owned proposal/admission/audit path. Raw or over-cap logs and stacks may be retained only in host-owned artifact/log stores and referenced from Canvas by redacted summaries and refs; missing, malformed, restricted, stale, or unverifiable log/error material fails closed as visible diagnostic status rather than falling back to raw display.
rationale: D504 permits bounded log displays and bounded component error displays while keeping iframe/postMessage/runtime capture host-private. D509 keeps raw source, source maps, scanner raw logs, and artifact material out of Canvas DTOs. D362 already establishes the broader runtime text pattern: raw stdout/stderr, stacks, provider responses, large diffs, and sensitive material use summary/ref artifacts with size/redaction evidence, while runtime-thrown messages are normalized. This decision applies that pattern to sandboxed UI so Workbench can support debugging without becoming a console collector, source-map expander, redaction engine, runtime owner, or graph error projector. Treating component failures as sandbox status preserves graph truth and avoids accidental repair, proposal, promotion, or execution side effects from display diagnostics.

layer: L6 / C-1 cross-runtime WireEdgeGroup facade and conformance split
question: How should Python join C-1 WireEdgeGroup publicly, and how should TS/Rust/Python expose and verify the C-1 surface without leaking raw bridge/protocol internals?
decision: C-1 uses public high-level WireEdgeGroup facades in all participating runtimes. TypeScript and Rust should expose their existing high-level wireEdgeGroup/wire_edge_group functions and WireEdgeGroup bundle/status/issue/edge option types as public adapter surfaces, while keeping them byte-valued, single-direction per D506, graph-visible through declared event/gate/projector lanes, and free of raw remote Node/Ctx/function/live-topology payloads. Python may add an idiomatic public wire_edge_group facade, but only as a wrapper over Rust/native-owned bridge and WireEdgeGroup semantics: edge values are bytes, declarations are inbound-only or outbound-only, returned material is a Python facade bundle with inbound edge nodes plus status/issues/release wrappers, and release follows the native source/topology release discipline. Python must not duplicate the wave core, construct protocol messages directly, expose raw WireBridge/WireEdgeFrame DTO construction as public API, expose PyO3 handles, expose raw Node.up/down or ctx.up/down, add Python-only protocol aliases, add a production value codec registry, or widen storage/checkpoint hydration. C-1 conformance should split before any honest pass flip: protobuf canonical byte helpers, WireEdgeGroup single-direction behavior, and explicit ack-timeout command ingress should be separate focused scenarios or arms so runtimes can pass only the behavior they actually expose and test. A public Rust/TS ack-driver helper remains optional ergonomics; conformance should require explicit graph-visible ack-timeout ingress, not a hidden timer pump or a helper name. Tombstone retention remains bounded recent-memory behavior from D506 and its numeric limit is not public conformance surface.
rationale: D498-D506 lock byte-valued bridge helpers, static one-cause WireEdgeGroup behavior, graph-visible timeout ingress, single-direction edge groups, and bounded recent replay guards. Once Python is allowed to expose WireEdgeGroup, the cross-runtime rule must become facade parity rather than raw structure parity: users get the same high-level behavior, but each runtime keeps its idiomatic wrapper and native ownership boundary. TS and Rust already expose high-level facades; Python should join at that level rather than reopening the raw native validation gate into a broad bridge protocol API. Splitting C-1 conformance prevents protobuf validation, WireEdgeGroup behavior, and ack timeout ingress from being collapsed into one all-or-nothing scenario, which would either overstate Python coverage or block honest TS/Rust progress.

layer: L6 / Python C-1 bridge and WireEdgeGroup facade exact shape
question: What exact Python public facade should expose C-1 wireBridge and WireEdgeGroup behavior without raw protocol/native leakage?
decision: Python adds high-level public wire_bridge(...) and wire_edge_group(...) facades over Rust/native-owned bridge semantics. wire_bridge(graph, *, session_id, name=None) returns an opaque Python WireBridge facade bundle sufficient for WireEdgeGroup composition and graph-visible status/issues/release, but does not expose raw WireBridgeEnvelope, WireBridgeCommand, WireEdgeFrame construction, PyO3 handles, or raw protocol ingress. wire_edge_group(graph, bridge, *, name=None, inbound_edges=None, outbound_edges=None) requires exactly one of inbound_edges or outbound_edges; inbound_edges is a non-empty iterable of edge ids, outbound_edges is a non-empty mapping of edge id to bytes-valued Node. It returns a Python WireEdgeGroup bundle with inbound edge nodes, status, issues, and idempotent release(). Status/issues are Python facade dataclasses/enums mapped from native facts. Outbound non-bytes values, malformed remote frames, unknown edges, duplicate frames, competing causes, incomplete causes, and replay-window violations become graph-visible issue/status facts rather than local protocol terminals. The facade must not duplicate the Python wave core, expose raw Node.up/down or ctx.up/down, add Python-only protocol aliases, add a value codec registry, or widen storage/checkpoint hydration.
rationale: D511 permits Python to join C-1 only at the high-level facade layer, while D498-D506 forbid raw wire/protocol expansion and preserve byte-valued, single-direction WireEdgeGroup semantics. A keyword-only opaque facade gives Python users the same behavior as TS/Rust without inheriting TS/Rust structural details, and making inbound_edges/outbound_edges mutually exclusive encodes D506 directly in the API. Mapping native facts into Python dataclasses/enums keeps the surface idiomatic while preserving graph-visible fail-closed behavior and native ownership of bridge/topology release.

layer: L6 / Canvas sandbox network and storage permission boundary
question: How should Canvas represent sandboxed generated or pasted UI network and storage permissions without granting access by manifest, passing handles, or making Workbench a permission enforcer?
decision: Untrusted generated, pasted, or marketplace sandbox UI has no network access, persistent storage, credential access, host storage API, cookie access, or direct browser storage authority by default. Canvas may define data-only sandbox permission posture views, permission request intents, admission status views, allowed-capability summaries, quota summaries, redacted origin summaries, and blocked/denied reason material. Workbench may display permission posture and emit user or component permission request intents, but it must not enforce permissions, grant permissions, mutate sandbox policy, write allowlists, broker credentials, create storage namespaces, pass network/storage handles, or treat component-declared manifests as executable authority. Host-private sandbox/runtime infrastructure owns origin policy, CSP, iframe sandbox flags, network proxying, URL/origin allowlists, storage namespace allocation, quota, cookie isolation, credential mediation, permission admission, enforcement, revocation, and audit persistence. Canvas permission DTOs must not carry raw URL allowlists, credential material, cookies, tokens, connection strings, env vars, storage handles, IndexedDB/localStorage/sessionStorage handles, filesystem paths, clients, provider/query/storage handles, runtime handles, iframe/window references, permission objects, opaque cursors, or callback maps. Component manifests or source intake records may request or summarize desired capabilities, but access becomes effective only after host-owned admission and host-owned enforcement; summaries are display material, not permission proof. Sandbox messages and event payloads cannot override permissions or smuggle origin/storage policy. Missing, denied, unsupported, stale, revoked, over-quota, unauthorized, malformed, or unverifiable permission material fails closed as visible status/issues/audit refs and must not fall back to direct network, direct storage, host preview, graph truth mutation, proposal admission/application, WorkItem mutation, provider/runner execution, or generated truth facts.
rationale: D504 keeps actual iframe/postMessage/origin/CSP/permission enforcement host-private and allows Canvas only to name/display sandbox lifecycle material. D503 allows sandbox policy posture as typed settings/display material without making settings an enforcement owner. D509 keeps source refs/fingerprints as evidence only, and D510 keeps raw runtime capture host-private. This decision closes the network/storage gap: useful future widgets can request capabilities, but Canvas remains a data-only posture and intent surface rather than a permission engine, credential broker, network proxy, or storage allocator. Default-deny untrusted UI preserves the browser workbench boundary while leaving a reviewed host-admitted path for later marketplace/data widgets.

layer: L6 / Canvas sandbox session lifecycle and teardown boundary
question: How should Canvas represent sandbox session lifecycle, restart, teardown, crash, and stale-message handling without owning iframe runtimes, session maps, timers, or automatic repair/promotion behavior?
decision: Canvas may define data-only sandbox session descriptors, lifecycle status views, lifecycle diagnostics, restart/suspend/teardown request intents, stale-message summaries, crash summaries, audit refs, and evidence refs. Workbench may display sandbox lifecycle state and emit data-only lifecycle request intents, but it must not own the sandbox session map, create or dispose iframes/workers, hold iframe/window/MessagePort/timer/heartbeat handles, send runtime teardown commands directly, restart runtimes directly, retry crashes, or subscribe to post-teardown events. Host-private sandbox/runtime infrastructure owns sandboxSessionId allocation, generation fencing, iframe/worker/window/MessagePort handles, heartbeat and timeout policy, resource cleanup, actual start/suspend/restart/teardown, crash handling, stale message rejection, runtime maps, and retention of private lifecycle evidence. Canvas session refs are display/correlation material only, not runtime handles or permission to address a running iframe. Lifecycle DTOs may carry bounded fields such as sandboxSessionRef, componentId, sourceKind, generation, lifecycle state, reason, staleMessageCount, issue summaries, policy refs, evidence refs, and audit refs, but must not carry runtime handles, ports, window references, callbacks, timers, origin/CSP enforcement objects, permission objects, clients, credentials, storage/query/provider handles, opaque cursors, raw logs, raw errors, or raw source material. Host validation must treat sandbox messages as valid only when their session ref and generation match an active admitted session; old-generation messages, unknown sessions, post-teardown messages, post-crash messages, revoked sessions, or stale lifecycle material fail closed as diagnostics/status and must not lower into component events, proposal intake, repair actions, promotion decisions, graph truth, WorkItem mutation, provider/runner execution, or generated truth facts. Crash/restart/teardown status is lifecycle display material by default; if a host wants repair, audit, review, or retry orchestration, it must route bounded lifecycle refs through an explicit host-owned proposal/admission/audit path outside Workbench.
rationale: D504 keeps iframe/postMessage/runtime/teardown authority host-private while allowing Canvas to display sandbox lifecycle material. D510 keeps crash/error/log capture host-owned and bounded before display, and D512 keeps permission enforcement host-owned. The remaining runtime risk is lifecycle drift: once real sandbox sessions exist, session ids, stale messages, restart buttons, and teardown failures can easily become hidden runtime authority in Workbench. This decision preserves the useful observable shape while forcing all actual session maps, generation fences, handles, timers, cleanup, and retry policy into the host runtime. Treating lifecycle failures as status rather than graph/proposal semantics prevents accidental repair, promotion rollback, or execution side effects from sandbox crashes.

layer: L6 / Canvas sandbox message protocol and event-port bridge boundary
question: How should Canvas represent sandbox postMessage payloads and event-port bridging without letting iframe payloads own routing, callbacks, permissions, or Workspace mutation?
decision: Canvas may define data-only sandbox message envelope views, event-port bridge previews, validation diagnostics, and typed event-envelope preview material that connects host-normalized sandbox messages to the existing D417/D426 component event envelope and lowering preview path. Workbench may display message validation and bridge status, but it must not listen to iframe messages, parse raw postMessage payloads, mutate routing, dispatch actions, call callbacks, or own message transport. Host-private sandbox/runtime infrastructure owns raw postMessage listeners, origin checks, MessagePort handles, session and generation validation, raw payload capture, transport ordering, and any private runtime correlation. A sandbox message may enter Canvas only after host normalization and session/generation validation, and only as clone-safe data containing bounded correlation such as sandboxSessionRef, generation, componentId, event name, source kind, validation status, diagnostics, and optional payload material. Declared event ports remain the only routing authority: payload material may supply bounded draft/data content only after clone/data/schema validation, and it must not override actionId, loweringKind, targetRefs, policyRefs, actorRefs, rendererRef, componentId, contractId, sandboxSessionRef, generation, permission posture, lifecycle state, or host admission context. Unknown events, non-ready event ports, malformed or uncloneable payloads, unauthorized messages, stale sessions, old generations, post-teardown messages, revoked sessions, and unsupported message kinds fail closed as data-only diagnostics/status material. They must not lower into typed renderer events, proposal intake, SidePanelActionIntent dispatch, repair actions, promotion decisions, graph truth, WorkItem mutation, provider/runner execution, permission changes, or generated truth facts. This bridge is preview/validation material only; actual postMessage transport and runtime lifecycle remain host-private.
rationale: D417 locks component events as typed data-only intents, D426 locks event ports as routing authority and forbids payload-owned routing/callbacks/runtime handles, D504 keeps iframe/postMessage runtime host-private, D512 forbids payload-level permission overrides, and D513 requires session/generation validation before messages can be considered current. This decision closes the message bridge gap by allowing Canvas to validate and display host-normalized sandbox messages while preserving the existing typed event envelope and lowering path. It prevents untrusted iframe payloads from becoming a command bus, permission channel, router override, Workspace mutation path, or callback surface.

layer: L6 / Canvas sandbox and component focused public surface boundary
question: Where should Canvas expose sandbox/component source, promotion, permission, lifecycle, log/error, and message bridge DTOs without growing the root package API or leaking host-private runtime/registry authority?
decision: Canvas sandbox and component-admission public API remains focused-subpath-only and data-only. The package root must not grow with sandbox runtime, lifecycle, permission, source intake, promotion, log/error, message bridge, registry, or generated-component admission symbols. Focused subpaths such as the existing workspace-component-renderer surface may expose only data-only DTOs, builders, validators, preview helpers, status helpers, and manifest/descriptor summary helpers for generated, pasted, marketplace, sandboxed, and host-registered components. If the sandbox/admission surface outgrows the renderer-focused boundary, Canvas may add a separately reviewed focused workspace-component-sandbox subpath, but it must preserve the same data-only and no-runtime-authority constraints. Workbench UI components, host registries, runtime drivers, iframe/window/worker/postMessage/MessagePort transports, React component maps, executable renderer maps, host adapters, source stores, package installers, permission enforcers, credential brokers, network/storage brokers, runner/provider clients, callbacks, raw source/log/error captures, filesystem paths, opaque cursors, and runtime handles remain private/internal and must not be exported from the root or focused public subpaths. Focused public helpers may describe already-derived material and validate bounded DTO shapes, but they must not allocate sessions, install renderers, load source, execute code, mutate registries, enforce permissions, persist settings, dispatch actions, lower events, write graph truth, mutate WorkItems, or become generic selector/provider/registry APIs. Export cleanliness is part of the contract: root export tests and subpath tests should assert that public surfaces remain descriptor/DTO-oriented and free of host-private runtime authority.
rationale: D503 keeps settings public surface focused and data-only; D504, D508, D509, D510, D512, D513, and D514 split sandbox execution, promotion, source intake, log/error capture, permissions, lifecycle, and message bridge authority away from Workbench and into host-private runtime/admission paths. Without an explicit export boundary, these many adjacent DTOs could casually accrete into the package root and become a broad implicit sandbox runtime API. Focused subpaths let hosts import the data vocabulary they need while preserving root API stability, avoiding callback/registry/provider drift, and keeping experimental or runtime-adjacent material away from the main Canvas public contract. Requiring pure DTO/helper exports keeps implementation freedom for the host runtime and gives future tests a concrete line to defend.

layer: L6 / Canvas cross-capability status, audit, and approval display boundary
question: How should Canvas display approval, audit, blocked, denied, retryable, and host-waiting state across runner, credentials, sandbox, promotion, permission, lifecycle, source review, and log/error follow-up without becoming a workflow engine or audit authority?
decision: Canvas may define a focused data-only cross-capability status, audit, and approval display vocabulary for Workbench surfaces. The vocabulary may normalize host-derived status summaries, approval posture, audit refs, evidence refs, issue summaries, blocked/denied/retryable reasons, last host decision summaries, and next-intent affordances across runner commands, credential setup, sandbox permission requests, component promotion review, component source review, sandbox lifecycle restart/suspend/teardown, sandbox log/error follow-up, and other reviewed Canvas host-capability surfaces. Workbench may display this already-derived material and may emit data-only user intents that name the requested follow-up, actor refs, policy refs, target refs, evidence refs, idempotency material, and audit context, but it must not own approval lifecycle state, write audit records, mutate policy, grant permissions, validate credentials, execute retries, run commands, advance sandbox lifecycle, install or promote components, admit or apply proposals, lower component events, write graph truth, mutate WorkItems, or become the source of capability truth. The shared display vocabulary is not a generic workflow registry, state-machine engine, approval engine, policy engine, action dispatcher, or provider/runtime adapter. Status values are display/correlation material only; effective state remains host/project/runner/sandbox/admission owned according to the governing capability boundary. Missing, stale, contradictory, unauthorized, unsupported, or unverifiable status/audit/approval material fails closed as visible diagnostics and disabled/blocked affordances, never as implicit approval, retry, permission grant, lifecycle transition, proposal admission/application, graph mutation, WorkItem mutation, provider execution, runner execution, or generated truth facts.
rationale: D503, D505, D508, D509, D510, D512, D513, D514, and D515 repeatedly allow Canvas to show capability posture and emit data-only intents while keeping execution, permission, lifecycle, promotion, source, runtime capture, public surface, approval, and audit authority host-private or caller-owned. The remaining product risk is duplication and drift: every capability could invent its own approval/status shape and accidentally grow a hidden workflow engine inside Workbench. A small shared display vocabulary gives the UI consistent badges, panels, disabled reasons, and next-action affordances while preserving the authority split. By requiring host-derived material and data-only intents, this decision keeps status understandable without turning Workbench into an approval lifecycle owner, audit writer, policy mutator, retry executor, or cross-capability command bus.

layer: L6 / C-1 conformance scenario split
question: How should C-1 conformance split after protobuf, WireEdgeGroup, and explicit ack-timeout ingress became separate adapter capabilities?
decision: C-1 remains the required umbrella end-to-end cross-graph diamond coalesce scenario and must not be marked pass until the full mixed-locality diamond is implemented and tested through the bridge. Add focused scenarios before any honest pass flip: C-1a covers canonical protobuf bridge envelope and wire-edge frame bytes/golden vectors; C-1b covers public high-level single-direction WireEdgeGroup behavior, including bytes-only edges, DIRTY-before-DATA gating, fail-closed issues/status, describe-visible event/gate/projector topology, release, and bounded recent replay guard without making the numeric tombstone limit public; C-1c covers explicit graph-visible ack-timeout command ingress, stale/malformed no-op or issue behavior, retry/exhausted facts, and absence of hidden core timer pumps. Runtime arms may pass each focused scenario only when that runtime exposes and tests the corresponding behavior. Public ack-driver helper names are not conformance requirements; explicit ingress behavior is. Python C-1b remains todo until the D516 public facade lands.
rationale: D497, D501, D502, D506, D511, and D516 split the C-1 implementation surface into byte validation, WireEdgeGroup behavior, and timeout ingress. Keeping one all-or-nothing C-1 record would either overstate Python coverage or hide TS/Rust completed adapter behavior. Focused scenarios let conformance track behavior honestly while preserving the original C-1 diamond as the final mixed-locality proof.

layer: L6 / Canvas Workbench intent handoff and idempotency boundary
question: How should Workbench hand user intents to a host across settings, runner, credential, sandbox, promotion, lifecycle, status, and action affordances without becoming an outbox, callback bus, dispatcher, workflow owner, or runtime executor?
decision: Canvas Workbench intent handoff is data-only, typed, caller-owned, and idempotency-aware. Workbench may construct, display, and surface bounded user intent DTOs for reviewed Canvas affordances such as setting changes, runner commands, credential setup, sandbox permission requests, component promotion review, component source review, sandbox lifecycle requests, sandbox log/error follow-up, UI navigation, and cross-capability status follow-up. Each intent should name an explicit intent kind, target refs, actor refs, policy refs, evidence or audit refs when applicable, caller-supplied intent id or idempotency key, and bounded data parameters. Workbench must not own a durable outbox, retry queue, callback registry, action dispatcher, command bus, admission lifecycle, approval lifecycle, audit writer, persistence owner, workflow state machine, transport channel, or runtime executor. Hosts or callers own receiving intents, validating and deduplicating idempotency material, admitting or rejecting, persisting, auditing, executing, retrying, cancelling, and reporting host-derived status back to Canvas display DTOs. Intent DTOs must not carry callbacks, promises, raw shell, raw paths, secrets, credentials, tokens, env vars, clients, provider/query/storage/runner handles, iframe/window/MessagePort handles, runtime handles, registry objects, executable component maps, opaque cursors, raw source, raw logs, raw errors, or permission objects. Duplicate, stale, malformed, unauthorized, unsupported, missing-idempotency, or unverifiable intents fail closed as host-derived status/diagnostics and must not imply approval, retry, permission grant, lifecycle transition, proposal admission/application, graph truth mutation, WorkItem mutation, provider execution, runner execution, component promotion, or generated truth facts.
rationale: D503, D505, D507, D508, D509, D510, D512, D513, D514, D515, and D517 repeatedly allow Workbench to emit data-only intents while keeping settings persistence, execution, credentials, permissions, sandbox lifecycle, promotion, source handling, runtime capture, public surfaces, approval, audit, and status authority outside Workbench. The shared remaining risk is the handoff itself: without an explicit rule, intent emission can become a hidden callback bus, outbox, retry engine, or cross-capability dispatcher. This decision gives every Workbench affordance the same narrow shape: bounded typed intent out, host-owned admission/execution/audit/status back. Idempotency material makes host dedupe and replay handling possible without making Workbench the owner of retries or persistence.

layer: L6 / Canvas fixture and test material extension boundary
question: How should Canvas provide reusable test, fixture, snapshot, mockup, and dashboard example material that other sandbox, runner, Docker, CI, or code-definition extensions can use without making Canvas own execution or leaking runtime-private material?
decision: Canvas fixtures, tests, snapshots, mockups, dashboard examples, and optional fixture packs are reusable data material, not execution plugins. Canvas may publish or consume bounded redacted fixture material, DTO examples, expected diagnostics, expected status/audit/approval views, event-envelope examples, sandbox posture examples, runner/credential posture examples, source/promotion evidence examples, redaction/truncation evidence, and pure validators/builders for those shapes. External hosts, runners, sandbox extensions, Docker/CI harnesses, Playwright suites, local test tools, or code-definition test systems may consume that material and execute tests however they choose, but execution remains outside Canvas. Canvas must not own the test runner, sandbox/container/VM lifecycle, code-definition runner, dependency installer, filesystem/network permission enforcement, credential lookup, source hydration, runtime message transport, result persistence, artifact store, retry policy, or test admission workflow. Runnable work enters Canvas only as typed runner/sandbox/source/promotion/status intents under the governing handoff boundaries, and results return only as host-derived redacted status, diagnostics, evidence refs, artifact refs, and bounded display DTOs. Fixture material and snapshots must not contain raw secrets, tokens, passwords, env vars, connection strings, raw shell, raw filesystem paths, real local/user paths, raw component source bodies, executable modules as authority, package archives, raw logs, full stack traces, source-map-expanded frames, raw Error objects, clients, provider/query/storage/runner handles, iframe/window/MessagePort handles, runtime handles, callbacks, registry objects, opaque cursors, permission objects, or credential material. Snapshot tests should defend public DTO boundaries and redaction/truncation evidence rather than canonize host-private runtime fields. A fixture pack may be a data pack with examples and validators, but it is not a registry, callback hook, executable extension, test harness, sandbox adapter, or provider/runtime plugin.
rationale: D505, D509, D510, D512, D513, D514, D515, D517, and D519 keep runner execution, credentials, source intake, raw logs/errors, permissions, sandbox lifecycle, message transport, public surfaces, status/approval, and intent handoff outside Workbench authority while still allowing data-only DTOs and evidence refs. The product needs realistic reusable examples so hosts and third-party extensions can test Canvas integrations, but Canvas should not become a testing platform, Docker runner, sandbox orchestrator, code-definition executor, or fixture plugin registry. Treating fixtures as redacted data packs gives users maximum freedom to run tests in their preferred environment while keeping Canvas good at what it owns: stable DTO contracts, preview material, evidence shapes, redaction boundaries, and display semantics.

layer: L6 / Python C-1 private native binding boundary
question: How should PyO3 carry the Python C-1 bridge and WireEdgeGroup facade without making private native handles part of the public API?
decision: Python C-1 implementation uses private PyO3 foundation classes/functions for wireBridge and WireEdgeGroup, wrapped by public Python facade objects. Native private classes may own Rust wireBridge/WireEdgeGroup bundles, graph-local command-source attachment, native release, and status/issue node handles, but they must remain implementation details outside graphrefly.__all__ and outside documented public API. Public Python facade objects expose only the D516 high-level wire_bridge and wire_edge_group shape, Python Node facade instances, frozen dataclass/enum status and issue values, and idempotent release(). Native classes stay unsendable and graph-owned, matching the existing Python binding single-thread graph-domain pattern. The implementation must not expose raw Core handles, PyO3 object handles, raw WireBridgeEnvelope/WireBridgeCommand/WireEdgeFrame construction, raw protocol ingress/down/up methods, bridge command mutation methods, Python-only protocol aliases, or a Python wave-core reimplementation. Native methods may provide only the minimum private hooks needed for facade construction, subscription/status mapping, release, and tests that assert no public raw leakage.
rationale: D415 assigns Rust ownership of the synchronous native graph engine and Python ownership of the idiomatic public API. D511 and D516 allow Python to join C-1 only through high-level native-owned facades, while D498-D506 forbid raw wire/protocol expansion and Python wave-core duplication. A private PyO3 bundle layer lets the implementation reuse Rust bridge semantics and release discipline without exposing raw handles to users. Keeping public Python objects as wrappers preserves Python typing and lifecycle ergonomics, keeps conformance behavior-oriented, and gives tests a concrete line: _native may contain private machinery, but graphrefly.__all__ and documented facades must remain high-level and raw-protocol-free.

layer: L6 / Canvas extension capability descriptor boundary
question: How should Canvas display external sandbox, runner, fixture-pack, Docker/CI, Playwright, code-definition test, credential, review, and promotion capabilities without becoming a plugin registry, extension marketplace, permission engine, or execution owner?
decision: Canvas may define data-only extension capability descriptors for host-derived capabilities such as sandbox runners, Docker or CI harnesses, Playwright suites, code-definition test systems, fixture packs, credential providers, component reviewers, source scanners, and promotion pipelines. Descriptors may include display labels, capability kind, supported typed intent kinds, supported artifact/evidence kinds, compatibility summaries, version summaries, permission posture summaries, status/audit refs, disabled or blocked reasons, and redacted host posture. Workbench may display these descriptors, use them to enable or disable bounded affordances, and emit D519 typed intents that name the selected capability or capability kind, but it must not install, discover, load, invoke, configure, permission, version-manage, update, uninstall, retain handles to, or execute extensions. Hosts own extension discovery, installation, configuration, permissioning, version compatibility, lifecycle, execution, audit, result reporting, and any mapping from Canvas intent to concrete extension implementation. Capability descriptors are not plugin registry entries, executable modules, callback hooks, provider adapters, command refs, permission grants, credential refs, runtime handles, package manifests as authority, or marketplace records. Descriptor claims are display and routing hints only; effective access and execution require host-owned admission under the governing runner, sandbox, credential, promotion, source, status, and intent boundaries. Missing, stale, incompatible, unauthorized, unsupported, unverifiable, or disabled descriptors fail closed as visible status/diagnostics and disabled affordances, not fallback execution, automatic install, permission grant, graph truth mutation, WorkItem mutation, proposal admission/application, provider execution, runner execution, component promotion, or generated truth facts.
rationale: D503, D505, D508, D509, D512, D515, D517, D519, and D520 allow Canvas to show capability posture and emit typed intents while keeping settings, execution, credentials, permissions, source handling, promotion, public surfaces, status/approval, intent handoff, fixtures, and test execution host-owned. Once external runners, sandbox extensions, fixture packs, and code-definition test systems are allowed to consume Canvas material, the UI needs a way to show what a host says is available. A data-only descriptor gives users visibility and lets Workbench shape affordances without turning Canvas into a plugin platform. Keeping discovery, installation, versioning, permissioning, and execution outside Canvas preserves user freedom to bring any host/extension stack while avoiding a generic registry/provider/callback surface that Canvas is not meant to own.

layer: L6 / Python C-1 protobuf byte transport facade
question: How should Python expose canonical protobuf byte ingress/egress for C-1 without exposing raw wire DTO construction or a value codec registry?
decision: Python may add a public high-level wire_bridge_protobuf(graph, bridge, *, name=None) facade over Rust/native-owned canonical protobuf bridge helpers. The facade returns inbound_bytes, outbound_bytes, status, issues, and release material. inbound_bytes accepts only bytes through ordinary Python Node facade ingress; outbound_bytes emits canonical protobuf bytes for host transport subscribers. Malformed inbound bytes, outbound encode failures, non-bytes ingress, and canonical validation failures become graph-visible protobuf issue/status facts, not local protocol terminals. The facade must not expose public CanonicalWireBridgeEnvelope, CanonicalWireEdgeFrame, WireBridgeEnvelope, WireBridgeCommand, or field-level protobuf builders; must not add a production value codec registry; and must not make strict JSON fixture bytes a production value encoding contract. Native implementation details may remain private under D521, while public Python users see only byte nodes, status/issues dataclasses/enums, and release().
rationale: D497 defines canonical protobuf bytes and golden vectors, D498 keeps Python first on private/native validation, D511/D516 allow Python high-level C-1 facades but forbid raw wire/protocol leakage, and D518 splits C-1a as a protobuf byte scenario. A bytes-only facade gives Python a real transport boundary and honest C-1a coverage while preserving the raw DTO prohibition. It mirrors the existing TypeScript wireBridgeProtobuf shape at the behavior level without forcing structural API parity or creating a production value codec registry.

layer: L6 / Python C-1 ack-timeout driver facade
question: How should Python expose C-1 explicit ack-timeout ingress without exposing raw bridge commands or adding hidden timers?
decision: Python may add a public high-level wire_bridge_ack_driver(graph, bridge, *, clock, timeout_ms, name=None) facade over Rust/native-owned bridge semantics. The helper consumes graph-visible monotonic clock facts and the opaque Python WireBridge facade, derives ack-timeout facts for pending bridge attempts, and returns timeouts, status, issues, and release material. timeouts is a Python facade Node of WireBridgeAckTimeout dataclass facts for inspection, not a raw WireBridgeCommand node or command constructor. Native-private implementation may attach the derived timeout facts to the bridge's private ack-timeout command ingress and detach them on release. Invalid timeout_ms is a construction error; invalid or regressing clock facts become graph-visible driver issues/status. Stale or mismatched timeout facts remain bridge-owned fail-closed no-ops, and malformed ingress remains issue/status, not a protocol terminal. The facade must not expose raw WireBridgeCommand, generic command sources, imperative bridge.ack_timeout methods, PyO3 handles, raw protocol DTO construction, timers, sleeps, hidden retry pumps, missed/catch-up policies, or Python wave-core duplication.
rationale: D502 and D518 require explicit graph-visible ack-timeout ingress and absence of hidden timer pumps, while D516 and D521 forbid Python raw protocol/native leakage. A reactive ack driver keeps timeout derivation inspectable and composable, lets hosts decide how clock facts enter the graph, and preserves bridge ownership of retry/exhausted/status behavior. layer: L6 / Python C-1 facade release and lifetime semantics
question: How should Python C-1 bridge facade bundles release native graph resources without leaking retained sources, crossing graph lifetimes, or adding hidden cleanup behavior?

Construction requires all graph, bridge, clock, and edge Node inputs to belong to the same Python Graph lifetime and owner thread. Calling release() from a non-owner thread raises GraphReflyRuntimeError. Graph.close() releases any still-live C-1 bundles in reverse creation/attachment order. Releasing a child bundle detaches only that bundle's native command or inbound sources and releases its owned topology/nodes; it must not release the parent bridge or sibling bundles. Releasing a bridge facade cascades release to its still-live child bundles before releasing bridge-owned native topology/resources, and child release after bridge release is a no-op. Constructing new child facades from a released bridge or closed graph raises GraphReflyRuntimeError. Release is lifecycle cleanup only: it must not emit protocol TEARDOWN/COMPLETE/ERROR, synthesize graph truth, publish raw native handles, or mutate unrelated graph resources. Native detach must happen before releasing owned topology; if release fails, the facade must not be marked released and any detached source attachment must be restored when possible. No __del__, weakref finalizer, hidden timer, background cleanup task, raw PyO3 handle, command-source method, or Python wave-core hook may own release semantics.
rationale: D516, D521, D523, D524, and D526 expose Python C-1 bridge behavior through high-level native-owned facades while forbidding raw native/protocol leakage. Existing Python graph objects already enforce owner-thread and graph-lifetime discipline, while TS/Rust bridge helpers rely on explicit idempotent release and source-detach-before-topology-release behavior. Registering C-1 bundles with the graph lifetime prevents retained-source leaks on Graph.close(); child-only release preserves composability; bridge cascade gives users one safe parent cleanup path without making release a protocol event or hidden scheduler. Rejecting finalizer-driven cleanup keeps graph mutation explicit and owner-thread-bound.
